0.title: How to Behave in the Household of God
0.overview:
First Timothy is a letter from a seasoned apostle to a young pastor — and it is as practical and urgent as anything Paul ever wrote. Timothy had been left in Ephesus to deal with a crisis: false teachers were infecting the church with 'different doctrine,' with myths and endless genealogies, with a distorted use of the law and a spiritualised asceticism that forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul's letter is his pastoral briefing for a young man who has been given a very hard assignment in a very important city.

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia — a commercial and religious metropolis, home to the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. It was a city Paul knew intimately: he had spent nearly three years there on his third missionary journey (Acts 19–20), and the church he planted was one of the most strategic in the Roman East. Now, years later, that church was in danger. The false teachers were not outsiders; they had come from within — perhaps former elders or teachers who had 'made shipwreck of their faith' (1:19–20). Timothy's task was to confront them, silence them, and restore the church to sound doctrine and ordered life.

The letter's great themes weave together seamlessly. There is the primacy of sound doctrine — 'the glorious gospel of the blessed God' (1:11) — against which every false teaching must be measured. There is the ordering of the church: prayer, worship, the qualifications of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, the honour due to elders. There is the call to godliness — a word that appears more often in 1 Timothy than in any other New Testament letter — the practical Christlikeness that is the goal of all authentic teaching. And there are the five 'trustworthy sayings' (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Tit 3:8) — compact theological summaries that sound like early confessions of faith, already familiar in the church before Paul wrote them down.

Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters? Many scholars think a later follower wrote them in his name, arguing that their vocabulary and style differ from Paul’s other letters, that their church order with elders and deacons looks later, and that their travels cannot be fitted into Acts. But each letter names Paul as author, they were received as his by the early church, and the church order they describe is simple: plural elders and deacons, which Paul appointed from his first journey (Acts 14:23; Phil 1:1). Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to trusted co-workers on new subjects. And the travels fit if Paul was released from the imprisonment with which Acts ends, as the early church believed, and then travelled again, to Macedonia (1:3), Crete (Titus 1:5) and elsewhere, before a final arrest. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote them, in the mid-60s.

And what was Timothy’s role? Not a bishop of Ephesus in the later sense, but Paul’s delegate, sent with apostolic authority for a time, Until I come (4:13), to correct false teaching and see that qualified elders led the church (3:1–7; 5:17–22).

Above all, this is a letter about the church as 'the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth' (3:15). The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is the family of the living God, called to hold up the truth in a world drowning in falsehood. That is what gives urgency to every instruction about doctrine and order and godliness: the stakes are not institutional but cosmic. The household of God must be governed well — because the God who indwells it is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords (6:15).

1.title: The Glorious Gospel and the Worst of Sinners
1.overview:
Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain men teaching a different doctrine: myths, genealogies and confident talk about the law that produced endless speculation instead of love. The law is good, Paul says, when used for its purpose: to convict sinners, measured by the gospel of God’s glory.

Then Paul turns to himself as the proof of that gospel. He had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man, and Christ showed him mercy. “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” If Christ’s patience reached him, it can reach anyone, and the thought breaks into praise. The chapter ends with a charge to Timothy to fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience, unlike two men who wrecked their faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul writes as an apostle appointed by God our Saviour and by Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, whom he calls his true son in the faith, wishing him grace, mercy and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Our Saviour, and Mercy Added

The Pastorals call the Father ‘Saviour’ — salvation was his design, as the Son accomplished it — and only the letters to Timothy add ‘mercy’ to grace and peace: compassion for a struggling minister.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young, unwarlike Timothy (4:12; 2 Tim 1:7) needed the apostolic commission standing behind him.

Now: ‘Christ Jesus our hope’ tells anyone in a hard post where to look when the situation offers nothing to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 1 sets out why the letter was written and what is at stake. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to silence men teaching a different doctrine, myths, genealogies and a misuse of the law, which bred arguments instead of love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith (vv. 3–7). The law is good when used lawfully, to expose and restrain sin, and its list of sins tracks the Ten Commandments (vv. 8–11). Then Paul offers his own story as the proof of the gospel he guards: a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man shown mercy, because Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom he is the foremost; and the memory bursts into praise of the King of the ages (vv. 12–17). He closes by charging Timothy to fight the good fight, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, who made shipwreck of their faith and have been put out of the church (vv. 18–20). A chapter about false teachers turns out to be a chapter about mercy, because the only safe guardian of the gospel is a man who knows he needed it more than anyone.

The setting. 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters, because they are written to Paul’s co-workers about leading churches. After his first Roman imprisonment (Acts 28), Paul seems to have been released and to have travelled again, around AD 62–64, leaving Timothy in Ephesus and Titus in Crete. Timothy, son of a Jewish believing mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5), had served alongside Paul for some fifteen years, and was still relatively young (4:12), perhaps timid (2 Timothy 1:7), and often unwell (5:23). Ephesus, where Paul had spent three years (Acts 19; 20:31), was now troubled by exactly the false teachers he had warned its elders about at Miletus: from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things (Acts 20:29–30). The wolves had come, and some of them were wearing the elders’ clothes.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus. An apostle (apostolos) is one sent with authority, carrying the word of the one who sent him. The letter is personal, a father writing to a son, but it is also official. Timothy would read it to the church, and the men he had to correct needed to know that these instructions carried Christ’s authority and not merely an old friend’s opinion.

By command of God our Saviour. The word is epitagē, a royal order, the term for an edict issued by someone with the authority to compel. Paul did not volunteer and was not elected; he was commanded. That matters to a young man, by temperament not a fighter, left in Ephesus with a job he did not choose, facing men who did not want him there. The first thing Paul establishes is that the chain of command runs above them both. Neither of them is in charge of this church. They are both under orders.

God our Saviour. Here Saviour is said of the Father, a title characteristic of these letters (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4), and there is no confusion in it: the Father is Saviour in that salvation was his design and his will before the world began; the Son in that he accomplished it. It also echoes the Old Testament, where the LORD is the Saviour of Israel and there is no other (Psalm 106:21; Isaiah 43:3, 11). And it had an edge in Ephesus. Emperors were hailed as saviours on coins and inscriptions, and Artemis, whose temple dominated the city and was counted one of the wonders of the world, was hailed as saviour too. Paul gives the title to the living God alone, in the opening line of a letter that would be read aloud a short walk from her altar.

And of Christ Jesus our hope. Not our example or our teacher, though he is both: our hope (Colossians 1:27). Christ is not merely the one who gives hope; he is the hope, and the phrase faces forward. Christian hope is not wishful thinking but confident expectation fixed on a person who has risen and will return. Paul is writing to a man in a hard post about a difficulty that will not resolve soon, and before he names a single problem he names the direction to look. The Father and the Son together stand behind his commission, and the one who commands is the same one who is coming back.

To Timothy, my true child in the faith. The word is gnēsios: genuine, legitimately born, the real thing as against a counterfeit. Timothy was Paul’s spiritual son, probably converted through Paul’s first visit to Lystra, where Paul was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:6–20), and he had grown to be genuinely like his father in faith and service: I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare (Philippians 2:20–22). Ephesus was full of men who wanted to be teachers (v. 7) and were not. Timothy is the genuine article, and Paul says so publicly, in a letter he knew would be read aloud. It is a father’s hand on a nervous son’s shoulder in front of the whole room: this man is my legitimate representative; heed him.

Grace, mercy, and peace. A small alteration in the greeting, and a tender one. Paul’s letters to churches say grace and peace; mercy (eleos) is added only in the letters to Timothy. Grace is God’s favour to the undeserving; mercy is his pity on the miserable, his compassion toward the struggling; peace is the wholeness and reconciliation that follow. Whatever else the extra word signals, it is the right word for a tired minister. A man carrying a congregation like this one needs to be told that God’s disposition toward him is not measured by how well he is coping. Mercy is what God gives to people who are not coping, and he gives it first, before the instructions.

From God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. One preposition, “from”, governs both the Father and Christ. They are the single source of grace, mercy and peace, and only God gives these. So without stopping to argue it, Paul places Christ on the side of God and not of creatures. The man who would later be called the foremost of sinners prays to a Saviour who is himself God.

Did Paul really write this letter? Many modern critical scholars doubt that Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters, pointing to differences of vocabulary, church organisation and theology from his earlier letters. But the letters claim Paul as author repeatedly and personally (1:12–16; 2 Timothy 4:9–21); the early church accepted them without question (they are echoed by Polycarp and named as Paul’s by Irenaeus); differences of vocabulary are well explained by different subject matter, a different stage of life, and possibly a different secretary (perhaps Luke, who alone was with him, 2 Timothy 4:11); and a pseudonymous letter with forged personal details, such as the request for a cloak and some parchments, would have been regarded as a deception and rejected. We receive them as Paul’s, and as Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the letter is merely private advice to a friend. It is apostolic instruction for the church, written so that you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God (3:15).

Is this letter for me if I am not a pastor? Yes. It is addressed to Timothy, but it was read to the whole congregation, and most of it concerns them: how they pray (chapter 2), whom they choose as elders and deacons (chapter 3), how they treat widows, older men and younger women (chapter 5), what they do with money (chapter 6). A church member needs to know what sound teaching sounds like, so that he can recognise it and test what he hears; what a faithful elder looks like, so that he can choose one and honour him; and how God wants his household run, because he lives in it. Reading a letter to a minister is also the best way to learn how to pray for one.

How do I find, or become, a spiritual father or mother? Timothy had a mother and grandmother who taught him the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and then Paul. You do not need an apostle. Look in your own church for an older believer whose life you respect, and ask for an hour: to read the Bible together, to talk about how they have walked with Christ, to pray. Most will be surprised and glad. And if you are older, do not wait to be asked. Pick one younger believer, of the same sex where the friendship will be close, and simply begin: invite them to a meal, ask how their soul is, open the Scriptures. Paul did not run a programme. He took a young man with him.

In a sentence. From Paul, sent as an apostle of Christ Jesus by order of God our Saviour and of Christ Jesus, who is our hope, to Timothy, my genuine son in the faith: grace, mercy and peace to you from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord.

On a Tuesday. Thank God by name for someone who has been a spiritual father or mother to you, and if they are still living, tell them so this week, in a few plain sentences. Then think of the hard place you have been left in: the job, the family, the church, the illness you would leave tomorrow if you could. Paul’s opening is addressed to exactly that. You are under orders there, and the one who gave them is your Saviour and your hope, and the first thing he sends you is not a list of tasks but mercy.

For worship. Before a word of correction is written, the King has spoken his welcome. The Father who planned salvation is our Saviour; the Son who accomplished it is our hope; and from both together come grace for the undeserving, mercy for the struggling and peace for the reconciled. In a city that called a goddess of stone its saviour, a few believers heard the true Saviour named, and knew that he had sent them a man, a letter and a promise.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and joined Paul on his second journey. The letter seems to come from after the events of Acts, probably after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, in the early to mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Without his usual thanksgiving, Paul gets straight to the problem. He left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain people teaching a different doctrine and spending their energy on myths and endless genealogies, which breed speculation rather than God’s work, which is by faith. The goal of Paul’s instruction is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. These teachers have wandered into empty talk, wanting to be teachers of the law without understanding it. The law is good when used properly: it is aimed not at the righteous but at lawbreakers of every kind, at whatever contradicts the sound teaching of the gospel entrusted to Paul.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Teaching Is For

The telos of the whole charge is love (v.5) — Paul is not setting doctrine against love but saying what doctrine is for — and the law, good when used lawfully (v.8), convicts sinners and drives them to Christ rather than feeding speculation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul diagnoses the Ephesian teaching by its output — endless speculation rather than God's household well run (v.4).

Now: The vice list of vv.9–10 must be read where Paul put it: five verses before he calls himself the foremost sinner alive.

verseByVerse.quote: As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.

No thanksgiving. In most of his letters Paul begins by giving thanks for his readers; here he goes straight to the problem in the third verse. Galatians is the only other letter that does this, and there the gospel itself was being abandoned. That omission is itself a measure of how serious things were at Ephesus. Paul loves this church, he wept with its elders on a beach (Acts 20:36–38), but a father who sees a fire in the house does not begin with pleasantries.

As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus. The word for urged (parakaleō) means appealed, pleaded, encouraged; remain (prosmeinai) means stay on. Timothy may well have wanted to leave with Paul. Paul had asked him to stay once already and is asking again in writing, which suggests the first request had not settled it, and the New Testament records a young man’s reluctance without embarrassment. This journey to Macedonia is not recorded in Acts, which supports the view that Paul was released after his first imprisonment and travelled again.

So that you may charge certain persons. The word for charge (parangellō) means to command, to give an order with authority, and it is a key word in this letter (1:5, 18; 4:11; 5:7; 6:13, 17). Timothy is not asked to start a discussion with these men. He is to tell them to stop. And note “certain persons” (tisin): Paul knows exactly who they are and does not name them yet, perhaps hoping they will repent before their names are written down for ever. He will name two at the end of the chapter. Some were probably elders of the church itself, just as he had warned (Acts 20:30).

Not to teach any different doctrine. One compound verb, heterodidaskaleō, found in the New Testament only in this letter: to teach other-ly, to teach a different thing. From it comes the idea of heterodoxy. It does not necessarily mean teaching outright falsehood. It means teaching something of a different kind from what was handed down (6:3). The church’s doctrine is not open to endless variation. There is a fixed body of truth, the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3), and a teacher’s job is to deliver it, not to improve it.

Nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies. To devote themselves (prosechō) is to pay attention to, to be absorbed in. Myths (mythoi) are fables, invented stories; genealogies (genealogiai) are lists of ancestry. The precise content is debated. The false teaching seems to have had a Jewish flavour (v. 7; Titus 1:14; 3:9): elaborate speculations built on the Old Testament family trees and legends, like the imaginative expansions found in some later Jewish writings, and possibly early speculation about chains of spiritual beings between God and the world. Paul does not bother to describe it, and that is instructive. He diagnoses teaching by its output, not its content.

Endless. That word (aperantos) is the giveaway: without limit, never reaching a conclusion. Some subjects are designed never to conclude, and their attraction is precisely that. They can be pursued for ever, they make the pursuer feel sophisticated, and they never require him to do anything. A man can spend twenty years on the names in a genealogy and never once be told to forgive his brother.

Which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith. Here is the diagnosis, two words set against each other. Speculations (ekzētēseis) are controversial questions, disputes, open-ended enquiry that never lands; their fruit was argument and division, not faith and love (6:4–5; 2 Timothy 2:23). Stewardship (oikonomia) is the management of a household: the ordered, practical administration of what God has entrusted to someone, and more widely God’s own plan, his way of running his household and saving his people, received and carried out by faith. Some manuscripts read oikodomē, edification, building up, but the better reading is stewardship. The contrast is between human speculation and God’s revealed way of salvation.

A plan with a Head. Paul’s word for God’s stewardship, oikonomia, is the word he used when he wrote to this same church about God’s purpose: a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth (Ephesians 1:10). God’s household order does not float free; it has a centre, and the centre is Christ. That is why the genealogies were never meant to be endless. In Scripture they run somewhere: Matthew’s list walks down the generations from Abraham and stops at Jesus, who is called Christ (Matthew 1:16). The false teachers kept the family trees and lost sight of the Son they were written to reach.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Old Testament genealogies are useless. They are part of Scripture, and they serve the story of Christ (Matthew 1; Luke 3). The problem was using them as material for fanciful speculation divorced from the gospel. Nor does it forbid careful theological study. It forbids speculation that goes beyond Scripture and breeds quarrels.

What are the myths and genealogies today? Anything that turns the Bible into raw material for a system it does not teach, and keeps people busy without making them holy. Date-setting for the Lord’s return and charts that decode current events. Hidden numerical codes in the text. Conspiracy theories baptised with proof-texts. Endless online controversies whose main fruit is a following. Elaborate claims about angels and demons, or about the hidden meaning of names, that Scripture never makes. The test is Paul’s: where does it lead? If it leaves you more anxious, more superior and more argumentative, and no more prayerful, loving or obedient, it is speculation, however clever it sounds.

How do I tell healthy study from speculation? Healthy study stays with what Scripture actually says, reads each passage in its setting, and is content to stop where the Bible stops (Deuteronomy 29:29). It aims at the questions the text is answering, not the ones it leaves aside. It makes you know Christ better and love people more. It can be deep and demanding: Paul’s own letters are not light reading. But it lands. You close the book with something to believe, to repent of or to do. Speculation never lands, and its favourite questions are the ones God chose not to answer.

Should I stay in a hard church? Paul asked Timothy to stay in a difficult place, and that is a word to those of us who leave too quickly. A church with problems is not a reason to go; a church with problems may be exactly where God wants a faithful member. But this is not a rule that you must stay anywhere at any cost. Timothy stayed in order to correct error, and he had an apostle’s authority behind him. If the gospel itself has been abandoned and the leaders will not hear correction, or if you or your children are being harmed and the church will not act, leaving is not unfaithfulness. Take counsel from mature believers before you decide, and leave, if you must, without bitterness.

In a sentence. When I was leaving for Macedonia I asked you to stay on in Ephesus to order certain people to stop teaching a different doctrine and to stop being absorbed in legends and never-ending family trees, which only stir up arguments instead of advancing God’s saving plan, which works through faith.

On a Tuesday. Notice the topics that absorb your Christian attention: the videos you watch, the threads you read, the arguments you keep returning to. Ask of each one what it has produced in you over the last year. Faith and love, or only argument? Then give the time the second kind was taking to something that lands: one psalm read slowly, one prayer for a person by name, one act of kindness for someone who cannot repay it.

For worship. Blessed be the God who does not leave his household guessing. The men in Ephesus could have searched the family trees for a lifetime and found only more questions; God himself has opened the one secret that matters, and its name is Jesus. His plan was not discovered by clever readers but announced to sinners, and it is received not by speculation but by faith, so that a slave who could not read a genealogy could know the Head of the whole household as well as any scholar, and better than the teachers of the law.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, where Paul had spent about three years.

verseByVerse.quote: The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.

The aim of our charge. This is the key sentence of the paragraph, and one of the most important in the letter. The word for aim is telos: the end, the goal, the point of the whole exercise. The charge (parangelia) is Paul’s instruction to Timothy, and more broadly the whole apostolic teaching he is to give. Everything Timothy has been left in Ephesus to do, all the charging and correcting and teaching, exists to produce something. The point of sound doctrine is not winning arguments but producing a certain kind of person.

Is love. Not correct opinions, not a settled congregation, not the defeat of the opposition. Love (agapē): self-giving love for God and for others. It is the fruit of true teaching, in sharp contrast with the speculations of verse 4, which produced quarrels. And that is a startling thing to write at the head of a letter which is about to spend six chapters on doctrine, church order, elders, deacons, widows and false teachers. Paul is not setting doctrine against love. He is telling us what doctrine is for. A theology that does not arrive here has failed on its own terms, however correct it is.

Love with a face. Paul does not leave the word undefined. Ten verses later he names the love this charge exists to reproduce: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15); and in the next chapter, the man Christ Jesus gave himself as a ransom for all (2:5–6). By this we know love, John writes, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers (1 John 3:16). A doctrine that is accurate about the cross and cold toward people has learned the facts of Calvary without its shape.

That issues from a pure heart. Love issues from (ek, out of) three springs, and each blocks a specific counterfeit. Pure (katharos) means clean, unmixed. The heart in Scripture is the centre of the person: thought, desire and will together. A pure heart is one cleansed by God (Psalm 51:10; Acts 15:9) and wholly given to him, the heart Jesus said would see God (Matthew 5:8): the affections uncontaminated, wanting one thing. Without it you get love as a performance, done for an audience or for what it returns.

And a good conscience. Conscience (syneidēsis) is the inner moral awareness, the faculty that sits in judgment on our own actions. A good conscience is one that does not accuse us, because we have been cleansed by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 9:14; 10:22) and are walking in obedience: an inner court with nothing unresolved in it. The phrase recurs in these letters (1:19; 3:9; 2 Timothy 1:3), and at verse 19 a wrecked conscience is what sinks a man; the false teachers had consciences seared as with a hot iron (4:2). Without a good conscience you get love as compensation: the busy kindness of someone avoiding something.

And a sincere faith. Sincere (anypokritos) means un-play-acted, without a mask; the hypokritēs was the actor on the Greek stage. Genuine trust in Christ, not a show. Paul uses the same phrase of the faith that lived first in Timothy’s grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice and now in him (2 Timothy 1:5). Without it you get love as religion: the correct behaviour of a person who does not actually trust God.

What does teaching grow? So Paul’s test for teaching is not merely whether it is true, though it must be, but what it grows. The false teachers were producing speculation and controversy; the charge was given to produce people who love, out of clean hearts, clear consciences and unfeigned faith. Hold any teaching you are drawn to, and any you are inclined to fight about, against that measure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean doctrine is unimportant so long as people love. Love here is the fruit of sound teaching, not a replacement for it: the same chapter that names love as the goal will hand two men over to Satan for false teaching. Nor does it mean love is merely a feeling. It flows from a heart, a conscience and a faith that God has renewed.

Does love mean I should never confront false teaching? No. This verse comes in the middle of a command to stop false teachers, and it explains why the command was given. Error harms people, and love will not stand by and watch sheep being harmed. The father who lets his child drink poison because correcting him feels unkind does not love him. What love changes is the manner: gently, patiently, without quarrelling, correcting opponents in the hope that God may grant them repentance (2 Timothy 2:24–25). Love also changes the aim. You are not trying to win; you are trying to heal.

How can I have a good conscience when mine keeps accusing me? A good conscience is not one that has never been guilty. It is one that has been cleansed. Bring the specific thing to God, confess it plainly, and believe what he says: the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Where you have wronged someone, put it right as far as you can. Then refuse to keep paying for what Christ has paid for. If the accusation returns after you have confessed, it is no longer your conscience doing its proper work; it is the accuser, and you answer him with the cross. And keep your conscience tender by obeying it quickly the next time it speaks.

In a sentence. The whole goal of this instruction is love, flowing from a clean heart, a clear conscience, and faith that is genuine.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last theological conversation you had that grew heated. Run Paul’s three questions over it. Was my heart pure, wanting God’s glory and the other person’s good, or wanting to win? Was my conscience clear, or was I arguing loudly about one thing to avoid another? Was my faith sincere, or was I performing? Then do one thing that verse 5 would recognise: write to that person, or pray for them by name, or ask their forgiveness for the tone if not the content.

For worship. God does not only command love; he is love, and he has shown it. The pure heart he asks for, he creates; the good conscience he requires, he cleanses with his Son’s blood; the sincere faith he looks for, he gives. Every true doctrine in this letter is a window onto that love, and the goal of all of them is that we should become, in our small measure, like the God who so loved the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.

Certain persons, by swerving from these. The verb is astocheō: to miss the mark, to shoot wide. The image is an archer, and the target was named in verse 5: love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. Note carefully what that implies. These men are not described as enemies who attacked the target from outside. They aimed at it and missed. They were church people with ambitions to teach, and they went wide, which is a more uncomfortable diagnosis than malice, because it can happen to anyone who stops checking where he is pointing.

Have wandered away into vain discussion. Wandered away (ektrepō) is to turn aside, used of turning off a road, and in medical writers of a limb wrenched out of joint. Vain discussion (mataiologia) is empty talk, idle chatter. Not false talk necessarily; empty. Talk that has no content and goes nowhere, but generates a great deal of heat and occupies a great deal of time. Their teaching was impressive-sounding and hollow, words without substance, and like a dislocated limb it still moved, but it could no longer bear weight.

Desiring to be teachers of the law. Teachers of the law (nomodidaskaloi) is the word used of the Jewish rabbis (Luke 5:17; Acts 5:34). These men wanted the standing of authorities on the Old Testament law. And the order of the sentence is the whole diagnosis. First comes the desire to be a teacher. The content is secondary: a subject was needed, and the law provided one. Paul is describing men who wanted the standing that comes with teaching and then went looking for something to teach, which is the reverse of how it should work and is not confined to the first century.

Without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions. The double ignorance is precisely observed: they do not understand their own words, nor the matters they pronounce on. Yet the pronouncing is confident. The verb (diabebaioomai) means to insist strongly, to affirm emphatically, the tone of a man who has settled the question. That combination, certainty without comprehension, is the reliable signature of this kind of teacher. Genuine understanding usually makes a person more careful, not less. The more a man truly knows of God, the more often he says, I do not know.

Paul had been this man. These lines come from someone who knew the type from the inside. Before Damascus, Saul of Tarsus was as confident a teacher of the law as any in his generation: a Pharisee, advancing beyond his contemporaries, as to righteousness under the law blameless (Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:5–6). And he understood neither what he was saying nor the things he asserted, because the law he taught was pointing to the Christ he was hunting. Six verses later he will say he acted ignorantly in unbelief (1:13). What cured him was not a better argument but a meeting: the risen Jesus spoke his name. It is still the only cure for certainty without comprehension, and it lets Paul write of these men with severity but without contempt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean confidence in truth is wrong. Paul himself speaks with certainty: I know whom I have believed (2 Timothy 1:12). The problem is confidence without understanding, and teaching for status.

Is it wrong to want to teach? No. Paul will say in 3:1 that if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task. The difference is in what is wanted. One man wants the work: to feed people, to make Christ known, to see a church grow in love. Another wants the platform: to be listened to, quoted, deferred to. You can usually tell which you are by what happens when someone else is asked instead of you, and by whether you are willing to learn before you teach (James 3:1). A good teacher is first a good listener to Scripture and to wiser people.

How do I know if I am confident without understanding? Three signs. You find it easier to explain why others are wrong than to explain the passage in front of you. You have never seriously read the best case for the view you oppose. And you are rarely heard to say, I am not sure, or, I was wrong about that. The remedy is not timidity. It is to sit longer with the text before you speak, to check your reading against the faithful teachers of the church, and to hold firmly what Scripture says plainly and lightly what it does not.

In a sentence. Some have missed this target and drifted off into empty talk; they want to be known as experts in the law, yet they do not understand their own words or the matters they are so sure about.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak with confidence about a spiritual matter this week, in a home group, online or across the kitchen table, ask: do I actually understand this from Scripture, or have I only heard it said? If you are not sure, say so. It costs a little pride, and it guards you against becoming the man in this verse.

For worship. There is one Teacher who never spoke a word he did not understand, and who never sought the standing that his teaching earned. He was the Word made flesh, and he made himself nothing. The crowds marvelled that he taught as one who had authority, and he used that authority to wash feet and to die for the men who had been listening. Every true teacher in the church is only an echo of his voice.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,

Now we know that the law is good. Paul now guards himself against a misunderstanding, and does it in one sentence. He has just dismissed the would-be teachers of the law, and someone could easily conclude that the problem is the law itself: that the Old Testament is the difficulty and the sooner the church is clear of it the better. Marcion drew that conclusion in the second century, and many have drawn it since; Paul heads it off at once. The law (nomos), here the Law of Moses and especially its moral commands, is good (kalos): excellent, fine, beautiful. It is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12), because it reflects the character of the God who gave it. It is God’s, and it is not on trial here.

If one uses it lawfully. There is a deliberate play in the Greek: nomos used nomimōs. The law must be used law-fully. It is a small joke with a serious point. The problem is a misuse. The false teachers were using the law as a source of speculation, or perhaps as a ladder of merit, and the phrase implies there is a proper use and that it can be identified: the law is aimed at the lawless, to expose and restrain their sin.

Where the lawful use leads. A law used lawfully does not leave a man admiring his own record; it sends him to a Saviour. Paul knew this from his own life: the commandment that promised life proved to be death to him (Romans 7:10), and it drove him to Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4). Used as God meant it, the law is the guardian that walks a sinner to the door and hands him over to Christ (Galatians 3:24). The false teachers made it a puzzle and so never arrived there; Paul, convicted by it, would write a few verses later that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.

Where Christians differ: what is the place of the law for Christians? Some say the Old Testament law has no role for Christians at all; others make it a way of earning favour with God. Verdict: The Reformed tradition, following Scripture, speaks of three uses of the moral law. First, it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). Second, it restrains evil in society (the use in view here, vv. 9–10). Third, it guides believers in grateful obedience (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:2). The ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1–14); the civil laws of Israel expired with Israel’s state, though their principles of justice remain instructive. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains God’s will, but it is never the way of justification.

A fourth use. The false teachers had found a use unknown to Scripture: raw material for a speculative system that flattered the interpreter and left everybody’s heart exactly where it was. Their law never accused anyone, restrained anyone or guided anyone. It only entertained.

The remedy for bad use is good use. The instinct when something good is being handled badly is to withdraw it: to stop teaching it, to treat the subject as dangerous. Some churches have done this with election, with the law, with the Lord’s Supper, with the Holy Spirit. Paul does not do that. He does not respond to the abuse of the law by abandoning the law; he responds by explaining what it is for. The remedy for bad use is good use, and it always costs more effort than avoidance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are saved by keeping the law. No one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16). Nor does it mean the law is bad because it cannot save. The fault lies in us, not in the law: what the law could not do, weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3).

If I am not under the law, why should I read it? Because you are not under it as a covenant of works, a way of earning life, but you are still under God, and the law tells you what he loves. A believer reads the commandments the way a child reads a letter from his father: not to find out how to be adopted, but to learn how to please the one who already adopted him. Christ did not abolish the law but fulfilled it (Matthew 5:17), and the Spirit writes it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). The same commandments that once condemned you now describe the family likeness the Spirit is forming in you.

Do I need to keep the food laws, festivals and sacrifices? No. Those belonged to the ceremonial law, which was a shadow of the things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The sacrifices pointed to his one sacrifice and ended when it was offered (Hebrews 10:1–14). The food laws marked Israel off from the nations, and Christ has made the two one (Mark 7:19; Ephesians 2:14–15). You read those chapters to see Christ in them, not to obey them as rules. The moral law is different, because it is grounded in God’s own character and in creation, and it is repeated throughout the New Testament.

In a sentence. We know the law is good, provided it is used for the purpose it was given.

On a Tuesday. Read the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1–17) this week, slowly, once for each use. First as a mirror: where do they show you your sin? Take that to Christ. Then as a fence: thank God for the restraint his law has placed on the world you live in, on your street, your courts, your own worst impulses. Then as a path: choose one commandment and ask what it would look like to keep it gladly, as love for God and neighbour, before Friday.

For worship. The law is good because the Lawgiver is good. Every commandment is a ray of his own holiness, and every one of them was kept, perfectly and gladly, by his Son. The law that could only condemn us has been satisfied by him, and now it is given back to us, not as a ladder we must climb, but as a description of the life he lived for us and is living in us.

verseByVerse.quote: understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,
verseByVerse.commentary:
understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,

Understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just. Here is the proper use, and it deserves its weight. Laid down (keitai) is a legal term: set, enacted, on the statute book. The just (dikaios) are the righteous. Paul is not saying a righteous person may ignore God’s commands. He is saying the law in its convicting and restraining function, as accuser, as the thing that arraigns you, is not aimed at people already doing what it requires, as if it existed to make them more righteous through speculation. You do not post a warning notice for people who were never going to do it. Its sharp edge is directed against wrongdoing. Those justified in Christ do not live under the law’s condemnation (Romans 8:1), though they delight in its moral content (Romans 7:22).

But for the lawless and disobedient. Then the list, and its shape is deliberate. It falls into two halves that track the two tables of the Ten Commandments. The first six words come in three pairs, describing sin against God: lawless and disobedient (those who reject authority), ungodly and sinners (those without reverence for God), unholy and profane (those who treat sacred things as common, trampling what God calls holy). That is the first table, the commandments about God: no other gods, no idols, no taking his name in vain, his day kept holy.

For those who strike their fathers and mothers. Now the second table, sins against neighbours, and these run in the order of the commandments. Paul is walking down the Decalogue and naming who each one is for. The words (patrolōais kai mētrolōais) mean literally father-killers and mother-killers, or those who beat their parents: the fifth commandment, honour your father and your mother, at its most violent extreme (Exodus 20:12; 21:15). Murderers follow: the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13).

The sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality. The seventh commandment, broadened to all sexual sin. The sexually immoral (pornoi) are those who engage in any sexual relations outside marriage. Men who practise homosexuality translates arsenokoitai, a compound of male and bed. Paul appears to have coined it, and its parts come straight out of the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which forbid a man lying with a male as with a woman: arsenos koitēn, a male bed. It refers to same-sex sexual acts, not only to exploitative forms. Attempts to narrow it to exploitation or temple prostitution have to work against that derivation. The historic Christian reading has been the plain one, and it should be stated plainly rather than smuggled or softened.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative or abusive practices, such as pederasty, and not loving, committed same-sex relationships. Verdict: The word arsenokoitai comes from the Levitical prohibition, which concerns the act itself, regardless of the relationship. Romans 1:26–27 describes mutual desire, not only exploitation. Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union belongs to the marriage of one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). This is held with compassion: same-sex attraction is a real struggle for many, it is not itself the same as acting on it, and all of us stand in this list as sinners. The hope is the same for all: “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Where Paul put it. But it should also be stated in this list, which is where Paul put it, alongside liars and men who hit their parents, and five verses later he will call himself the foremost sinner alive. This is a passage about who the law arraigns, and the answer includes the writer. Any use of verse 10 that leaves the user feeling comfortable has misread the paragraph it sits in.

A list of people Christ came for. The list does not have the last word, and Paul will not let it. Six verses on, the same pen writes that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15), using the very word that stands in this catalogue (v. 9). Every kind of person named here is the kind of person the Son of God came for: the parent-beater, the murderer, the sexually immoral, the slave-trader, the respectable liar. The law arraigns the lawless so that the gospel can acquit them, and it can acquit them only because Christ became a curse for us and bore the sentence himself (Galatians 3:13).

Enslavers. The eighth commandment, do not steal, in its most extreme form. Enslavers (andrapodistai) are kidnappers, slave-traders, men who steal human beings to sell them. The law punished man-stealing with death (Exodus 21:16). Note what Paul counts as the worst form of theft: not a purse but a person. And Paul, writing inside an empire built on slavery, puts slave-trading in a list of things contrary to sound doctrine. That deserves to be said out loud, given how often the New Testament is assumed to have nothing to say on the subject. Scripture condemns the trade that built so much of history’s slavery, including the Atlantic trade that men professing Christ carried on for three centuries against the plain words of this verse.

Liars, perjurers. The ninth commandment, false witness. Perjurers (epiorkoi) are those who swear falsely, the lie told under oath where justice depends on the truth.

And whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine. The catalogue was never meant to be complete; the list is representative. And then a word that will become a refrain in these letters. Sound (hygiainousa, from which comes hygiene) is a medical word: healthy, whole, wholesome (6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13; 4:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1). Paul’s standard for teaching is not merely accuracy but health: doctrine that makes people well. False doctrine is a disease that spreads like gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17). Everything on this list makes people ill. And notice that sound doctrine and moral behaviour are inseparable: Paul does not say these sins are contrary to good manners, but to sound doctrine. What a church believes and how its people live are one organism, and sickness in either spreads to the other.

What it does not mean. It does not single out one sin as worse than all others, or suggest that those who commit these sins are beyond grace. Paul goes on immediately to call himself the foremost of sinners (v. 15). Nor does it mean the law has no relevance to believers; it means the law’s condemning and restraining force is aimed at sin.

What if I am a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction? It means you are not in this list for your temptations; you are in Christ, and the list is about practice. Being tempted is not sin: our Lord was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Your calling is the one every Christian has, to say no to sexual sin and yes to Christ, whether in faithful celibacy or, for some, in marriage to someone of the opposite sex. That is costly, and the church must not pretend otherwise. It must be a family to you: homes open to you, friendships deep enough to carry the weight, no jokes or contempt tolerated. Many faithful believers walk this road, and Christ is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters.

Did the Bible approve of slavery? Not of the slavery most people picture. The trade that seized Africans and shipped them across the Atlantic was man-stealing, and this verse and Exodus 21:16 condemn it outright. Old Testament servitude was mostly a form of working off debt, limited in time and protected by law (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12–15; 23:15–16). In the New Testament Paul did not lead a revolt against Roman slavery, which would have been crushed in a week, but he planted the gospel that dissolved it: masters and slaves equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28), a runaway sent back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), slaves told to gain their freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21). The Christians who fought to end the trade were reading these verses rightly.

In a sentence. We know that the law is not aimed at the righteous but at people who break it and rebel, who are godless and sinful, irreverent and profane; at those who attack their parents, at murderers, at the sexually immoral and men who have sex with men, at people-traffickers, liars and perjurers, and at anything else that opposes healthy teaching.

On a Tuesday. Read the list slowly and find yourself in it somewhere. You may not have struck a parent, but have you despised one? You may not have perjured yourself, but when did you last shade the truth to protect yourself? Jesus taught that the commandments reach the heart (Matthew 5:21–30). Then remember verse 15, and speak of sin to others, and especially of sins that are not yours, as one who has also been forgiven.

For worship. The law names the sins; the gospel names the Saviour. Every one of these commandments was kept by Christ: he honoured his mother from the cross, he gave life and did not take it, he was pure, he stole nothing and gave everything, he never once lied. And the man who was all that the law requires was numbered with the lawless, so that the lawless who trust him could be numbered with the just.
verseByVerse.note: The list follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from the first table (God) to the second (neighbour).

verseByVerse.quote: in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.

In accordance with the gospel. This is the standard against which the whole chapter has been measuring. The myths and genealogies, the confident assertions, the misuse of the law: all of it is judged by whether it accords with this. What is sound doctrine (v. 10)? Whatever agrees with the gospel. Paul does not refute the false teachers point by point. He holds them up against the gospel and lets the mismatch do the work. And the law and the gospel are not at war. The law exposes sin; the gospel announces the remedy. They agree in their verdict on sin: the gospel does not approve of sin but saves from it.

Of the glory of the blessed God. The phrase is often quoted as the glorious gospel, and that is not quite what Paul wrote. Literally it is the gospel of the glory: the gospel that concerns God’s glory, that displays it, that has it as its content. The difference matters: God’s glory is not an adjective describing the message but the thing the message is about. And the glory is seen in a face: the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4, 6). When the gospel is preached, God is showing what he is like.

The blessed God. A phrase Paul uses only in this letter (here and 6:15). The word is makarios, the same word that opens each of the Beatitudes: happy, supremely fortunate. Applied to God it means he is perfectly and self-sufficiently happy: not needing anything, not waiting on circumstances, complete in himself, the Father delighting in the Son and the Son in the Father in the fellowship of the Spirit from all eternity. Hold onto that. God did not save anyone out of loneliness or deficiency. He was entirely blessed before he made anything, and the gospel is the overflow of that fullness rather than the remedy for a lack. The good news comes from a God who is himself overflowing with joy, and it invites us into it.

With which I have been entrusted. The verb (pisteuō, here in the passive) is the language of a deposit placed in someone’s keeping, the same idea he will press on Timothy at the end of the letter: guard the deposit (6:20; 2 Timothy 1:12–14). Paul did not devise this message and does not own it. He is holding something for its owner, which is the only posture from which anyone can safely correct anybody else’s doctrine. And that word turns the paragraph. Paul has been describing men who wanted to be teachers. Now he remembers that he was made one, and the memory sets off the most personal passage in the letter.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gospel is Paul’s own invention. It was entrusted to him by God, received by revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:11–12).

Is it irreverent to call God happy? No; it is Paul’s own word, and it guards us against two errors. One pictures God as stern and joyless, tolerating us with a frown, so that the Christian life becomes a matter of keeping a grim master satisfied. The other pictures him as needy, as if he made us because he was lonely and saves us because he could not bear to be without us. Neither is the God of the Bible. He is holy and he is happy, and these are not in tension: his joy is joy in what is good. That is why his commands are not burdensome, why his presence is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11), and why the servant who is faithful is told to enter into the joy of his master (Matthew 25:21).

In a sentence. Healthy teaching is measured by the gospel that displays the glory of the blessed God, the gospel that was placed in my care.

On a Tuesday. If your picture of God this week is of someone tired of you, read this verse again. The God you pray to is not irritable, depleted or reluctant. Begin your prayers by remembering what he is, before you tell him what you need. And when you share the gospel, remember that you are not selling a rescue scheme; you are telling people about the glory of a God who is happy, and who has made a way for them to share it.

For worship. Blessed is the God who needs nothing and gives everything. His joy was full before the first morning of creation, and out of that fullness he sent his Son, not to fill an emptiness in himself but to bring us into the fellowship he had always enjoyed. The gospel is the glory of that God, shining in the face of Jesus Christ, and it has been placed in the hands of sinners to carry.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:12–17 – Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and appointing him to service, though he had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man. He was shown mercy because he acted in ignorance and unbelief, and the Lord’s grace overflowed to him with faith and love. Here is a saying to be trusted: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul counts himself the worst. He was shown mercy so that Christ could display his patience in him as an example for all who would believe. Paul bursts into praise of the eternal, immortal, invisible King, the only God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Present Tense of Verse 15

‘Of whom I am the foremost’ — not was. Nearness to light shows more dust, not less, and only a man who sees himself so can correct others without contempt.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The persecutor became the pattern (v.16): Christ's patience with him is the outer limit that no later case exceeds.

Now: The doxology of verse 17 comes from a man remembering his own conversion and unable to finish the sentence without worship.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord. The thought of the gospel entrusted to him makes Paul stop and give thanks, and the first thing he thanks Christ for is strength. The verb (endynamoō) means empowered, put power into. Paul’s ministry was not his own achievement but Christ’s power in him (Philippians 4:13; 2 Timothy 4:17). The man who planted churches across the empire took no credit for the energy.

Because he judged me faithful. Stop on this. Judged (hēgeomai) is considered, regarded; faithful (pistos) is trustworthy. That is an extraordinary thing for this man to say, and he immediately explains why it is extraordinary. It was not because Paul had earned it; he was a persecutor. Christ, by grace, made him trustworthy and then entrusted him with the work (1 Corinthians 7:25). The Lord does not find faithful men; he makes them, and then he treats them as what he has made.

Appointing me to his service. Service (diakonia) is ministry, the word from which deacon comes. A gracious appointment, given on the Damascus road: he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name (Acts 9:15; 26:16).

Though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. Three words, and they escalate: in word, in deed, in attitude. Blasphemer (blasphēmos): he had spoken against the name of Christ, and worse, had tried to force others to do it (Acts 26:11). Persecutor (diōktēs): he had hunted people down; Acts records him approving an execution and going house to house dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:1, 3; 9:1–2; Galatians 1:13). Insolent opponent is hybristēs, from which we get hubris: the violent, arrogant man who takes pleasure in hurting and humiliating people. It is the ugliest of the three, and Paul chose it about himself.

But I received mercy. The verb (eleeō) is passive: he was shown pity. It is the pivot of the verse. Paul deserved judgment; he received mercy. He did not find it, earn it or ask for it. On the road to Damascus he was not seeking Christ; he was seeking Christians.

Because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief. This needs care, because it can be misread as an excuse, and Paul is not making one; he has just used three brutal words about himself. He did not fully know what he was doing: he thought he was serving God (Acts 26:9; Romans 10:2). In the Old Testament there was provision for sins committed unwittingly, and none for sins committed with a high hand, in deliberate defiance (Numbers 15:27–31). Paul is saying he was on the first side of that line: catastrophically wrong, and sincerely so. Not innocent. Reachable. Jesus prayed for the men who crucified him in the same terms: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34).

And the grace of our Lord overflowed for me. The verb is enormous: hyperpleonazō, super-abounded, more than filled, flooded beyond measure. It is one of Paul’s hyper words, and he stacks the prefixes because ordinary words will not carry it. Where his sin had been extreme, grace was more extreme. Grace did not merely match his sin; it overwhelmed it, as where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

With the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Notice what came with the flood. Faith and love were not what Paul contributed in response; they arrived in it. Faith in place of his unbelief; love in place of his violence. Both are found in Christ Jesus, given through union with him. The man who had neither was given both, which is the exact answer to the question raised by verse 5, where love from sincere faith was named as the goal of everything. Here is where such love comes from. It is not produced by teaching alone. It is poured in by grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s ignorance earned or caused God’s mercy, as if ignorance made him deserving. Ignorance is not innocence; Paul still calls himself the foremost of sinners (v. 15). The point is that his sin, though terrible, was not the deliberate, knowing rejection of the Spirit that Jesus calls unforgivable (Mark 3:28–29). Mercy remained possible, and God freely chose to give it. Paul’s conversion was God’s sovereign, effectual call (Galatians 1:15–16), not a response to his deserving.

Could I have committed the unforgivable sin? If you are worried that you have, you have not. The sin Jesus warned of (Mark 3:28–30) was committed by men who watched the Spirit’s work in Christ and deliberately called it the devil’s, and who were so hardened that they had no desire to repent. It is a settled, knowing hostility to Christ, not a single dreadful thought, a terrible season of backsliding, or a past as violent as Paul’s. The very fear that you have gone too far is evidence that the Spirit is still at work in you. Paul blasphemed, persecuted and enjoyed hurting people, and he was received. Come to Christ now, and you will find that he does not cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Can God really use someone with my past? Look at who wrote this. God did not merely forgive Paul and leave him in a back pew; he put him in the front line, among the very people he had hunted. Your past does not disqualify you from belonging to Christ or from serving him. It may shape how you serve: some offences have lasting consequences, and some roles, such as eldership, require a good reputation over time (3:2, 7). But grace does not only pardon; it appoints. The stories you are most ashamed of may be the ones God uses to show someone else that there is hope.

In a sentence. I give thanks to Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, because he counted me trustworthy and put me into his service, although I used to slander him, hunt his people and treat them with violent contempt; yet I was shown mercy, since I acted in ignorance and unbelief, and our Lord’s grace flooded over me, bringing the faith and love that are found in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. No one you know is too far gone for grace. Name the most hostile person you know toward Christ: the relative who mocks, the colleague who sneers, the public figure who rages. Pray for them today by name, and pray for more than their restraint. Pray that Christ would do to them what he did to Saul. Then thank him, specifically, for what you were when he found you.

For worship. Christ went looking for his worst enemy and turned him into his greatest apostle. He did not wait for Saul to soften; he met him at full speed on the road to Damascus, with letters of arrest in his bag, and spoke his name. Grace overflowed, and it is still overflowing. The same Lord who strengthened the persecutor holds every one of his people, and not one of them was found worthy. Every one was made so.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.

The saying is trustworthy. Trustworthy (pistos) is faithful, reliable, the same word Christ used of Paul in verse 12. This is the first of five such formulas in the Pastoral Letters (3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), and it appears to flag a line already in circulation: something the churches said, perhaps sang or taught to new believers, which Paul now endorses with his apostolic authority.

And deserving of full acceptance. Full acceptance (pasēs apodochēs) is total welcome, wholehearted reception. This truth is not only to be agreed with but embraced with the whole self, the way a starving man does not merely agree that bread is nourishing.

That Christ Jesus came into the world. Nine words in English that hold the gospel. Came into the world: he was somewhere else first. This is a claim to his pre-existence and incarnation made in passing (John 1:9; 3:17). He existed before he came; he came from the Father into our world as a man.

To save sinners. The purpose of his coming: not merely to teach or to set an example, but to save, to rescue from sin and its penalty (Matthew 1:21; Luke 19:10). And to save sinners: not the promising, not the religious, not the nearly good. Jesus said it himself: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners (Mark 2:17). This is the gospel in a sentence, and the only qualification for it is the one thing everyone has.

Of whom I am the foremost. Then Paul adds words of his own, and they are the reason the verse is unforgettable. Foremost (prōtos) is first, chief, worst. And the tense is the thing. Not was the foremost, which is what we would expect after verse 13’s list of past crimes. I am. Present. Decades into an apostleship, having planted churches across the empire and written much of the New Testament, Paul’s settled estimate of himself is present tense. Mature believers see their sin more clearly, not less: the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9), the very least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8), and now the foremost of sinners. The sequence of those letters runs downward.

Nearness to light. This is not theatrical humility, or a man fishing for contradiction. It is what happens to self-knowledge over a long life with God. Nearness to light shows you more dust, not less. John Bunyan took the title of his own spiritual autobiography from this verse: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners. And John Newton, the slave-ship captain who became a minister of the gospel, is remembered as saying near the end of his life that his memory was nearly gone, but he remembered two things: that he was a great sinner, and that Christ was a great Saviour.

How Paul uses it. And see how it functions here. Paul is about to discipline two men (v. 20) and has been dismantling a group of false teachers for ten verses. He does it from this position. A man who genuinely considers himself the foremost sinner in the room can correct other people without contempt, and nobody else can.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was literally the worst sinner who ever lived, as a statistical claim. It is the honest confession of someone who knew the depths of his own heart. Nor does it mean Christ came to save everyone without distinction in such a way that all will be saved; he came to save sinners, and those he came to save he actually saves (Matthew 1:21; John 10:11, 27–29).

Isn’t it unhealthy to call myself the worst of sinners? Not when it is said the way Paul says it, in the same breath as Christ Jesus came to save. Self-hatred looks at sin and stops there; it ends in despair or in self-punishment. Paul looks at his sin in order to look at his Saviour, and it ends in a doxology two verses later. Nor is it a false humility that refuses to see God’s work in you: Paul also says he worked harder than all the apostles, though it was not he but the grace of God (1 Corinthians 15:10). The healthy Christian holds both: I am a great sinner, and I am greatly loved. Each truth keeps the other from going wrong.

What if I do not feel that bad? The question is not how you compare with Paul, but how you stand before God. A respectable sinner is still a sinner, and the danger of feeling not that bad is that you never come to Christ as one who needs saving. Paul’s first opinion of himself was that he was blameless (Philippians 3:6); that was his worst condition, not his best. The door of this verse is marked Sinners, and the only people who cannot go through it are those who think the sign does not apply to them.

In a sentence. Here is a statement you can rely on and should welcome with all your heart: Christ Jesus entered the world to rescue sinners, and I am the worst of them.

On a Tuesday. When you next find yourself despising someone, the political opponent, the neighbour, the church member who has failed publicly, say this verse under your breath with your own name in it. It changes the tone of what you say next. And if you are carrying a sin you think is too heavy for this verse, read it again: it does not say Christ came to save sinners, except for the worst. The worst signed it.

For worship. Christ Jesus came into the world. He left the glory he shared with the Father, took our flesh and walked into a world of sinners, not to inspect them but to save them, and he did not stop until he had borne their sin on the cross. The foremost of sinners was found by him; the chief of sinners became the herald of his grace. There is no one so lost that the Son of God has not come looking for him.
verseByVerse.note: The first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters.

verseByVerse.quote: But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

But I received mercy for this reason. Paul now gives a further purpose of his conversion, and explains why he of all people was chosen. God had a reason for choosing such an enemy, and the reason was you.

That in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience. Display (endeiknymi) is to demonstrate, to put on show. Perfect patience (tēn hapasan makrothymian) is all his long-suffering, the whole extent of it: long-temperedness, the slowness to boil that endures provocation. And it was on display for years. Christ was patient with Saul of Tarsus for the whole time Saul was doing his worst, and he did not intervene until the moment he had chosen. If Christ could be patient with Paul, he can be patient with anyone. Paul is the showcase of Christ’s patience.

As an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. Example (hypotypōsis) is a pattern, a sketch, an outline drawn so that others can see the shape of a thing: the prototype. Paul’s conversion is the template. He was made an exhibit. The logic is generous and worth following. If Christ’s patience stretched to a man who hunted his people and tried to make them curse his name, then nobody who comes after can reasonably say their case is too hard. Paul’s biography stands as a fixed outer limit: the worst case on record was received. Whatever anyone brings, it has already been exceeded. Those who were to believe looks ahead to all future believers, chosen and called by God, and eternal life is the goal of faith.

To the King of the ages. Then the sentence breaks into praise, and note where the doxology comes from. It is not attached to a doctrine of God in the abstract; it erupts out of the memory of his own conversion. Paul thinks about what he was and what he received, and cannot get to the end of the paragraph without worshipping. That is a fair test of whether the gospel has been understood or merely learned. Four titles follow, and each one answers something. King of the ages (basileus tōn aiōnōn): the eternal King, ruler over all the ages of history. He governs every era, including this troublesome one in Ephesus, and including yours.

Immortal, invisible, the only God. Immortal (aphthartos) is literally incorruptible, not subject to decay, unlike everything else Timothy is dealing with: the church, the false teachers, his own body with its frequent illnesses. Invisible (aoratos): no one has ever seen God in his essence (John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16). That is exactly the difficulty of pastoral work: the one you serve cannot be seen, while the opposition is entirely visible. The only God: there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), and in a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis, that is not a philosophical statement but a stand. Some later manuscripts add wise, the only wise God, borrowed from Romans 16:27; the earlier reading is the only God.

Be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. Forever and ever (eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn) is to the ages of the ages, the strongest phrase Greek has for endlessness. The King of the ages receives glory for the ages of the ages. And Amen: so be it, it is true. Paul expects the congregation to say it back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only notorious sinners are examples of grace. Every believer is saved by the same patience. Nor does Christ’s patience mean he is indifferent to sin; his patience gives time for repentance (Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9).

What if I was converted quietly as a child? Is my story worth anything? Yes. Paul’s story is the outer limit, set there so that the worst may hope. But a child brought up in the faith and kept from great sins has received just as much mercy; it was simply given earlier, before the damage could be done. Being kept is as much grace as being rescued. Your story displays Christ’s patience in a different way: patience with all the small, stubborn sins of a long ordinary life, and faithfulness through every year of it.

If God is invisible, how can I know him? Because the invisible God has made himself known. John says that the only Son, himself God and at the Father’s side, is the one who has made the unseen Father known (John 1:18). Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). You meet him in the Scriptures, which testify to Christ, and you know him by faith, through the Spirit, who opens the eyes of your heart. The invisibility of God is not his absence. It is his greatness: he is not one more object in the world, and he cannot be captured in an image, but he has come close in his Son.

In a sentence. Yet for this very reason I was shown mercy: so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus could show the full extent of his patience, as a pattern for all who would later trust him and receive eternal life. Now to the eternal King, deathless, unseen, the one and only God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

On a Tuesday. If you know someone who believes they are beyond hope, tell them Paul’s story this week, in your own words, and then tell them yours. And notice what happened to Paul when he remembered his conversion: he worshipped. Spend five minutes today remembering what you were when Christ found you, and what he has given you since, and let it end the way Paul’s did, with honour and glory to the King.

For worship. To the King of the ages, who reigned before the first age began and will reign when the last has ended; to the one who cannot decay, in a world where everything decays; to the one no eye has seen, who has shown his face in Jesus Christ; to the only God, beside whom every saviour of stone is nothing; who was patient with his enemy for years and then made him a pattern of mercy for us all: be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul entrusts this charge to Timothy, in line with the prophecies once spoken about him, so that he will fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience.
