Some have rejected conscience and wrecked their faith, among them Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan so that they learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Goes First — Conduct or Doctrine

In verse 19 the conscience goes first and the faith goes down after it; and even the severest discipline, handing over to Satan, is remedial — ‘that they may learn’ (v.20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was to fight by the prophecies once made over him (cf. 4:14).

Now: Shipwreck is what happens when a man keeps sailing while ignoring what his conscience tells him about the rocks.

verseByVerse.quote: This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.

This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child. Paul returns to where the chapter began, and the vocabulary of deposit returns with it. The charge (parangelia) is the same word as verse 5: the commission to guard sound doctrine. Entrust (paratithēmi) is to deposit with someone for safekeeping. As the gospel was entrusted to Paul (v. 11), he now entrusts the charge to Timothy, who must later entrust it to faithful men who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). It is being handed on, and that is how it has always travelled: one faithful person to another, down every generation, until it reached you.

In accordance with the prophecies previously made about you. When Timothy was set apart for ministry, prophetic words had been spoken about him, presumably at his commissioning, when the elders laid hands on him (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). We are not told what was said, but Timothy is to fight by them, to use them as ammunition on hard days. When the ministry goes badly and a man wonders whether he should be doing this at all, one legitimate answer is to remember what was said when he began.

That by them you may wage the good warfare. Wage warfare (strateuomai) is to serve as a soldier, to fight a military campaign. The military note is deliberate and will come back (6:12; 2 Timothy 2:3–4; 4:7; Ephesians 6:10–17). Ministry here is not administration; it is a campaign, and there is an enemy. Good (kalē) means noble, worth fighting.

Holding faith and a good conscience. Holding (echōn) is keeping, retaining, not letting go. These are the two things named back in verse 5, and here they are two weapons. Faith is both personal trust and the content of the faith; a good conscience is the clear inner court. They belong together. When conscience is violated, faith soon suffers.

By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith. Rejecting (apōtheomai) is thrusting away, deliberately pushing aside, and this is the good conscience. Made shipwreck (nauageō) is to suffer shipwreck. Paul, who had been shipwrecked three times before he ever sailed for Rome (2 Corinthians 11:25; Acts 27), uses a vivid image: they deliberately threw overboard their conscience, and their faith broke up on the rocks.

The conscience goes first. Note the order carefully, because it is the most practical thing in the chapter. The conscience goes first, and the faith goes down after it. Paul does not describe men who reasoned their way out of Christianity and then began living badly. He describes men who rejected a good conscience, who kept doing what they knew to be wrong, and whose doctrine followed their conduct onto the rocks. Wrong living has to build itself a theology eventually, and it usually manages one. Many who announce that they have lost their faith for intellectual reasons lost their conscience first.

Among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander. Two names, after twenty verses of certain persons. Hymenaeus later taught, with Philetus, that the resurrection had already happened, and upset the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:17–18). Alexander may be the coppersmith who did Paul great harm (2 Timothy 4:14), though the name was common.

Whom I have handed over to Satan. The phrase is severe, and it is used elsewhere of putting someone outside the church’s fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:5): out of the sphere where God’s people gather under Christ’s protection, and back into the world, the domain of darkness where Satan operates (Colossians 1:13). This is excommunication, the most serious act of church discipline.

A defeated enemy on a short chain. Handing a man over to Satan could only be remedial if Satan is not free, and he is not. At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The devil still prowls, but inside the limits his conqueror sets, as Paul learned when a messenger of Satan was made to serve his good (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Timothy fights under a Captain who has already won the battle that decides the war, and even the enemy’s ground can become a school in which Christ teaches a blasphemer to stop.

That they may learn not to blaspheme. But read the purpose clause, because it changes the colour of the whole thing. Learn (paideuō) is to be disciplined, trained, as a child is trained. It is remedial, not punitive. Even excommunication aims at restoration: experiencing life outside the church might bring them to their senses and to repentance. It is the same logic as 2 Thessalonians 3:15, where the disciplined man is warned as a brother and not treated as an enemy. And note the word blaspheme. Their false teaching dishonoured God, and it is what Paul called himself in verse 13, before he received mercy. He hands them over hoping for what happened to him.

Where Christians differ: do prophecies like these continue today? Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians see the prophecies over Timothy as a model for prophetic words in churches today. Verdict: The New Testament prophets belonged to the foundation-laying era of the church, alongside the apostles (Ephesians 2:20), when Scripture was still being given. With the completion of the canon, God guides his church through the sufficient written Word, not through new revelations (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). This is held charitably: brothers who differ often love Christ deeply, and God still guides through his Word, wise counsel, providence, and the inward witness of the Spirit to Scripture. But no word claiming to be prophecy may add to or stand alongside Scripture.

What were these prophecies? Spirit-given words, in the apostolic age, that marked Timothy out for his ministry, probably spoken when the elders laid hands on him (4:14). They belonged to that founding time. Today the church recognises a man’s call to ministry by his gifts, character and fruit, tested by Scripture, not by new prophecies.

Were Hymenaeus and Alexander true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians read made shipwreck of their faith that way. The more likely reading is that they held the faith outwardly but never truly trusted Christ; as John says of such people, if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19). Paul’s discipline was meant to bring them to repentance, that they might learn not to blaspheme. The warning is for every believer to hold faith and a good conscience.

What it does not mean. Made shipwreck of their faith does not mean true believers can be lost. Those who finally abandon the faith reveal that their faith was not genuine saving faith (1 John 2:19), and the aim of the discipline was still their recovery. Nor does handed over to Satan mean cursing them to hell; it is a remedial step, not a final sentence.

What if I am afraid my own faith could be shipwrecked? The fear itself is a good sign; the men in this verse were not afraid, they were careless. Christ keeps his sheep, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he keeps them by means, one of which is this warning. So do what verse 19 says. Keep your conscience clean: when it accuses you, do not argue with it or bury it; take the thing to the cross, confess it and turn from it. Keep near the means of grace, the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. And tell a trusted believer when you are drifting. Ships rarely sink in one wave; they take on water slowly, and someone who loves you can see the list before you can.

What does church discipline look like today? It begins quietly, as Jesus taught: a private word, then one or two others, and only then the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Most discipline ends at the first step, with repentance and restoration. Excommunication is the last step, for serious, unrepented sin or for persistent false teaching, and it is carried out by the church under its elders, not by individuals. It means the person is no longer received as a member or at the Lord’s Table. It does not mean hatred or shunning in every form: you may still greet them, and you should pray for them and call them back, warning them as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15). And it must never be used to silence the victims of abuse or to protect leaders; that is a perversion of it.

In a sentence. Timothy, my son, I am placing this commission in your hands, in line with the prophetic words once spoken about you, so that, strengthened by them, you may fight the noble fight, keeping hold of faith and a clear conscience; some have thrown conscience overboard and their faith has been wrecked, Hymenaeus and Alexander among them, and I have handed them over to Satan so that they will be taught not to blaspheme.

On a Tuesday. Guard your conscience. When it accuses you, deal with it quickly at the cross, before the rot spreads to your faith. Is there one thing you have been doing that you know is wrong and have stopped thinking about? That is where shipwrecks start. Name it to God today, and if it involves another person, put it right this week. And remember the call God placed on your life when you first believed: when the fight is hard, fight by it.

For worship. The gospel has come down to us through a long chain of trembling hands, Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, and on through every century, and not one link was strong in itself. Christ kept it. Paul knew what it was to be on a ship breaking up in the surf, and to see every soul on board brought safe to land as God had promised (Acts 27:24, 44). The same Lord stands by his people in every storm of doubt and sin. Even his discipline is mercy, a hand reaching after the wanderer, and the blasphemer who wrote these lines is the proof that it can bring him home.
verseByVerse.note: To hand someone “over to Satan” means putting him out of the church, in the hope that he will be brought to repentance.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,<sup>2</sup>To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine,<sup>4</sup>nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.<sup>5</sup>The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.<sup>6</sup>Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion,<sup>7</sup>desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.<sup>8</sup>Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,<sup>9</sup>understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers,<sup>10</sup>the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,<sup>11</sup>in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.<sup>12</sup>I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service,<sup>13</sup>though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief,<sup>14</sup>and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.<sup>15</sup>The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.<sup>16</sup>But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life.<sup>17</sup>To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>18</sup>This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare,<sup>19</sup>holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith,<sup>20</sup>among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.

2.title: One Mediator, Many Prayers
2.overview:
Paul turns to the church’s gathered life. First, prayer for everyone, including rulers such as Nero, because God our Saviour desires all people to be saved, and there is one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. Then conduct in worship: men are to pray without anger or quarrelling; women are to be adorned with good works rather than displays of wealth.

Finally the most debated verses: women are to learn, but not to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, and Paul grounds this in creation, not in Ephesian culture. Here, as throughout, the app holds the complementarian reading, respectfully stated, and insists that a restriction on a role is never a verdict on a person’s worth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul makes prayer the church’s first priority: every kind of prayer, for every kind of person, including rulers and officials, so that believers may live peaceful lives marked by godliness and seriousness. Such prayer pleases God our Saviour, who desires people of every kind to be saved and to come to know the truth. Paul grounds this in the heart of the gospel: there is only one God, and only one go-between for God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave his life to set people free, a message announced at God’s chosen time, for which Paul was made a herald and teacher to the nations.
verseByVerse.theology:
‘Desires All People to Be Saved’

Verse 4 has been read as all kinds of people, or — more often in the Reformed tradition — as God's revealed will set beside his decretive will. Either way there is one mediator, and his ransom is a substitute's (vv.5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Nero, the church was told to pray — and give thanks — for kings (v.2; cf. Jer 29:7).

Now: The aim is modest: a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified. Paul thought that enough to pray for.

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 2 sets the church’s public worship in order. First, prayer (vv. 1–7): the church is to pray for all kinds of people, even rulers who might persecute it, because God our Saviour wants all kinds of people to be saved, and there is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all; Paul was appointed to carry that message to the Gentiles. Second, men and women in worship (vv. 8–15). Men are to pray with holy hands, without anger or quarrelling. Women are to adorn themselves with good works rather than display, and to learn quietly and submissively; Paul does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, and he grounds this not in culture but in creation and the fall (vv. 11–14). He closes with a hard sentence about women being saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love and holiness (v. 15). At the centre of it all stands the one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself.

The setting. The false teachers in Ephesus seem to have been exclusive in outlook (perhaps thinking salvation was for a spiritual elite or for Jews), contentious in spirit, and particularly influential among some women (5:13–15; 2 Timothy 3:6–7). They may also have forbidden marriage (4:3). Paul’s instructions answer each of these: pray for everyone, because God’s salvation reaches all kinds of people; stop quarrelling; women are to learn, but not to take over the teaching office; and marriage and motherhood are good. When Paul wrote, the emperor was Nero (AD 54–68), who would soon begin persecuting Christians.

First of all, then, I urge. Paul has dealt with the false teachers; now he turns to how the church is to conduct itself, and the first item is prayer. Not strategy against the opposition, but prayer, and prayer for outsiders. First of all (prōton pantōn) means first in importance, not just first in a list: prayer is the church’s first priority in worship. Urge (parakaleō) is to exhort, to appeal. And then (oun) connects to chapter 1: in the light of the battle for the truth, the church must pray. A church fighting error without praying for the world has already lost something the false teachers wanted it to lose.

That supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made. Four words are stacked, and while they overlap they are not identical. Supplications (deēseis) are requests arising from need, the asking of someone who lacks something. Prayers (proseuchai) is the general word, the God-ward address. Intercessions (enteuxeis) carries the idea of approaching a superior on someone else’s behalf, a word used of bringing a petition before a king. And thanksgivings (eucharistiai), the surprising one, since those to be prayed for, and given thanks for, include Nero. Together they describe full, rich, many-sided prayer: not a brief mention of the government before the real business, but the church on its knees, bringing the world before the throne.

For all people. That scope governs the paragraph: everyone (pantōn anthrōpōn). No one is excluded from the church’s prayers: friends and enemies, believers and unbelievers, rulers and slaves, Jews and Gentiles. The context, which immediately names kings, shows that Paul means all kinds and classes of people, not least those we might be tempted to leave out.

For kings and all who are in high positions. Then verse 2 makes it concrete in the least comfortable way available. Kings includes the emperor; high positions (hyperochē) are places of authority and prominence: governors, magistrates, officials. This letter belongs to the reign of Nero. Paul is telling a church in Ephesus to pray, and to give thanks, for the emperor who would shortly use Christians as living torches in his gardens, and who would eventually have Paul himself executed. Paul does not say pray for good kings, or pray that God would remove bad ones. The instruction is unqualified, and it matches what he wrote to Rome about governing authorities (Romans 13:1) and what Jeremiah told the exiles about Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jeremiah 29:7). God’s people have usually lived under governments they did not choose, and this is the standing instruction.

That we may lead a peaceful and quiet life. Peaceful (ēremos) is tranquil, free from outward disturbance; quiet (hēsychios) is calm, settled within. The purpose is modest. Not that the church may prosper or gain influence, but peace and quiet: room to get on with living well, a setting in which the church can worship and the gospel can spread without hindrance. That is a smaller ambition than a modern church often has for its nation, and Paul thought it enough to pray for.

Godly and dignified in every way. Godly (eusebeia) is godliness, reverent devotion to God shown in life, a key word of these letters, used ten times. Dignified (semnotēs) is seriousness, respectability, a life worthy of respect. The purpose of peace is not comfort but godliness. Paul does not ask for quiet so that Christians can be left alone to enjoy themselves. He asks for it so that they can be holy in public, and so that their neighbours can see what a life given to God looks like.

Praying for the power that judged him. Later Paul reminds Timothy of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession (6:13). The church’s Lord stood before a Roman governor, was condemned by Roman authority and nailed up by Roman soldiers, and he prayed for the men who did it (Luke 23:34). A church that prays for Nero is doing what its Master did. And it prays through him: its supplications and intercessions reach God only because there is one mediator between God and men (v. 5), who lives for ever to intercede for his people. Our prayers for rulers ride on his prayers for us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should only pray for good rulers, or that praying for rulers means approving all they do. Nor does it mean the church’s goal is political influence. The goal is peaceful conditions for godly living and gospel spread.

What do I actually pray for a ruler I think is wicked? Pray what Paul prays. For their salvation first: Nero was beyond the church’s reach, but not beyond God’s, and the prayer that a persecutor might be converted was answered spectacularly in Paul himself. For wisdom and justice in their decisions. For restraint on their evil, and for protection of the weak who suffer under it. For peace, so that the church can worship and the gospel can run. And give thanks for whatever good they do, and for the order that even a bad government preserves, because the alternative is chaos. You can pray all this without pretending to admire them.

Does praying for rulers mean I must never oppose them? No. Praying for a ruler is not the same as agreeing with him. Christians may vote, campaign, protest lawfully and speak out against injustice, as the prophets confronted kings and Paul appealed to Caesar for his rights (Acts 25:11). Where a ruler commands what God forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). But prayer changes the spirit in which we do all this. It is very hard to hate a man you have prayed for by name every week, and very hard to put your hope in politics once you have spent time before the King of the ages.

In a sentence. My first and chief request, then, is that the church bring requests, prayers, pleas and thanks to God on behalf of everyone, including kings and all in authority, so that we may live calm, undisturbed lives marked through and through by godliness and seriousness.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for your head of state, your local leaders, and one public figure you find hard to like. Pray for their good and their salvation, and thank God for one specific good thing that has come through them. Notice what happens to your conversation about them afterwards.

For worship. The Lord who rules the kings of the earth is never threatened by them. He turned the heart of Cyrus, humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and used a Roman census to bring his Son to Bethlehem. And his church, praying for Nero in a house in Ephesus, was not a frightened minority pleading for its life. It was a royal priesthood interceding for the world, under a King whose kingdom no emperor could touch.
verseByVerse.note: Christians were to pray for rulers such as Nero, under whom they would later suffer.

parallels.desc: seek the welfare of the city

verseByVerse.quote: This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior. This is the prayer for all people (vv. 1–2). Good (kalos) is fine, right; pleasing (apodektos) is acceptable, welcome. The logic connects: pray for everyone, because God’s saving concern reaches everyone. God delights in such prayer, because it fits his own character as Saviour. The church’s prayers are to be as wide as God’s desire.

Who desires all people to be saved. Desires (thelō) is wants, wills, wishes. All people (pantas anthrōpous) is the same phrase as verse 1. God is not grudging toward sinners. He is a saving God, whose heart is open to all kinds of people, including kings who persecute and Gentiles whom the false teachers may have excluded. And this is one of the most discussed sentences in the New Testament, because it sits alongside the Bible’s equally clear teaching that God chooses and that his purposes do not fail. If God desires all to be saved, and not all are saved, what follows? Serious Christians have answered in more than one way, and honesty requires setting them out.

And to come to the knowledge of the truth. Knowledge (epignōsis) is full knowledge, recognition. The truth is the gospel (2 Timothy 2:25; 3:7; Titus 1:1). Salvation comes through knowing and believing the truth, not apart from it. This is why prayer and preaching go together: God saves people by bringing them to know the truth, and he brings them the truth by sending people to tell it.

The desire with tears in it. To see what God’s desire for the lost looks like, look at his Son. Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–42) and said, How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing (Matthew 23:37). Those were real tears over real people. The same Lord said that he would lose none of all that the Father had given him (John 6:39). Both are true in one Christ, and many Reformed preachers have pointed to those tears as the clearest window onto the sincerity of God’s call. The knowledge of the truth that God wants people to reach is, in the end, the knowledge of this Saviour.

Where Christians differ: if God desires all to be saved, why are not all saved? Arminians argue that God wills to save every individual equally, and that the difference lies in human free will: God does his part, and each person decides. Universalists argue that, since God desires it, all will eventually be saved. Verdict: Universalism contradicts Scripture’s plain teaching on final judgment (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). As for the Arminian view, Scripture distinguishes between what God desires in the sense of what pleases him and what he commands (his revealed will), and what he has decreed will happen (his decretive will). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11) and sincerely calls all to repent; yet he has, for wise and holy reasons, chosen to save some and not all (Romans 9:18; Ephesians 1:4–5). Two further points help. First, all people in context means all kinds of people, including rulers and Gentiles (vv. 1–2, 7), as all often means in Scripture (Titus 2:11; compare Revelation 5:9). Second, God’s desire here is the ground for the church’s universal prayer and preaching: we do not know who the elect are, so we pray for and preach to all, knowing that God is pleased to save through that means. The Reformed view does not make God less loving; it makes him the sovereign author of every salvation.

Two ways of speaking about God’s will. The distinction is not an evasion invented for this verse. It is required by any reading of the Bible that takes seriously both God’s sincere offer and his sovereign accomplishment. Scripture itself shows both at work in one event: the cross was the most wicked act men ever committed, which God commanded them not to do, and it was the very thing his hand and his plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). God genuinely takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; he genuinely commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30); and he has also purposed to save a people, and he will not lose one of them. We cannot see how all of this fits together in the mind of God. We are not asked to. We are asked to believe both, and to pray accordingly.

The pastoral force. What must not be lost, whichever reading you hold, is the pastoral force Paul intends. He is not writing a lecture on the divine will. He is telling a small, harassed congregation that there is nobody they may treat as beyond praying for: not the magistrate who fined them, not the emperor, not the neighbour who reported them. God’s disposition toward the world is not what a frightened church assumes it to be. Both readings agree that the church must pray for everyone and preach to everyone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is frustrated, wishing for what he cannot achieve. God works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11). Nor does it mean that God’s offer of the gospel to all is insincere; the call is genuine, and anyone who comes will be received (John 6:37).

If God has chosen whom he will save, why should I pray and evangelise? Because God ordains the means as well as the end. He has chosen to save people through the prayers and the preaching of his church, just as he has chosen to grow crops through farmers. Paul believed in election more firmly than anyone, and he was the greatest missionary in history; election was what gave him confidence that his preaching would not be wasted (Acts 18:9–10; 2 Timothy 2:10). You do not know who God’s elect are, and you are not meant to. You are meant to pray for everyone and tell everyone, and to trust that God will use it.

How can I be sure the offer includes me? Because it is addressed to you. The gospel does not say Christ died for the elect, find out if you are one. It says come, believe, repent, and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). You never have to look into God’s secret decree to know whether you may come. You look at his open invitation, and you take him at his word. Everyone who has ever come to Christ has been received, and you will not be the first to be turned away.

In a sentence. Such prayer is right and delights God our Saviour, whose will is for all kinds of people to be saved and to come to know the truth.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you have quietly decided will never be saved: the hardened relative, the mocking colleague, the man in the news. Ask yourself why you stopped praying for them. Then begin again today, and add one more name, someone from a group your church usually forgets. God’s desire is wider than our habits.

For worship. God our Saviour is not reluctant. He takes no pleasure in the death of anyone, he sends his gospel to the ends of the earth, and he calls kings and slaves alike to come to him. And he does not merely wish; he saves. Every person who will stand before his throne, from every tribe and language and people and nation, will be there because this God desired it and accomplished it, and gave his Son to make it so.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.

For there is one God. For gives the reason for praying for all (vv. 1–4). This has the ring of something already in circulation: compact, balanced, easily memorised. Paul is very likely quoting a confession the churches used. One God is the Shema, the first line of Israel’s faith (Deuteronomy 6:4), and it lands with force in Ephesus, a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis and whose riot in Acts 19 was a two-hour chant: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians. Since there is only one God, he is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 3:29–30), of rulers and slaves alike. He is not the tribal God of one group, and so the church must pray for every group.

And there is one mediator between God and men. A mediator (mesitēs) is a go-between, one who stands in the middle and brings two estranged parties together. Sinners are separated from a holy God; a mediator is needed who can represent both sides. And the word one is doing heavy work. It excludes every other candidate: not angels, not the speculative intermediary beings the false teachers seem to have been fascinated by, not Mary, not the saints, not a priest, not the church itself. Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Hebrews 8:6; 9:15; 12:24). There is a single point of access, and it is a person.

The man Christ Jesus. Then the astonishing phrase. Not the Son, not the Lord: the man (anthrōpos, a human being). A mediator must have a genuine footing on both sides, and Paul presses the human side because that is the side in question. To represent humans, the mediator had to be truly human; to bring us to God, he had to be truly God (Hebrews 2:14–17; John 1:1, 14). He is one person in two natures. Whatever else the incarnation achieved, it produced someone who could stand between. And note the tense of the phrase: Paul does not say the mediator was a man. He remains a man now, in heaven, with a body that bears the marks of the nails, and he always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25).

Who gave himself. Christ’s death was voluntary self-giving (Galatians 1:4; 2:20; Titus 2:14). The phrase rules out any picture of a reluctant victim. He was not taken; he handed himself over, and he said he had authority both to lay his life down and to take it up again (John 10:18). The ransom was a gift, not a seizure.

As a ransom for all. The word is antilytron, found nowhere in Greek before this: lytron, a ransom price, the word Jesus used of himself (Mark 10:45), with anti, in place of, fixed on the front. A substitute-ransom: a ransom price paid in place of another. Jesus did not merely pay for us; he stood where we were standing. It is substitutionary, and this is penal substitution: he bore the penalty we owed, to set us free. For (hyper) is on behalf of; all (pantōn) picks up verses 1 and 4.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many hold that Christ died for every individual equally, making salvation possible for all, with each person’s decision determining whether it becomes effective. Verdict: In context, all means all kinds of people, Jews and Gentiles, rulers and subjects (vv. 1–2, 7), as when Revelation 5:9 says he ransomed people “from every tribe and language and people and nation.” Scripture teaches that Christ’s death was a real ransom that actually frees those for whom it was paid, not a mere possibility. He laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), for the church (Ephesians 5:25), for many (Mark 10:45). A ransom paid for someone who is never released would be a ransom wasted. This is definite atonement: Christ died with the intention and effect of saving all whom the Father had given him. Yet his death is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and so the gospel is to be offered freely and sincerely to every person.

Which is the testimony given at the proper time. Testimony (martyrion) is witness: Christ’s self-giving is God’s witness to his saving purpose. At the proper time (kairois idiois) is literally at its own appointed seasons. Kairos is the right moment, not merely a date. History was not marking time until something happened; it was being brought to a particular hour. At the right moment God sent his Son, the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4), and now in this age the message is proclaimed (Titus 1:3).

What it does not mean. One mediator does not mean believers cannot pray for one another; Paul has just commanded intercession (v. 1). Praying for others is not mediating salvation; Christ alone does that. And the man Christ Jesus does not mean he is only a man; he is the eternal Son made man.

To whom was the ransom paid? Not to the devil, as some early writers suggested, as if God owed Satan anything. The ransom was paid to the justice of God. Our debt was to God’s law, which we had broken, and the penalty was death (Romans 6:23). Christ paid it by bearing that penalty himself, so that God could be both just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The Father did not extract the price from an unwilling Son, and the Son did not buy a reluctant Father’s love. The Father so loved the world that he gave, and the Son gave himself. The whole Trinity planned and paid the ransom.

Can I pray to Mary or the saints to help me? No, and you do not need to. They were sinners saved by the same mediator, and they are not commanded or promised to hear our prayers. Scripture never directs a single prayer to anyone but God. More than that, you need no one to soften Christ toward you, because he is not hard. He is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, and he invites us to draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:15–16). Go to him directly. Ask fellow believers to pray for you, as Paul did; but bring your prayers to God through Christ alone.

In a sentence. For there is only one God, and only one go-between who can bring God and humanity together, the man Christ Jesus, who handed himself over as the ransom price in the place of all kinds of people: that is the witness God gave at the time he chose.

On a Tuesday. When you pray today, notice whether you approach God as if you need to make yourself presentable first, or as if you had no standing at all. Neither is right. You come through a mediator who has already brought you near. Begin your prayer by naming him: I come through Jesus Christ, who gave himself for me. And when you pray for someone who seems far from God, remember there is only one way to God, and it is open.

For worship. There is one God, and he is not far off; there is one mediator, and he is not a stranger. The eternal Son took our flesh so that one of us could stand in the gap, and he did not stand there as a negotiator but as a ransom, giving himself in the place of the captives. He is a man still, at the right hand of the Father, with our nature and our name, and he has never lost a single one of those he bought.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle. For this is the testimony of verse 6, the message of Christ the ransom. The ransom was for all kinds of people, Gentiles included, and Paul’s own commission is the proof that God meant it. He was sent specifically to the outsiders. Three titles, and they are not synonyms. A preacher (kēryx) is a herald: the man who announces a king’s decree in the public square, whose job is accurate delivery and who has no licence to edit. An apostle (apostolos) is an authorised messenger, one sent with authority. A teacher (didaskalos) is the one who explains and instructs over time. Announcing, authorisation, patient explanation: the three together describe the whole task.

Appointed. Note the verb (tithēmi, set, placed). God placed Paul in this ministry. Set that against 1:7, where the men causing the trouble were desiring to be teachers of the law. One man was placed; the others placed themselves. The whole difference between apostolic ministry and religious ambition is in the voice of that verb, and it explains why Paul can insist on his credentials in one breath and call himself the foremost of sinners in the next. He is not defending a position he took.

(I am telling the truth, I am not lying). The parenthesis is the strange thing in the verse, a solemn assertion like Romans 9:1. Nobody had accused him in this sentence. Why the protest? Because of what he has just claimed, and where. That God desires all to be saved, that the ransom was for all kinds of people, and that Paul is teacher of the Gentiles: these were the fighting words of his ministry. He had been mobbed in Jerusalem for less; the crowd listened to him until the word Gentiles, and then shouted for his death (Acts 22:21–22). The false teachers in Ephesus wanted to be teachers of the law (1:7), and the church needed to hear Paul’s credentials affirmed. The protest tells us that even here, late in his life, this was still the contested ground.

A teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. Paul’s special calling was to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9; Acts 9:15). In faith and truth could mean faithfully and truthfully, or teaching the faith and the truth. Either way, it is not in speculation, which is what the rivals dealt in (1:4). The two nouns are the atmosphere his teaching is conducted in: trust toward God, and honesty about what is actually so.

The herald’s voice is Christ’s. A herald speaks in another’s name, and Paul knew whose. Writing to this same church, he said that Christ came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near (Ephesians 2:17). The Gentiles of Ephesus never saw Jesus in Galilee, yet Paul says Christ preached to them, because when his herald announced the ransom, the King himself was speaking. The risen Lord who stopped him on the Damascus road and sent him to open the eyes of the Gentiles (Acts 26:16–18) was making his own voice heard through him in every market square.

What he will fight for. There is something quietly moving in it. The man who has just called himself the foremost of sinners, and who elsewhere refuses to defend his own reputation, will fight for this. He does not much mind what people think of him. He minds a great deal that they believe the Gentiles are genuinely included. And if you are not Jewish, he was fighting for you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only apostles may share the gospel. All believers are witnesses. But the apostolic office was unique and foundational, and it has not continued.

Does God still call people to preach? Yes, though not as apostles. The church still needs heralds and teachers, and God still gives them (Ephesians 4:11; Romans 10:14–15). A call to preach is not normally a voice or a vision. It is a desire for the work, the gifts and character Scripture requires (3:1–7), and the recognition of the church, which tests a man and sets him apart. If you sense that desire, talk to your elders, ask them to test you, and take every opportunity to serve and learn. And whether or not you are called to preach, you are called to speak of Christ to the people around you.

In a sentence. And this is why I was made a herald and an apostle (I am speaking the truth, not lying), a teacher of the nations in faith and truth.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is for every nation. Pray for one people group that has little gospel witness, by name: look one up if you need to. And think of the nations that have come to your own street, the family from overseas, the international student, the colleague from another faith. A herald announces the King’s message to whoever is in the square.

For worship. The King has sent heralds to every nation, because the ransom was paid for people from every nation. The persecutor of the church became the teacher of the Gentiles, and a message that began in a corner of Judea has reached the ends of the earth. Every believer from the nations is a living proof that God meant what he said, and that the one mediator gave himself for all kinds of people, even us.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:8–15 – Men and Women in the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul addresses conduct in the church’s gatherings. Men are to pray with clean lives, not in anger or dispute. Women are to dress with modesty and good sense, making good works rather than expensive display their adornment. Women are to learn quietly and submissively, and Paul does not allow them to teach men or hold authority over them in the church. He bases this on the order of creation, Adam first, and on the account of the fall, in which Eve was the one deceived. Yet women will be kept safe through bearing children, if they persevere in faith, love and holiness with self-control.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Contested Passage, Read Slowly

The crux of verse 12 is authentein; the ESV and the historic Reformed consensus read it as plain authority, restricted rather than abused, and Paul grounds it in the order of creation (vv.13–14) — an order that concerns function, not worth (Gen 1:27; Gal 3:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The braided hair, gold and pearls of verse 9 imported social rank into the assembly; Paul replaces that currency with good works, which nobody can outspend.

Now: Whatever a church concludes about who teaches, a restriction on a function is never a verdict on a person.

verseByVerse.quote: I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;
verseByVerse.commentary:
I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;

I desire then. Desire (boulomai) is to will, to intend, a word of authoritative direction. Paul is not offering a preference but giving an apostolic instruction. And then draws it out of what he has just said: since God desires all to be saved, and there is one mediator, here is how the church is to pray.

That in every place. In every place likely means every place where the church gathers, all the house churches in and around Ephesus, and beyond them the churches generally (1 Corinthians 1:2). There is an echo of Malachi’s promise that in every place incense will be offered to God’s name among the nations (Malachi 1:11). Paul is not describing a local Ephesian arrangement but what he expects of the churches everywhere, which matters for how his instructions to men and women are read.

The men should pray. The men (tous andras) are males specifically, not people in general. Paul now addresses men and women in turn. Men are to lead the congregation in public prayer. This does not forbid women from praying in church (1 Corinthians 11:5), but it gives men a particular responsibility to lead. And it is a responsibility many men leave to others: the prayer meeting in many churches is attended mostly by women. Paul’s first instruction to Christian men is not to take charge but to pray.

Lifting holy hands. The posture is the ordinary one of the ancient world: standing, hands raised and open, palms up. Jews prayed like this (1 Kings 8:22; Psalm 28:2; 141:2), and so did early Christians; it is the natural attitude of someone asking. Nothing here forbids kneeling or bowing, which the Bible also describes. The adjective is where the weight falls: holy (hosios, pure, devout). Hands lifted to God must be clean from sin. God told Israel that when they spread out their hands he would hide his eyes, because their hands were full of blood (Isaiah 1:15).

Without anger or quarreling. And Paul immediately says what would make the hands unholy, and it is not what we might expect. Not ritual impurity. Not scandalous sin. Anger (orgē) is settled wrath, resentment. Quarrelling (dialogismos) is disputing, argument, or the internal churn of a man rehearsing his case. The hands are disqualified by the state of the man’s relationships. The false teaching had stirred up controversy (1:4; 6:4–5), and men in Ephesus were apparently carrying that into worship. So the picture is a congregation in which the men stand with hands lifted while carrying grievances against each other, and Paul says the raised hands do not compensate for it.

The same track. This is the consistent biblical order and it never changes. Leave your gift at the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift (Matthew 5:23–24). Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone (Mark 11:25). Husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, so that your prayers may not be hindered (1 Peter 3:7). Worship does not run on a separate track from how you treat people; it runs on the same track, and a blockage in one is a blockage in the other. And there is a plain, unglamorous test here for any Christian man. If your praying feels obstructed, the first place to look is not your technique or your discipline. It is whether there is somebody you are angry with.

The one who can ascend the hill. Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? asks Psalm 24, and answers: he who has clean hands and a pure heart (Psalm 24:3–4). Only one man has ever fully answered that description. Our high priest is holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26), and he has gone into the true sanctuary on our behalf. That is why men can lift their hands in every place, as Malachi foresaw: not because they have qualified themselves, but because the one mediator has opened the way and they come in his name. Holy hands are not hands that never sinned. They are hands that have been cleansed by him and are no longer clenched against a brother.

What it does not mean. It does not require raising hands in every prayer; the point is holiness, not posture. Nor does it mean women never pray in public; it addresses men’s particular failing and responsibility.

May women pray aloud in church? Yes. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in the gatherings at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:5), and in Acts the women were praying with the apostles before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). What this verse does is lay a particular duty on the men: to lead in prayer, and to do it with clean hands. A church where only women pray has not obeyed this verse, and a church where women are silenced from praying has misread it.

What if I want to be reconciled and the other person refuses? Then do what lies with you, and leave the rest with God. Paul’s own limit is realistic: as far as it depends on you, be at peace (Romans 12:18). Go to them, admit your part honestly without excusing it, forgive them from the heart whether or not they ask, and refuse to nurse the grievance or talk about it to others. If they still will not be reconciled, your hands can be holy even though the relationship is broken, because what defiles them is your anger, not their refusal. Keep praying for them. And if the conflict involves abuse or danger, reconciliation does not mean putting yourself back in harm’s way; forgiveness and safety can go together.

In a sentence. So it is my instruction that wherever the church meets, the men should lead in prayer, lifting up hands that are holy, free from anger and arguing.

On a Tuesday. Is there resentment in your heart toward someone in your church, or your home? Deal with it before you next lead or join in prayer: a phone call, a message, an apology, or at the very least an honest prayer of forgiveness. And men, if your church has a prayer meeting, go to it this week.

For worship. The hands that were lifted up for us were holy. Christ prayed for his enemies with his arms stretched out on the cross, and he did it without anger and without quarrelling: Father, forgive them. Because his hands were pierced, ours are washed, and we may lift them to the Father in his name, a family at peace with God and learning to be at peace with each other.
verseByVerse.note: Standing with raised hands was a common posture for prayer.

parallels.desc: the lifting up of my hands

verseByVerse.quote: likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.

Likewise also that women should adorn themselves. Likewise (hōsautōs) ties this to verse 8: as the men have their besetting problem in the assembly, anger, so the women have theirs, display. Both address what was actually going wrong in that room. Adorn (kosmeō, from which comes cosmetic) is to arrange, to make beautiful. Paul is not against beauty; he directs it.

In respectable apparel. Respectable (kosmios) is orderly, well-arranged, decent, from the same root as adorn: Paul is saying, let your adornment be adorned. Clothing appropriate to the gathering of God’s people.

With modesty and self-control. Modesty (aidōs) is a sense of shame in the good sense, reserve, the instinct not to draw improper attention. Self-control (sōphrosynē) is soundness of mind, good sense, the settled self-mastery that was among the most prized virtues in Greek moral thought. Paul is using vocabulary his readers admired. Both are inner qualities expressed outwardly.

Not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire. The specifics tell us what the problem was. This is not a rule against tidiness or against jewellery as such. In the first century, elaborately braided hair threaded with gold and pearls was a recognised display: it required slaves and hours to produce, and it existed to announce wealth and rank. Ephesus was a prosperous city and its church evidently contained women who could afford the display. Peter makes a similar point (1 Peter 3:3–4).

Ranking in the assembly. So the issue is not vanity in the abstract but the importation of social ranking into the assembly. A poor woman, perhaps a slave, entering a room where wealth was being advertised knew exactly where she stood. It is the same problem James addresses when a man with gold rings gets the good seat (James 2:1–4), and the same problem at Corinth, where the Lord’s Supper had become a display of who had more (1 Corinthians 11:21–22).

But with what is proper for women who profess godliness, with good works. Then the positive, which is the point of the whole paragraph. Profess (epangellomai) is to claim, to make a public declaration; godliness (theosebeia) is reverence for God. A woman who claims to worship God should be known not for her outward display but for her good works: kindness, hospitality, service, like Dorcas, who was full of good works and acts of charity, and whose widows showed Peter the garments she had made (Acts 9:36–39; 5:10). Paul does not tell them to dress down or to look poor. He tells them to change what they are adorned with. The ornament of a Christian woman is her good works, and that is a genuinely levelling standard: a wealthy woman can outspend a poor one on pearls, but nobody can outspend anybody on kindness. Paul has taken the currency of the room and replaced it with one everybody can trade in.

Adorning the Saviour’s teaching. Paul uses this same verb in Titus, where Christian slaves are to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in everything (Titus 2:10). A woman’s good works do not merely decorate her; they decorate the gospel, making the beauty of Christ visible in a city that knew only the beauty of money. And the works themselves are his gift: we are his workmanship, Paul told the Ephesians, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). The Saviour who came without outward splendour, with no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2), is still shown to the world in the plain kindnesses of his people.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all braiding, jewellery, or nice clothes. Rebekah received gold jewellery from Abraham’s servant as a sign of God’s blessing (Genesis 24:22), and the bride in the Song of Songs is adorned. The issue is extravagant display, status-seeking, and immodesty. Nor is it only for women; men too must avoid vanity. And it does not mean appearance is irrelevant; it means character matters far more.

How do I decide what is modest and appropriate? Ask three questions, of any outfit. What is it saying? If the honest answer is look how wealthy I am, or look at my body, it is saying the wrong thing in the house of God. Whom does it serve? Clothing that makes a poorer sister feel shabby, or that pulls attention away from worship, does not serve the church. And what does it cost, in money and in time? If your appearance absorbs more of both than your good works do, the balance is wrong. Within those questions there is freedom, and cultures differ. Do not judge other women by your own preferences, and do not make rules Scripture has not made.

Does this make women responsible for men’s lust? No. Every man is responsible for his own eyes and his own heart; Jesus put the guilt of the lustful look on the man who looks (Matthew 5:28), and Job made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). A woman is never to blame for a man’s sin against her, and no one may ever excuse harassment or abuse by pointing at what a woman wore. Paul’s concern here is different: that a Christian woman’s aim should not be to draw attention to herself, whether by wealth or by immodesty, but to adorn the gospel with a godly life. Modesty is a woman’s gift to God and to the church, not a fence she must build around men.

In a sentence. In the same way, women should make themselves beautiful with decent clothing, modestly and sensibly, not with elaborate hairstyles, gold, pearls or expensive outfits, but with what suits women who claim to worship God: good deeds.

On a Tuesday. Before you dress for church, ask: will this help others focus on God, or on me? Then ask the more important question: what good work can I do this week that matters more than any outfit? A meal for a new mother, a visit to a widow, a card to someone grieving. That is the adornment that lasts.

For worship. God himself is the great adorner. He clothed Adam and Eve with garments of skin after their shame, he clothes the lilies more splendidly than Solomon, and he has clothed his people with the robe of Christ’s righteousness. The church is being made ready as a bride adorned for her husband, and her fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). A woman adorned with good works is wearing, already, the clothes of the wedding.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.

Two contested verses. These two verses are among the most contested in the New Testament, and they should be read slowly, with the actual words in front of us, and with care for the many Christian women who read them with a lump in the throat.

Let a woman learn. Begin with what is easily missed because it sounds restrictive to us. Learn (manthanō, be a disciple, study) is an imperative: a command, not a grudging permission. In the first century it was a generous one. Formal religious education for women was not assumed in either Jewish or Greek settings. In first-century Judaism, women were often not taught the law at all, and some rabbis spoke with contempt of teaching it to a woman. Paul requires it. Whatever else this passage does, it puts women in the class rather than outside the door. Christianity elevated women as full disciples, as Jesus did when Mary sat at his feet and he said she had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:38–42).

Quietly. The word (en hēsychia) is in quietness, calmness, a settled spirit. It is the same word root as verse 2, a peaceful and quiet life, which Paul wants for the whole church. It does not mean absolute silence, as if women could never speak, but a receptive, peaceable attitude, not disruptive or contentious.

With all submissiveness. Submissiveness (hypotagē) is ordering oneself under. It describes the posture of any learner under teaching, which is how a disciple sits: submission to the teaching and to the church’s order, under the elders who teach. Not submission of every woman to every man, but a recognition of God’s order for the church.

I do not permit a woman to teach. Permit (epitrepō, allow) is present tense: I am not permitting, as my settled practice. Teach (didaskō) in the Pastoral Letters refers to the authoritative teaching of doctrine in the church, the work of elders (3:2; 4:11; 5:17; 2 Timothy 2:2). Paul is forbidding women to hold the teaching office in the gathered church.

Or to exercise authority over a man. The crux is authenteō, have authority, take authority, a rare word found only here in the New Testament. Some argue it carries a negative shade, to domineer or usurp, so that Paul forbids only overbearing authority rather than a woman’s teaching as such. That is a serious reading held by serious Christians, and it should not be caricatured. But two things weigh against it. The wider evidence of the word’s use in that period points to plain authority, without built-in negative force. And the grammar of the sentence tells: the two activities joined by or must carry the same value, and didaskein, to teach, is a good thing throughout these letters. If teaching is good, then having authority is good too, and Paul is not forbidding an abuse of a thing but restricting the thing itself. Man (andros) here means the adult males in the congregation. The two activities together describe the eldership: teaching and governing (3:2, 5; 5:17).

Rather, she is to remain quiet. Again en hēsychia: she is to have a quiet, receptive disposition, not taking the place of public teacher over men.

Where Christians differ: may women be pastors and elders? Egalitarians argue that this verse addressed a temporary situation in Ephesus (uneducated women spreading false teaching), so that once women are educated, they may teach and lead equally. Verdict: The complementarian view is the natural reading. Paul grounds the restriction not in local culture or women’s lack of education but in the order of creation (v. 13) and the account of the fall (v. 14), which apply to all times and places. The same principle appears elsewhere (1 Corinthians 11:3; 14:33–35; Ephesians 5:22–33), and the qualifications for elders assume men (3:2; Titus 1:6). This does not mean women are inferior: men and women are equally made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), equally heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), and equally gifted for ministry. Women may teach other women (Titus 2:3–5) and children (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), share the gospel, explain Scripture privately (Acts 18:26), serve as deaconesses or in a diaconal role, and exercise a vast range of gifts. The restriction concerns the office of elder: authoritative teaching and governing of the whole church.

The scope. Note the scope, which is narrower than it is often made. Paul is addressing the gathered assembly (in every place, v. 8) and the two functions named: authoritative teaching, and governing authority. He is not saying women may not speak: the same letter assumes they pray, and elsewhere he assumes they prophesy (1 Corinthians 11:5). He is not saying women may not teach at all: Priscilla, with her husband Aquila, took Apollos aside and explained the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26); Timothy’s own faith came through his mother and grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5); and older women are commanded to teach younger ones (Titus 2:3–4).

Every disciple sits at one Teacher’s feet. Whatever the order of the assembly, it is ordered under Christ. Jesus told his disciples not to be called rabbi, for they have one teacher, and they are all brothers (Matthew 23:8). An elder does not teach his own word but Christ’s, as an under-shepherd answerable to the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:1–4). So the woman who learns in quietness and the man who teaches are both, first and last, disciples of the same Lord. The authority Paul restricts was never a man’s possession to boast of; it is a stewardship of Christ’s word, and teacher and hearer alike will give account to him.

So may women be pastors or elders? The more likely reading is no. Paul grounds the restriction in creation, Adam was formed first, then Eve (v. 13), not in the culture of Ephesus, and in the next chapter an overseer must be the husband of one wife (3:2). The office of elder, with its authoritative teaching and governing of the church, belongs to qualified men. Egalitarian Christians read the verse as a temporary restriction on uneducated women in Ephesus; but Paul does not argue from their lack of education.

What of a woman teaching a Sunday school class, leading a Bible study or reporting on mission? Complementarians draw the line at the authoritative teaching of the gathered church and the office of elder, and churches apply it with some differences. Women may teach women and children (Titus 2:3–4), share their testimony, and explain the faith in many settings, as Priscilla did privately with her husband (Acts 18:26). Many churches also welcome women to teach mixed groups under the elders’ oversight, as long as they are not exercising the elder’s authority. The aim is to honour both the gifts God gives women and the order he has set.

Doesn’t this make women second-class Christians? No, and a church where it feels that way has misunderstood it. A restriction on a function is not a verdict on a person. Within the Trinity, the Son submits to the Father, and he is not less God (1 Corinthians 11:3; 15:28); within the church, the members submit to their elders, and they are not lesser Christians (Hebrews 13:17). The New Testament is full of women honoured for their faith and service: the women who stayed at the cross when the men fled, and were first at the empty tomb; Lydia, whose home became the church at Philippi; Phoebe, servant of the church at Cenchreae and bearer of the letter to the Romans; Priscilla, named before her husband; the women who laboured side by side with Paul in the gospel (Philippians 4:3). Eldership is one calling. The church depends on a thousand others, and on the women who fill them.

What about Deborah, Phoebe and Junia? Deborah was a prophetess and judge in Israel at a time when, as the story itself notes, the men were failing to lead (Judges 4:4–9); she is honoured, but the priesthood of Israel remained male, and her story is not about the office of elder in the church. Phoebe was a servant (diakonos) of her church, likely a deaconess, and Paul commends her warmly (Romans 16:1–2); serving in that way is not the teaching and governing office of elder. Junia (Romans 16:7) is described as well known to the apostles, or well known among them; even if she is called an apostle, the word is used there in the broader sense of a sent messenger or missionary, not one of the Twelve or Paul. None of them overturns the reason Paul gives, which is rooted in creation.

What if a man uses these verses to control or abuse? Then he is defying them. Paul has just told men to lift holy hands without anger; he will require elders to be gentle, not violent and not quarrelsome (3:3); he tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). Headship in Scripture is self-giving love and responsibility, never domination. This passage concerns the office of elder in the church; it does not put every woman under every man. Abuse is never tolerated: a woman being harmed should seek safety and tell the authorities and her church leaders, and a church that protects an abuser or tells his victim to submit to him has betrayed Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women may never speak in church, never pray aloud, never share a testimony, or never teach anyone. It does not mean women must submit to every man. It does not mean women’s gifts are lesser, or that women are more easily deceived by nature. It is about the office of teaching and governing elders in the church.

In a sentence. Women should be taught, with a calm and receptive spirit, accepting the church’s order; I do not allow a woman to hold the office of teaching and exercising authority over the men of the church; rather, she should keep a quiet disposition.

On a Tuesday. If you are a woman, use the gifts God has given you in every way Scripture opens to you, and there are many: teaching women and children, hospitality, mercy, counsel, evangelism, prayer, administration, music, care for the sick. If you are a man in leadership, encourage and train women to serve, make sure they are well taught, ask their counsel, and honour them publicly. If your church has never thanked the women who keep it running, start.

For worship. The God who designed men and women is wise, and his order is not a cage but a gift. Christ, who has all authority in heaven and on earth, used it to wash his disciples’ feet; he welcomed Mary to sit at his feet as a disciple; he appeared first to women on the morning of his resurrection and sent them to tell the apostles. In his church every gift is his, every member is honoured, and every office, from the least to the greatest, is a way of serving the one who served us all.

verseByVerse.quote: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.

For Adam was formed first, then Eve. The word to watch is the first one: for. Paul is giving his grounds for verse 12, and they determine how far the instruction reaches. He does not appeal to Ephesian culture, or to the education available to women, or to the false teaching in that city, all of which would have been available to him and would have limited the application to that situation. He goes to Genesis. Formed (plassō) is moulded, shaped, as a potter shapes clay, the verb used in the Greek translation of Genesis 2:7. Paul’s first reason is the order of creation: God made Adam first and then made Eve from him and for him as his helper (Genesis 2:18–23; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). In Scripture, the firstborn carries responsibility for leading. This reason comes from before the fall, so it is not a result of sin or culture, but part of God’s good design.

Order, not worth. In Scripture, order in creation carries weight. It is the same logic Paul uses at 1 Corinthians 11, and it is about ordering, not worth. Genesis is emphatic that both are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and Paul is emphatic that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Galatians 3:28). Whatever verse 13 establishes, it cannot mean women are lesser, because the same apostle denies it. And the word helper, which Genesis uses of Eve, is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself, the helper of Israel (Psalm 33:20; 121:1–2). It is not the title of a servant but of one who brings what is lacking.

And Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived. Deceived (apataō) is tricked, misled, intensified in the second case as exapataō, thoroughly deceived. Paul’s second reason comes from the fall (Genesis 3:1–6, 13). This is harder, and it should not be read as a claim that women are more gullible. Paul nowhere says that, and elsewhere he lays the fall squarely at Adam’s door, twice, in the passages where he is assigning responsibility (Romans 5:12–19; 1 Corinthians 15:22).

What happened in the garden. What the verse observes is what happened there. The serpent went around the order God had established, approaching Eve and bypassing Adam’s headship, and she was deceived. Adam, who was not deceived, went along with it anyway: he sinned with his eyes open, which made his sin, if anything, worse. He was with her (Genesis 3:6), and he said nothing. In the fall, God’s order was reversed: the woman took the lead, and the man followed and failed to protect. The result was catastrophe. Paul’s point is about what occurs when the given order is bypassed, and both parties in Genesis failed in it. The church should not repeat that reversal.

The man who did not stand by. Paul himself calls Adam a type of the one who was to come (Romans 5:14), and this garden scene shows why a second Adam was needed. The first man stood silent while his wife listened to the serpent; the last Adam stepped between his bride and the enemy and took the blow himself. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The first man hid among the trees; the second was lifted up on a tree in her place. That is headship done perfectly: not passivity and not domination, but a husband who protects at the cost of his life. The order broken in a garden was restored at a cross.

And became a transgressor. The phrase (en parabasei gegonen) is came to be in transgression: stepping over the line God had drawn.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are by nature more gullible or less intelligent than men. Paul does not say that; and men are deceived all the time (2 Timothy 3:13; Titus 1:10). Nor does it blame Eve more than Adam; Scripture places primary responsibility for the fall on Adam (Romans 5:12; 1 Corinthians 15:22). The argument concerns the order God established and what happened when it was overturned.

Two guards. Whatever conclusion a church reaches about who teaches, it settles nothing about the value, gifting or standing of the women in it. A restriction on a function is not a verdict on a person, and any congregation where it is felt as one has failed to read the rest of the letter. And Christians who read verse 12 differently generally do so because they weigh the words and the situation in Ephesus differently, not because they think less of Scripture. They are to be answered from the text, with patience, as brothers and sisters.

Isn’t the appeal to creation just Paul’s culture talking? That is exactly what Paul rules out by going to Genesis. When Jesus was asked about divorce, he did the same thing: from the beginning it was not so (Matthew 19:4–8). Going back to creation is the Bible’s way of saying, this is not a custom of our time, but how God made things. If Paul had argued from Ephesian conditions, we could set his instruction aside when the conditions changed. He did not. He argued from the way God made the first man and the first woman, and that has not changed.

How can there be order without inferiority? Look at the Trinity, and at Christ. The Son is equal with the Father in every way, God from God, and yet he delights to do the Father’s will: I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). He is not less for obeying. On earth he submitted to Joseph and Mary as a boy (Luke 2:51), and he was not less than them. Order is the way love arranges itself in a family. The world assumes that whoever leads is worth more, and whoever follows is worth less; the gospel has abolished that arithmetic. The greatest among you shall be your servant.

In a sentence. The reason is that God made Adam first and Eve afterwards, and that it was not Adam who was taken in, but the woman, who was thoroughly deceived and fell into sin.

On a Tuesday. Men, read Genesis 3 this week and notice where Adam was standing while his wife was being deceived: right there, silent. Godly headship is not control; it is the courage to protect, to speak and to take responsibility. Ask where in your home or church you have been silent when you should have spoken, or passive when you should have served. Women, ask how you can honour God’s design gladly, and where your gifts are most needed.

For worship. Blessed be the Son who met the same serpent in another wilderness and was not deceived. Where Eve was talked out of trusting God’s word, he answered every lie with what is written; where Adam said nothing, he spoke the truth and kept it. The serpent’s first lie was that God was holding back something good. At the cross God held back nothing, not even his own Son (Romans 8:32), and the transgression that began with a lie believed was carried away by the one who is the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

Yet she will be saved. This is one of the genuinely difficult verses in the New Testament, and the first duty is to say what it cannot mean. It cannot mean that women are saved by having babies. Paul has just said, in this very letter, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners and that there is one mediator between God and men (1:15; 2:5). Whatever verse 15 means, it does not add a second route. Yet (de, but): after mentioning Eve’s transgression, Paul gives hope. Saved (sōzō) is the normal word for salvation in Paul. She at first refers to Eve, and through her to women generally; the change to they in the next clause shows he means Christian women.

Through childbearing. Childbearing (teknogonia) is bearing children. It is one of the hardest phrases in Paul. Main readings: (1) women will be kept safe physically through childbirth, which killed a great many women in that world, though Paul’s word saved is normally spiritual, and many godly women have died in childbirth; (2) women will be saved through the childbearing, that is, the birth of the Messiah, the offspring of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15, which reads beautifully against verses 13–14, which have just been in the garden, though the article is not clearly emphatic; (3) women will be saved, that is, will work out their salvation and show its genuineness, by embracing their God-given role, of which motherhood is a central example, rather than seeking the role of elder. The third reading fits the context best: the curse on Eve touched childbearing (Genesis 3:16), and the false teachers were apparently forbidding marriage (4:3). Paul is dismantling a teaching that despised ordinary life, and against it he insists that a woman is not saved by escaping her circumstances but within them. Women need not take on men’s roles to be saved; they will persevere to final salvation in the path of godly womanhood, typified by motherhood, if they continue in faith, love and holiness.
