Reading 2 is also attractive, and the two can be combined: the Child born of a woman reversed the curse, and in him women’s ordinary calling is redeemed.

From she to they. Then the grammar does something significant that the ESV preserves: the verse begins with she and ends with they. Whatever the childbearing clause means, the condition attaches to a plural, to Christian women generally.

If they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control. The condition itself is the sentence’s real anchor. Not if they bear children; if they continue in faith. Continue (menō) is abide, remain. Salvation is not by childbearing as a work; the conditions are spiritual: faith (trust in Christ), love, holiness (hagiasmos, sanctification), and self-control (sōphrosynē, the same word as v. 9). Perseverance in these is the evidence of genuine salvation (Colossians 1:22–23). Whatever weight the first half carries, the evidence Paul asks for is exactly what he has asked for from everybody in this letter.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are saved by having children. Salvation is by grace through faith alone (Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 3:5). Nor does it mean that unmarried or childless women are second-class or cannot be saved. Paul honoured singleness (1 Corinthians 7:7–8, 34). Motherhood here represents the whole sphere of women’s God-given calling, not a requirement for every woman.

What is clear. It is honest to say that this verse is not fully clear and that good readers differ. What is clear is enough: no woman is saved by anything other than the one mediator, and the life that proves salvation is the same for her as for anyone: continuing in faith, love and holiness.

Where does this leave me if I am single or cannot have children? Exactly where it leaves every believer: saved by Christ, and called to continue in faith, love and holiness. Motherhood is a central example of a woman’s calling, not a condition of salvation. Some of the most fruitful women in the church’s history were unmarried, and Paul himself commended singleness as a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:32–35). Many childless women are spiritual mothers to dozens. If your childlessness is a grief, it is a real one, and Scripture does not dismiss it: Hannah wept before the Lord, and he heard her. But you are not less in his eyes, and your calling is just as real.

Does if they continue mean I could lose my salvation? No. The condition describes what true faith does, not a test it might fail. Those whom God has justified he will also glorify (Romans 8:30), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). But he brings it to completion through our continuing, and warnings like this are one of the means he uses to keep us. The person who is anxious to continue in faith is the person God is keeping. The one who should fear is the one who has stopped caring.

In a sentence. But women will be brought through to salvation in the path of motherhood and their God-given calling, provided they keep on in faith, love and holiness, with good sense.

On a Tuesday. If you are a mother, see your work as holy service to God, not a lesser calling: the nappies, the meals, the patient answers to the same question, the prayers at the bedside are where your faith is being worked out, and where God is at work. If you are childless or single, know that you are not less in God’s eyes; your calling is just as real. And whoever you are, thank a mother in your church this week, and especially one who is weary.

For worship. The woman who was deceived was given a promise in the same breath as her sentence: her offspring would crush the serpent’s head. Through childbearing, in the long line of mothers that ran from Eve to Mary, the Saviour came. He was born of a woman, carried and nursed and raised by a woman, and on the cross he made sure his mother was cared for. He has redeemed the curse at its root, and every woman who trusts him will be brought safely home, not through her own labour but through his.
verseByVerse.note: One of the harder verses in Paul. Suggested readings include: kept safe through childbirth; saved through the Childbirth, the birth of Christ; or saved while fulfilling her calling. It cannot mean earning salvation.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,<sup>2</sup>for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.<sup>3</sup>This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,<sup>4</sup>who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.<sup>5</sup>For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.<sup>7</sup>For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.<sup>8</sup>I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;<sup>9</sup>likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire,<sup>10</sup>but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.<sup>11</sup>Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness.<sup>12</sup>I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.<sup>13</sup>For Adam was formed first, then Eve;<sup>14</sup>and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.<sup>15</sup>Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

3.title: The Household of God
3.overview:
Paul sets out who may lead God’s household. Overseers (elders) must be men of proven character: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not lovers of money, managing their homes well, mature in faith and respected by outsiders. Only one requirement is a skill: “able to teach”. Deacons, who serve rather than teach, must meet the same standard of character and be tested first.

Then Paul says why it matters. The church is the household of the living God, the pillar that holds up the truth for the world to see. And the truth it holds up is Christ himself, sung in an early hymn: “manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit … taken up in glory.” The rules about wine and money exist so that the pillar stands straight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul calls the work of an overseer, or elder, a good and worthy aim, and lists what such a man must be. His life must give no grounds for accusation: faithful to his wife, clear-headed, disciplined, respected, welcoming, and able to teach. He must not drink too much, be violent or quarrelsome, or love money, but be gentle. He must lead his own family well, with children who respect him, because a man who cannot care for his own home cannot care for God’s church. He should not be a new believer, lest pride trip him up as it did the devil, and outsiders should think well of him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Character, Not Competence

Of some fifteen requirements only one — ‘able to teach’ — is a skill; everything else concerns what a man is, and the vices named are the kind a congregation cannot see for years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Overseer’ and ‘elder’ name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7).

Now: Verse 7 gives outsiders a say: what would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 3 sets out who may lead the church, at a time when false teachers had arisen, probably including some of the elders themselves (Acts 20:30). Paul describes two offices. The overseer or elder (vv. 1–7) does a noble work but needs proven character: above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach, gentle rather than violent or quarrelsome, free from love of money, a good manager of his household, not a new convert, and well regarded by outsiders. Deacons (vv. 8–13) serve the church’s practical needs and must likewise be serious, honest, sober, free from greed, sound in the faith and tested first; the women associated with them (either their wives or women deacons) must be similarly trustworthy. Then Paul says why this matters (vv. 14–16): the church is God’s household, the pillar and support of the truth, and that truth is the mystery of godliness, sung in an early hymn about Christ. The chapter that begins with job descriptions ends with a song, because the ordinary machinery of a church exists to hold up one glorious person where the world can see him.

The setting. In the New Testament, overseer (episkopos, from which come bishop and episcopal) and elder (presbyteros, from which come presbyter and Presbyterian) appear to be two names for the same office. Paul summons the elders of Ephesus and tells them the Holy Spirit has made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus 1:5–7 moves between the two words in consecutive verses. One office, two words: elder stresses maturity and dignity; overseer stresses the function of watching over the flock. Churches were led by a plurality of elders, not a single ruler (Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1; James 5:14). The later system of one bishop over several churches developed in the second century.

The saying is trustworthy. The second of the five trustworthy sayings in these letters (1:15; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). Paul is again quoting something already in circulation. It may refer to what follows, the nobility of the office, or, less likely, back to 2:15. Most take it as introducing verse 1.

If anyone aspires to the office of overseer. Two different verbs, and both are positive. The first, aspires (oregō), means to reach out for, to stretch toward something. The office of overseer (episkopē) is oversight, the work of supervising, watching over. Paul does not treat wanting this as suspicious. Register that, because there is a strain of Christian thinking that regards any ambition for office as disqualifying, the only safe candidate being the man who has to be dragged to it. It is right to desire this work, and it is not pride to want to serve as an elder, provided the motive is to serve Christ and his people.

He desires a noble task. The second verb, desires (epithymeō), is to set one’s heart on, to long for. Noble (kalos) is good, fine, excellent; task (ergon) is work. A work, not a title or a rank. Eldership is hard labour (5:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12), not honour for its own sake. Everything that follows in this chapter is about character rather than ability precisely because the job is not a platform but a labour. And in a culture where church leadership brought danger rather than prestige, the desire was a mark of devotion: the first men to be arrested when persecution came were the leaders.

A flock bought with blood. Why is the work noble? Because of whose flock it is. Paul told the elders of this very church to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). The overseer watches over people for whom Christ died, and that makes the job both splendid and frightening. The office itself is a gift of the risen Lord: when he ascended on high, he gave shepherds and teachers to equip his people (Ephesians 4:8, 11). A man who desires to be an overseer is asking to become one of Christ’s gifts to his church, which is a noble thing to want, and a humbling one.

Keeping the office. There is also a quiet dignity in calling it an office at all. Ephesus had just been described as full of men who wanted the standing of a teacher (1:7). Paul does not respond by abolishing the position or treating leadership as inherently corrupting. He keeps the office, affirms the desire, and raises the bar, which is the harder and better answer to the abuse of authority than pretending authority should not exist. The desire is welcome; the qualifications are not negotiable.

Where Christians differ: how should the church be governed? Episcopal churches have bishops over priests and deacons (three orders); congregational churches vest final authority in the members; presbyterian churches govern through elders in local sessions and wider courts. Verdict: The New Testament knows two ongoing offices in the local church: elders (overseers), who shepherd, teach and govern, and deacons, who serve practical needs (Philippians 1:1). Each church should be led by a plurality of qualified elders, men who meet these qualifications (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5). Apostles were a unique, foundational office that has ceased. Within this, churches differ charitably on how much authority the congregation holds and how churches relate to one another.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ambition for position is good. The desire must be for the work, not the power. Nor does it mean the desire alone qualifies someone; the qualifications that follow must be met and tested.

What does an elder actually do? He shepherds the flock: knowing the people, praying for them, visiting the sick, warning the wandering, comforting the grieving (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2–3). He teaches, in public and in private, and guards the church from error (Titus 1:9). He leads, with his fellow elders, in the decisions that shape the church’s life (5:17). And he will give an account for the souls in his care (Hebrews 13:17). That is why the work is noble and why it is heavy. An elder is not a board member who attends meetings; he is an under-shepherd of Christ’s sheep.

How do I know whether I should aspire to this? Begin with the desire, and examine it: do you want to care for people and feed them God’s Word, or do you want to be recognised? Then hold your life up against the list that follows, honestly, and ask others who know you well to do the same. Look at what you already do. Men who will make good elders are usually already doing elders’ work without the title: opening their homes, teaching a group, visiting the lonely, praying for the flock. Tell your elders of the desire, ask them to watch and test you, and be content to wait. The call is confirmed by the church, not by the man alone.

In a sentence. Here is a reliable saying: anyone who sets his heart on being an overseer is longing for a fine work.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your elders by name today. Their work is noble and hard, and much of it is invisible: the hospital visit at night, the conversation with a couple in crisis, the hours over a passage that you will hear in forty minutes on Sunday. Send one of them a note this week to say you are praying for him, and mention one specific thing he has done that has helped you.

For worship. Christ is the chief Shepherd and the true Overseer of our souls (1 Peter 2:25). Every faithful elder is a small reflection of him: watching, feeding, guarding, carrying. He did not wait to be dragged to the noble task; he came from heaven to do it, and he still watches over every sheep the Father gave him. He gives his church shepherds after his own heart, and when the chief Shepherd appears, every one of them who served well will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.note: “Overseer” and “elder” appear to be two names for the same office.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,

Therefore an overseer must be above reproach. The list begins with the heading that governs everything after it. Must (dei, it is necessary): these are requirements, not ideals. Above reproach (anepilēmptos) means not able to be taken hold of: there is nothing to grab, no handle by which he can be seized. Not sinless, which would empty every pulpit, but with no glaring, ongoing pattern of sin that could be fairly charged against him. Nothing available to be used against him. This is the headline; the rest of the list explains it.

Character, not performance. Notice how little of the list concerns gifts and how much concerns character. And then the single item that is a skill rather than a character trait: able to teach. One. Out of some fifteen requirements in these verses, nearly all concern what a man is, and one concerns what he can do. Any church selecting leaders by gifting, competence or platform has inverted the proportions Paul set, and given what chapter 1 says about men who wanted to teach without understanding, the emphasis is deliberate.

A life the flock can follow. The reason for the proportions lies in what an elder is for. He shepherds Christ’s flock as an example to it (1 Peter 5:3), and the sheep learn their Shepherd partly by watching his under-shepherds. Paul could say, Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). An elder’s marriage, his table, his temper and his teaching are meant to show the congregation, in small and imperfect measure, what Christ is like: faithful, self-governed, open-handed, truthful. A gifted man of poor character teaches one thing with his mouth and another with his life, and the flock usually believes the life.

The husband of one wife. Literally a one-woman man (mias gynaikos andra), and this is the most argued-over phrase in the list. Several meanings have been proposed: (1) he must not be a polygamist; (2) he must not have remarried after divorce or the death of his wife; (3) he must be married; (4) he must be sexually faithful to his wife, devoted to one woman. The fourth best fits the wording and the context. Polygamy was rare in the Greek world; Paul encourages remarriage of younger widows (5:14), which sits badly with a ban on any second marriage; and he himself was unmarried and commends singleness (1 Corinthians 7:8), so he cannot mean must be married. The phrase stresses marital and sexual faithfulness: a man of one woman in heart and conduct. It fits the tenor of the whole list, which is about present character rather than an audit of a man’s history. What the phrase requires is a marriage nobody can point at. And the qualifications assume that elders are men, which agrees with 2:12.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced and remarried man be an elder? Some churches forbid it absolutely; others ignore the question. Verdict: The phrase concerns present faithfulness and character, not merely marital history. A man who was divorced on biblical grounds (adultery or desertion by the other spouse, Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15) and has since lived faithfully may be considered. But a man whose divorce was sinful, especially recent, or whose marriage history brings reproach, would not be above reproach. Each case requires wise judgment by the church.

A widower and the past. A widower who remarried is plainly not excluded. And a man divorced long ago, before he came to Christ, may qualify if his life now is above reproach and his past is not a present scandal; the church must judge each case carefully, and must not pretend that a man’s history is irrelevant or that it is unforgivable.

Sober-minded. The word (nēphalios) means temperate, clear-headed, and is sometimes used literally of abstinence from wine. Alert, balanced, not given to excess. A shepherd who is not awake cannot see the wolf.

Self-controlled. The word is sōphrōn: sensible, prudent, of sound judgment, the soundness of mind Paul commended in the women of 2:9. It is a key word of these letters (2:9, 15; Titus 1:8; 2:2, 5): a man in possession of his own judgment, not driven by his moods or appetites.

Respectable. The word (kosmios) means orderly, well-behaved, of good arrangement, the same word as 2:9. A life that is not chaotic. His days, his finances and his commitments are in order, and people can rely on him to do what he said.

Hospitable. Literally a lover of strangers (philoxenos), and in the first century it was a serious matter. Inns were dangerous and often little better than brothels; travelling Christians and itinerant preachers depended on households opening to them. An elder’s home was to be one of them (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 1 Peter 4:9), which means his family bore the cost of his office. An elder whose home is closed cannot shepherd a flock, because the flock is mostly shepherded around tables.

Able to teach. The word (didaktikos) means skilled in teaching, apt to teach. It is the one gift-based qualification, and it distinguishes elders from deacons. Elders must be able to hold firm to the trustworthy word, to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). Not every elder must be a gifted preacher, but every elder must be able to teach sound doctrine, whether to a congregation, a small group or a troubled man across a kitchen table.

What it does not mean. It does not require that elders be married or have children; it describes how they behave if they are. Nor does it describe sinless perfection; it describes mature, consistent Christian character. And these qualities are expected of every Christian; elders must model them.

Does a terrible past before conversion disqualify a man? Not in itself. Paul, a former persecutor, wrote these words, and he had been the foremost of sinners. Above reproach describes the man’s present life and reputation, not a record with nothing in it. What matters is whether he has been changed, whether that change has been tested over time, and whether his past still brings reproach on the church: some offences, such as the abuse of children, rightly bar a man from office permanently, because the trust the office needs cannot be restored and the vulnerable must be protected. The church must judge with both grace and wisdom.

In a sentence. An overseer, then, must give no grounds for accusation: he must be faithful to his wife, clear-headed, sensible, orderly, open-handed with hospitality, and capable of teaching.

On a Tuesday. Use this list as a mirror for your own life. Which of these qualities does God want to grow in you? Pick one. If it is hospitality, invite someone to eat with you this week whom you would not normally invite. If it is faithfulness in marriage, ask what you are letting your eyes and your thoughts rest on. If it is self-control, name the appetite that is ruling you and take one concrete step against it.

For worship. These qualities describe a man, and there has been one man in whom every one of them was perfect. Christ was above reproach: which of you convicts me of sin? He was faithful to his one bride, the church, and gave himself up for her. He was clear-headed in the wilderness, self-controlled under every provocation, hospitable to sinners at his table, and the greatest teacher who ever spoke. Every elder is a copy, and every copy is imperfect; but the Original is the Shepherd of us all.

verseByVerse.quote: not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.

Not a drunkard. Four more, and they come in two pairs that describe how a man behaves when things are difficult. Drunkard (paroinos) is literally beside wine: one who lingers over wine, addicted to it. Drinking wine was normal in the ancient world, and the Bible does not forbid it; this letter will shortly tell Timothy to take a little for his stomach (5:23). What is in view is the man whose relationship with drink has become the governing fact about his evenings. Drunkenness disqualifies.

Not violent but gentle. Violent (plēktēs) means a striker, a bully, a man quick to use his fists. That such a thing needed saying about candidates for church office tells us something about the world Paul was working in. Against it he sets epieikēs, that hard-to-translate word from Philippians 4:5: gracious, reasonable, forbearing, yielding; the man who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed, who knows when the strict letter would do an injustice. An elder deals with people patiently, not harshly, not domineering over those in his charge (2 Timothy 2:24–25; 1 Peter 5:3).

The gentleness of Christ. Paul chose this word knowing whose it was. When he appealed to the stubborn Corinthians, he did it by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1), using the noun of this same word. Gentleness is not a temperament Paul happened to prefer in leaders; it is the character of the Lord they serve. The one who has the right to judge everyone did not insist on it among us: he would not quench a smouldering wick (Matthew 12:20), and he restored Peter with questions by a charcoal fire rather than a rebuke (John 21:15–17). An elder is to be gentle because the church already has a Shepherd who is.

Not quarrelsome. The word (amachos) is literally not a fighter, peaceable, and here it means with words rather than fists. Given chapter 1, this is pointed. Ephesus was full of vain discussion and confident assertion (6:4–5), and it would be easy to conclude that what the church needed was a leader who could out-argue them. Paul says the opposite. A man who enjoys the fight is disqualified from the office, however right he happens to be.

Not a lover of money. The word (aphilargyros) means without love of silver. Money runs through this letter: the false teachers imagining that godliness is a means of gain (6:5), the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils (6:10), the rich charged not to be haughty (6:17). Greed was a mark of the false teachers (Titus 1:11). Elders may be paid (5:17–18), but they must not be in it for money. A man who loves money will eventually be bought, and everyone will find out what the price was.

What they have in common. Drink, violence, arguing, money: each is a way of handling pressure or appetite badly, and each is invisible to a congregation until it is far too late. That is why the qualifications are for character rather than performance. You can assess a man’s preaching in twenty minutes; these take years to see. Ask his wife, his children, his employees and the people who have disagreed with him.

What it does not mean. It does not require total abstinence from alcohol; Paul later advises Timothy to drink a little wine (5:23). Nor does not quarrelsome mean an elder never contends for the truth; he must refute error (Titus 1:9). The difference is between a contentious spirit and faithful defence of the truth.

What if my pastor is harsh, controlling or a bully? Then he is failing one of the plainest requirements of his office, and it should not be excused as strong leadership. Elders are not to domineer over the flock (1 Peter 5:3), and a man who manipulates, intimidates, shames people from the pulpit or punishes disagreement is not gentle. If it is a single incident, speak to him privately and humbly. If it is a pattern, take it to the other elders, or to whatever wider body your church answers to. If you have been harmed, you are not being disloyal by speaking up, and abuse of any kind, spiritual, emotional or physical, must never be covered up to protect a leader’s reputation. The flock belongs to Christ, not to the shepherd.

Should Christians drink alcohol at all? Scripture permits it and warns against its abuse. Jesus made wine at a wedding, and the Psalms praise wine that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15). But drunkenness is sin (Ephesians 5:18), and wisdom may call for abstinence: if you have a history of addiction, if drink runs in your family as a destroyer, if you are with someone who is struggling, or simply for the sake of a weaker brother (Romans 14:21). Many godly Christians choose not to drink, and many godly Christians drink moderately. Neither should judge the other, and both should watch that the thing never becomes their master.

In a sentence. An overseer must not be given to heavy drinking, not a bully but gracious, not combative, and not greedy for money.

On a Tuesday. Are you known as gentle? Ask someone close to you, and listen honestly to the answer without defending yourself. Then look at your bank statement and your diary, and ask what they say about your relationship with money. If either answer stings, take it to Christ before you take it anywhere else.

For worship. The Lord of glory came gentle and lowly in heart. He had every right to the last inch of what he was owed and insisted on none of it. He would not quarrel or cry aloud in the streets; when he was reviled he did not revile in return. And the one man who never loved silver was sold for thirty pieces of it by a man who did. His gentleness is not weakness. It is the strength of a King who has nothing to prove, and it is how he shepherds us still.

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church?

He must manage his own household well. Manage (proistēmi) is to lead, to preside over, to care for, the same word used of elders who rule well (5:17). The household in the ancient world included family, servants and property. A man’s leadership at home is a testing ground for leadership in the church.

With all dignity keeping his children submissive. Submissive (hypotagē) is under order, obedient. With all dignity (meta pasēs semnotētos) could describe the father’s manner (he leads with dignity, not harshness) or the children’s behaviour (they are respectful). Probably the father: he maintains order in a dignified way, not by shouting or force. A house kept in line by fear would meet the letter of this requirement and fail its spirit entirely, and Paul has already ruled out the violent man in verse 3. This concerns children still at home and under his authority.

For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? Then the reason, put as a question that answers itself. The argument runs from lesser to greater, and it assumes something the modern church often does not: that home and congregation are the same kind of thing. Both are households, and Paul will call the church the household of God eleven verses later (v. 15). If a man cannot lead his small family well, he will not lead God’s family well.

Care for. Note the verb Paul chooses for the church, though, because it changes at the crucial moment. He does not ask how a man will manage God’s church. He asks how he will care for it (epimeleomai, take care of, look after), the same word used of the Good Samaritan taking charge of the wounded man at the inn (Luke 10:34–35). Church leadership is not corporate management but tender care. Managing a household qualifies a man for something warmer than management.

The Son over the house. Hebrews draws the comparison plainly: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house (Hebrews 3:5–6). An elder is never the master of the church, only a steward in a house that belongs to the Son, caring for brothers and sisters whom the Son is not ashamed to call his brothers (Hebrews 2:11). That is why the qualification looks at a man’s home. The church is to be cared for by someone who answers to its true Head, and he must first have learned at his own table what faithful, gentle care looks like.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must have perfect children who never sin, or that he is disqualified because an adult child has chosen to rebel. Children have their own wills. It means his household should show a pattern of godly, loving leadership, and his children at home should generally be respectful and orderly. Nor does it mean an unmarried or childless man cannot be an elder.

Handling a painful requirement. This requirement has caused a great deal of pain, and it should be handled honestly. It is not a guarantee that a good father’s children will all believe; Scripture nowhere promises that, and godly parents have watched children walk away since Genesis. What Paul is describing is the present ordering of a household still under a man’s charge: whether his home is a place of evident care and order, or whether it is visibly out of control.

The place where character is known. And the principle reaches past elders to everyone. The place where a person’s real character is known is the house he lives in. Public competence is easy to manufacture for a few hours a week; nobody sustains a performance in front of the people who see him tired. If you want to know what a man is like, ask how his children speak of him when he is not in the room.

Have I failed if my child has walked away from the faith? Not necessarily, and you must not assume it. Every parent fails in many ways, and it is right to confess those failures to God and, where it helps, to your child. But a child’s faith is not manufactured by parenting; it is the gift of God, who calls whom he wills. Adam and Eve had a perfect Father and walked away. Keep loving your child, keep the door open, keep praying without ceasing, and do not turn every conversation into a sermon. Many prodigals have come home years later, remembering a father or mother who never stopped loving them. Leave the outcome with God, who loves your child more than you do.

In a sentence. He must lead his own family well, keeping his children in order with a dignified manner; after all, if a man does not know how to lead his own family, how can he look after the family of God?

On a Tuesday. Fathers: is your leadership at home marked by dignity and care, or by harshness or neglect? The home is the first place of ministry. This week, pray with your family once more than you usually do, apologise to one of your children for something you got wrong, and spend an evening with them doing something they love. Children learn what God the Father is like by watching their fathers.

For worship. God is the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. He rules his household with perfect dignity and perfect tenderness, never harsh, never neglectful, disciplining his children for their good and running to meet the prodigal on the road. The church is his household, and he has never once mismanaged it. Every earthly father, and every elder, is learning to do in small what he does perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.

He must not be a recent convert. Two final requirements, and each is guarded by a warning about the devil: the only two places in the list where Paul explains what happens if you get it wrong. Recent convert (neophytos) is newly planted, our neophyte. A young believer, however gifted, has not yet been tested or matured. The church at Ephesus was about a dozen years old, so it had mature believers available. (In Crete, a younger church, Paul omits this requirement, Titus 1:5–9.)

Or he may become puffed up with conceit. The danger is named exactly. Puffed up (typhoō) is to be wrapped in smoke, clouded by a fog of pride: an inflation word, swollen with air, larger than the substance warrants. Quick promotion can go to the head. Give a new believer standing and authority quickly, and you may not be honouring him. You may be endangering him.

And fall into the condemnation of the devil. Two possible meanings: the condemnation the devil received (pride was the devil’s sin, which brought his downfall), or the condemnation the devil brings (accusation by the devil). Most take it as the first: the new convert, swollen with pride, might fall under the same judgment as the devil (Isaiah 14:12–15 and Ezekiel 28:17 are often applied to Satan’s fall, though their primary reference is to earthly kings). The sin that ruined the devil was pride, and a man promoted before he is ready is being walked along the same road.

A church in a hurry. This is a hard rule for a church in a hurry, especially a young or growing one that needs leaders now. Paul’s answer is that the shortage is not a reason to promote early, because the cost of doing so falls on the man himself.

Thirty quiet years. The church has a better example of patience than any rule. The Son of God, sinless from the cradle, spent some thirty years in a carpenter’s home before he began his public ministry (Luke 3:23), increasing in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52). Even then, the Spirit first led him into the wilderness, where the devil offered him every shortcut to glory and he refused them all (Luke 4:1–13). If the Lord of the church was content to wait for his Father’s hour, his under-shepherds can wait for theirs.

Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders. Then the most surprising qualification in the chapter. Well thought of (martyrian kalēn echein) is to have a good testimony, a good reputation; outsiders (hoi exōthen) are those outside the church. The church does not get to assess its leaders on its own. Paul makes the opinion of non-Christians, neighbours, tradesmen, employers, the people who see the man when he is not being religious, a formal qualification for office. Not that they must approve of his beliefs; the gospel will always offend. But they must not be able to say he is dishonest, or cruel, or unreliable. The world watches church leaders, and a man whom non-Christians know to be dishonest or immoral brings shame on the gospel.

So that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil. Disgrace (oneidismos) is reproach, insult; snare (pagis) is a trap, the word for a bird-snare. The devil sets traps for leaders, and a poor reputation can be one: accusations, scandal, ruined witness (2 Timothy 2:26). A leader with a bad reputation outside the church is already caught: everything he says about Christ is discounted by the people who know what he is like, and he cannot free himself by arguing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must be popular with everyone. The world may hate him for the gospel’s sake (John 15:18). It means his conduct should give non-believers no honest grounds for accusation.

How long is a recent convert? Scripture gives no number of years, and wisely, because people mature at different speeds. The question is whether a man’s faith has been tested by time and trouble, whether his character has been seen under pressure, and whether he has shown humility when corrected. In an established church that will usually mean years, not months. Paul himself, after his conversion, spent years in relative obscurity before his great missionary work began (Galatians 1:17–18; 2:1).

Should a famous convert be put on the platform straight away? No, and churches do great harm when they do it. A celebrity, an athlete or a public figure who comes to Christ is a cause for joy, and his testimony may be told. But to give him a pulpit, a book contract or a leadership role before his roots have grown is to do exactly what this verse forbids, and many such men have fallen publicly, to the gospel’s shame and their own harm. Love him by letting him be an ordinary church member for a good long while: learning, serving, being known.

In a sentence. He must not be a new believer, or he may be blinded by pride and fall under the devil’s own condemnation; and he must have a good name among those outside the church, so that he does not fall into disgrace and into the devil’s trap.

On a Tuesday. How do your non-Christian neighbours and colleagues see you? Let your daily life make the gospel credible. Ask the question honestly: what would they say about you if the subject came up? Are you the one who pays on time, keeps his word, does not gossip about the boss, and treats the cleaner with the same respect as the director? Then do one thing this week that would make a neighbour think well of the Christ you follow.

For worship. The Son of God never needed to grow out of pride, because there was none in him. He who was in the form of God did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself; and outsiders, even his enemies, could find no true charge against him. Because he humbled himself, the proud are judged and the humble are lifted up, and the devil’s condemnation will never touch those who are hidden in him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deacons too must be worthy of respect, sincere, not given to much wine or greedy for gain, holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. They should be tested first and serve only if blameless. The women (either deacons’ wives or women deacons) must likewise be dignified, not slanderers, sober and faithful in everything. Deacons should be faithful in marriage and manage their children and households well. Those who serve well gain a good standing and great confidence in their faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

The gynaikas of verse 11 may be deacons' wives (so the ESV) or women serving as deacons (cf. Phoebe, Rom 16:1). The passage does not settle it; the standard of character is the same either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Missing from the deacons' list is ‘able to teach’: they serve rather than teach, under standards just as demanding.

Now: Test first, then appoint (v.10) — the order most churches reverse, to their cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.

Deacons likewise. The word ties the second office to the first: same seriousness, different function. Deacons (diakonoi) are servants, ministers. The roots of the office are often traced to Acts 6:1–6, where seven men were chosen to handle the daily distribution of food to widows so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. Deacons care for the practical and material needs of the church, freeing elders to shepherd and teach.

What is missing. Notice at once what is missing from this list. There is no able to teach. That single skill separated the overseer, and its absence here defines the deacon’s work: he serves rather than teaches. Everything else, the character, the testing, the blamelessness, is just as demanding.

Must be dignified. Dignified (semnos) is serious, worthy of respect, the same root as the dignity of the overseer’s household manner (v. 4).

Not double-tongued. Literally two-worded (dilogos): saying one thing to one person and another thing to another. It is a precise hazard for men who move between households collecting and distributing, hearing everybody’s business. A deacon who repeats in one house what he heard in another destroys the trust the job runs on.

Not addicted to much wine. Literally not devoted to much wine. The same concern as for the elder, and for the same reason: a servant who cannot master his appetite cannot be trusted with other people’s needs.

Not greedy for dishonest gain. The word (aischrokerdēs) means fond of shameful profit, eager for it, and it is exact for the office. Since deacons handled the church’s money and gifts to the poor, they must be scrupulously honest. The temptation is obvious: funds passing through your hands with no ledger anybody checks. The disciples had a treasurer once who helped himself to what was put into the bag (John 12:6).

They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. This is the positive at the centre. Mystery (mystērion) is a truth once hidden, now revealed by God; the faith is the body of Christian truth. Deacons are not required to expound the faith, but they must hold it, firmly, and hold it with a conscience that is clean. That phrase has already appeared twice (1:5, 19), and it is the letter’s steady concern, linking belief and behaviour. A man may distribute bread faultlessly while carrying something unresolved, and Paul will not have it.

The mystery is a person. What exactly do deacons hold? Paul answers at the end of this chapter, when he names the mystery of godliness and it turns out to be a hymn about Christ: he was manifested in the flesh, and taken up in glory (3:16). The mystery of the faith is not a secret doctrine for insiders but the open secret of the Son of God made man, crucified, raised and reigning. So a deacon carrying bread to a widow is not doing something less theological than preaching. He is holding Christ while he does it, and his clean conscience is the evidence that his grip is real.

And let them also be tested first. The procedure: tested (dokimazō) is examined, proved, the assayer’s word for testing metal. Not tested by an examination necessarily, nor a formal probation, but by time: an observed track record. The church should know a person’s character before appointing them.

Then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless. Blameless (anenklētos) is unaccused, without charge, similar to above reproach for elders. Paul’s order is: observe the man, then appoint him. The reverse order, appoint him and find out afterwards, is how many churches actually do it, and it is how many of them come to grief.

What it does not mean. It does not mean deacons are junior elders or that the diaconate is a stepping stone. It is a distinct office of service. Nor does it mean deacons have no spiritual role; Stephen and Philip, among the seven, preached powerfully (Acts 6–8).

What do deacons do in a church today? Whatever practical service frees the elders to pray, teach and shepherd. In many churches deacons care for the poor and those in need, manage the church’s finances and buildings, organise care for the sick and the elderly, welcome newcomers, run the practical side of the Lord’s Supper and baptisms, and coordinate the many volunteers who keep a church running. The details vary, and Scripture leaves room for that. What does not vary is the spirit: deacons serve, and they serve so that the Word can run and no one in need is forgotten, as in Acts 6, where the widows were being overlooked.

Is serving less spiritual than teaching? No. The word deacon means servant, and the Lord of the church took that title for himself: I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:27). The seven in Acts 6 were required to be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to wait on tables. Carrying meals to a widow, fixing a leaking roof, counting the offering honestly and driving an old man to church are as much the work of Christ as preaching, and they are often how the gospel becomes visible to a watching world.

In a sentence. In the same way, deacons must be serious people, not two-faced, not given to much wine, not out for shameful profit; they must keep hold of the revealed truth of the faith with a clear conscience. They too should first be tested, and then, if nothing is found against them, they may serve as deacons.

On a Tuesday. Deacons serve quietly. Thank one this week, by name, for something specific, and ask how you can help them serve. Then look for one practical need in your church that nobody has noticed, and meet it without telling anyone.

For worship. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. He took a towel and a basin and knelt at the feet of the men who would desert him that night. Every deacon who carries a meal or keeps an honest ledger is following the steps of a Servant-King, who emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and whom God has highly exalted.
verseByVerse.note: Deacons (“servants”) cared for the church’s practical needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

Their wives likewise. The Greek simply says women (gynaikas), which can mean either wives or women; the language does not distinguish, and there is no possessive their in the text. So the verse is genuinely ambiguous, and the choice matters. Two readings are held by serious Christians: (1) the wives of deacons, who would assist their husbands in ministry; or (2) women deacons, often called deaconesses. In favour of the second: likewise introduces a new group, as with deacons in verse 8, as though a third category is being named; the qualities listed match the deacons’ own point for point; no qualifications are given for elders’ wives, which would be odd if deacons’ wives needed them; and Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1). In favour of the first: the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph, and verse 12 returns to male deacons as husbands of one wife, suggesting the women of verse 11 belong to them. The ESV reads their wives, with a note that the word can mean women. Both views are held by faithful complementarians, since the diaconate is not an office of teaching or governing authority over men.

Must be dignified, not slanderers. Dignified (semnos), as with deacons. Slanderers (diaboloi) are accusers, malicious gossips, and the same word is used of the devil, whose name means accuser. It is the counterpart to the deacons’ not double-tongued. Careless talk about people is given the devil’s own title, which should sober anyone who has ever enjoyed passing something on. Women who visit homes and care for needs hear a great deal, and must not spread what they hear.

But sober-minded, faithful in all things. Sober-minded (nēphalios), as with elders (v. 2). Faithful in all things (pistas en pasin) is trustworthy in every respect: the woman to whom you could give the keys, the money and the secret, and sleep well. The qualities are the ones this letter keeps returning to, and the same standard of character is required whichever reading of the verse is right.

Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. The same requirements as elders (vv. 2, 4): faithful in marriage, a good leader at home. The one who serves the household of God must first serve his own well.

For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves. Then verse 13, and it is a promise rather than a requirement. Good standing (bathmon kalon) is a good step, a good rank, good ground to stand on. Faithful deacons gain respect in the church, and perhaps a good standing before God.

And also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus. Confidence (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech: the boldness of a man who can speak freely, the word used of Peter and John before the council (Acts 4:13). Faithful service grows assurance and boldness in faith, toward God and in speaking to others. That is a striking thing to attach to practical service. Paul does not promise deacons promotion; he promises them assurance. A man or woman who has carried food to widows for years, quietly and honestly, ends up with a settledness in the faith that no amount of study produces on its own. Serving well does something to the server.

Boldness that rests on Christ. Paul is careful to say where the confidence lies: in the faith that is in Christ Jesus. Writing to this same church, he used the same word: in Christ we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him (Ephesians 3:12). A faithful deacon does not grow bold by admiring his record of service. He grows bold because, year after year, he has watched Christ keep his promises in the homes of the poor and the sick, and his confidence has moved off himself and onto the Lord he was serving.

Where Christians differ: may women serve as deacons? Some say the diaconate is for men only; others allow women deacons. Verdict: Either reading of verse 11 is within faithful bounds. Since deacons do not hold the authority to teach and govern the church (2:12), women may serve in a diaconal capacity, as Phoebe did. Churches should decide wisely and charitably, without treating the question as a test of orthodoxy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women serving in this way are elders. The teaching and governing office remains limited to qualified men (2:12; 3:2).

So may my church have women deacons? It may, and many faithful churches do; others keep the office for men and have women serve alongside in diaconal work without the title. Paul calls Phoebe a servant of the church and asks the Romans to help her in whatever she needs, for she has been a patron of many (Romans 16:1–2). Whatever your church decides, the work matters more than the title. The early church soon had women formally serving in this way, caring for women in need, visiting the sick and assisting at the baptism of women. If your church is divided on the question, do not let it become a cause of quarrelling; Paul has just said that a quarrelsome man is unfit to lead.

How do I share a prayer need without gossiping? Ask three questions before you speak. Is it mine to tell? If it was told you in confidence, it is not, and asking for prayer does not change that. Would they be glad to hear me telling it? If not, keep it between you and God. And what is my aim: that this person be helped, or that I be the one who knows? Often the best prayer request is the vaguest: please pray for a friend going through a hard time. Gossip disguised as concern is still gossip, and the devil’s name is on it.

In a sentence. In the same way, the women must be serious and respected, not malicious gossips, but clear-headed and dependable in everything. A deacon must be faithful to his wife and lead his children and household well. Those who have served well as deacons win a good standing for themselves and great boldness in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Guard your tongue this week. Do not repeat what was told you in confidence. When a conversation turns to someone who is not there, change the subject, or say something kind about them. And thank God for the women in your church whose faithful, unseen service holds it together: the ones who visit, cook, pray, teach the children and notice the lonely. Tell one of them.

For worship. The accuser’s name is slanderer, and his work is to spread what will wound. Christ’s name is Advocate, and his work is to speak for us before the Father, covering our sins rather than exposing them. He knows every secret of every household in his church, and he has never once betrayed a confidence or brought up again a sin he has forgiven. He is faithful in all things, and the accuser’s whispers fall silent before the one who has answered every charge against his people with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: “Their wives” may also be translated “women,” that is, women deacons; the Greek can mean either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he is writing: he hopes to visit soon, but if delayed he wants Timothy to know how God’s household should conduct itself, because the church of the living God supports and upholds the truth. And the truth it holds is great. Paul summarises the mystery of the faith in what sounds like an early Christian hymn about Christ: his appearing in human flesh, his vindication by the Spirit, his being seen by angels, his being preached among the nations and believed in the world, and his ascension in glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress

The church does not create the truth; it holds it up where it can be seen (v.15). And the hymn of verse 16 is six passive lines — God does all of it — from ‘manifested in the flesh’ to ‘taken up in glory’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a city of Artemis's hundred-odd columns, house churches are called the pillar of the truth.

Now: The chapter's rules about wine, money and reputation exist so that the pillar stands straight and the mystery of godliness can be seen from the street.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.

I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you. Here is the letter’s own statement of purpose, and the honesty of it should be noted. Paul intends to come. He may not. The letter stands in for his presence, and now stands in for it for the whole church in every generation. It exists because of a contingency, which is how a great deal of Scripture came to be written: Paul could not get to Thessalonica either, and we have two letters because of it.

So that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God. This verse is the key to the whole letter. Behave (anastrephō) is to conduct oneself, to live. Household (oikos) is house, family. Everything in chapter 3 has been building here. The overseer must manage his own household because the church is one; the deacons serve in it; and now the whole is named. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but an extended body, kin, servants, dependants, with an order to it and a head. The church is that, and it is God’s: God as Father, believers as brothers and sisters, elders as stewards (Titus 1:7).

Which is the church of the living God. Then two further descriptions, and they lift the sentence enormously. Church (ekklēsia) is the assembly, the gathered people. Of the living God: the adjective has teeth in Ephesus, whose great temple housed an image that could not move, and whose craftsmen made a living selling silver shrines of it (Acts 19:23–41). The Ephesians boasted that their image had fallen from the sky (Acts 19:35). The true God is alive and present among his people, and the Thessalonians turned to him from idols, to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

A pillar and buttress of the truth. Pillar (stylos) is a column, which holds up and displays. Buttress (hedraiōma) is a foundation, support, bulwark, which keeps it from shifting. The temple of Artemis, according to Pliny, had 127 enormous columns, each sixty feet high, and was counted one of the seven wonders of the world. Paul takes the architectural vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and applies it to a congregation meeting in houses. The church holds up the truth for the world to see and holds it firm against attack.

The right way round. Get the relation the right way round, though, because it is often inverted. The church does not create the truth or authenticate it. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own, and the church’s task is to hold it visibly in place, which is exactly what the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do.

A temple with a cornerstone. Paul had already told the Ephesians what this temple stands on: the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–22). The living God of this verse does not live in a marble shrine; he lives among a people joined to his Son. And the truth the pillar holds up is not finally a system but that same Son, who said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). A congregation is not primarily a service provider, a campaign or a community centre. It is a pillar of the truth to the degree that it lifts Christ up where the town can see him.

Where Christians differ: does the church stand above Scripture? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse to argue that the church, through its teaching office, is the infallible guardian and interpreter of truth, and that Scripture and tradition together form the rule of faith. Verdict: The church supports the truth; it does not create it or stand over it. The truth is God’s Word, which the church receives, guards, and proclaims (2 Timothy 1:13–14; Jude 3). When a church departs from Scripture, it ceases to be a pillar of truth, as the false teachers in Ephesus showed. Scripture alone is the final authority over the church (sola Scriptura).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church is a building. The household is people. Nor does it mean the church is the source of truth; Christ and his Word are.

Why do I need to belong to a local church? Because this is what God has made for you to live in. You cannot be a member of a household by yourself. The New Testament knows nothing of Christians who believe privately and belong nowhere: every letter is written to a gathered church or its leaders, and every command about loving one another, bearing burdens, submitting to elders, using gifts and sharing the Lord’s Supper assumes you are in one. Online sermons can feed you, but they cannot know you, visit you when you are ill, correct you when you wander or need your gifts. Find a church where the Bible is taught faithfully, join it, and commit yourself to its people.

What if my church is a poor pillar? Every church is imperfect, and Timothy’s church was troubled by false teachers when Paul wrote this. Do not leave over preferences, disappointments or ordinary weakness; pray, serve, and be part of the remedy. But if a church has abandoned the gospel itself, denying the truths about Christ that the church has always confessed, or refusing to submit to Scripture, it has stopped being a pillar of the truth, and you should find one that still is. The question is not whether the church is impressive but whether it is holding up Christ.

In a sentence. I hope to visit you soon, but I am writing this in case I am held up, so that you will know how people are to conduct themselves in God’s household, which is the assembly of the living God, the column and support that holds up the truth.

On a Tuesday. Think of your local church as it really is, with its weak points and its awkward people, and ask what it is holding up in your town. Then ask what part you play in that: are you a column that bears weight, or a spectator in the forecourt? Find one way this week to strengthen the household: a meal for a family, a conversation with someone new, an honest word to an elder about something that needs attention.

For worship. The living God has a house, and it is not made of marble. It is made of forgiven people, gathered in his Son’s name, and he lives among them by his Spirit. The temple of Artemis lies in ruins, a single reconstructed column standing in a marsh; the household of the living God still stands in every nation on earth, in rented halls and village chapels and crowded flats, holding up the truth about Jesus. Empires have fallen around it, and its foundation has never moved, because the one it rests on is alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness. We confess (homologoumenōs) means by common confession, undeniably, as all agree. Paul introduces what the whole church confesses. Mystery (mystērion) is a truth hidden in the past and now revealed. Of godliness (tēs eusebeias) is the truth that produces godliness, the revealed secret at the heart of true religion. And the opening may be a deliberate contrast with the cry that filled the theatre at Ephesus for two hours: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! (Acts 19:28, 34). The mob shouted the greatness of a goddess who could not hear them. The church confesses the greatness of a Saviour who came.

A hymn. What follows is rhythmic, balanced, and almost certainly an early Christian hymn or creed the churches sang, and Paul quotes it whole. It has six lines, each beginning with a verb in the same form, arranged perhaps in three pairs that contrast earth and heaven: flesh and Spirit, angels and nations, world and glory. The movement is from the incarnation to the exaltation. And every verb is passive: he was manifested, vindicated, seen, proclaimed, believed on, taken up. Christ is the subject throughout, and God is doing all of it.

He was manifested in the flesh. The truth at the centre of godliness is not a principle but a person: Christ. He (hos) is literally who. Manifested (phaneroō) is made visible, revealed, which means he existed before he appeared. And in the flesh: in true human nature, not a semblance, not a costume, but the real thing. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The first line rules out the two errors the early church had to fight: that he was not truly divine, and that he was not truly human.

Vindicated by the Spirit. Vindicated (dikaioō) is declared righteous, justified, shown to be in the right. He had been condemned by a Jewish council and a Roman court and executed as a criminal; the resurrection by the Spirit was the higher court overturning the verdict. He was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4; 1 Peter 3:18). Or it may mean in the spirit, in the realm of the Spirit, the new life of resurrection.

Seen by angels. The unseen world watched. Angels appear at every hinge of his life: the announcement, the birth, the wilderness, Gethsemane, the empty tomb, the ascension (Matthew 28:2–7; Acts 1:10–11), and perhaps the whole of his triumphant entry into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him (Ephesians 1:20–21; 1 Peter 3:22). The salvation they watched unfold, Peter says, is something they long to look into even now (1 Peter 1:12).

Proclaimed among the nations. Proclaimed (kēryssō) is heralded; nations (ethnesin) are the Gentiles. The message went to the whole world; Paul himself had been appointed its herald to the Gentiles (2:7).

Believed on in the world. Not merely proclaimed but believed. And this is the astonishing pair, because it is the least likely thing on the list. The other lines are about him; these two are about what happened next. A crucified provincial was announced to the empire, and people believed it. Paul is writing to a church in Ephesus that exists because that line came true, and so are you.

Taken up in glory. Taken up (analambanō) is the word used of the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22). The hymn ends where he now is. He reigns in glory at the Father’s right hand.

Textual note. Many later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read God was manifest in the flesh (theos) instead of He who was manifested (hos). In ancient manuscripts, the abbreviation for God (ΘΣ) looked very like who (ΟΣ) with a small line added. The earliest and best manuscripts read who, and this is the more likely original. The deity of Christ does not depend on this verse; it is clearly taught elsewhere (John 1:1; Romans 9:5; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8), and the hymn itself assumes his pre-existence.

What it is all for. Notice where this sits. Paul has spent a chapter on overseers, deacons, wine, money, household management and reputation: the unglamorous machinery of a working church. Then he says: and this is what it is all for. The rules about drink and quarrelling are not religious housekeeping. They exist so that the pillar stands straight and this can be seen from the street.

What it does not mean. It does not mean mystery is something unknowable or puzzling. It is a revealed secret, now openly confessed. Nor is godliness a technique; it is the fruit of knowing Christ.

What is godliness, and how does a hymn about Christ produce it? Godliness (eusebeia) is a life turned toward God in reverence, love and obedience: the whole person living before his face. Paul calls this hymn the mystery of godliness because godliness grows from it and from nothing else. You do not become godly by trying harder to be religious, as the false teachers taught; you become godly by beholding Christ. As we see the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The incarnate, risen, ascended Christ is not only the object of your faith but the pattern and the power of your new life.

In a sentence. Beyond all doubt, great is the revealed secret from which godliness springs: he appeared in a human body, was proved right by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was announced among the nations, was trusted throughout the world, and was taken up into glory.

On a Tuesday. When you are weary of the ordinary business of church life, the meetings, the rotas, the disagreements about small things, come back to this verse. Read the six lines aloud slowly. Then go back to the rota with these lines in your heart. And take one line a day this week, Monday to Saturday, and let it fill your prayers.

For worship. Great indeed is the mystery. The eternal Son was manifested in our flesh, born in a stable and laid in a manger. He was condemned by men and vindicated by the Spirit, raised in power on the third day. Angels watched him rise and saw him enter heaven. He was proclaimed to nations who had never heard of Israel’s God, and believed on by Greeks and barbarians, slaves and kings, in every corner of the world. And he was taken up in glory, where he reigns now, and from where he will come again. Great is the Lord Jesus Christ, and greatly to be praised.
verseByVerse.note: Probably an early Christian hymn or creed, with six lines in three pairs. “He” is literally “Who” in Greek; some manuscripts read “God,” others “Which” (ESV note).

3.text: <sup>1</sup>The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.<sup>2</sup>Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,<sup>3</sup>not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.<sup>4</sup>He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive,<sup>5</sup>for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?<sup>6</sup>He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.<sup>8</sup>Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain.<sup>9</sup>They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.<sup>10</sup>And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.<sup>11</sup>Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.<sup>12</sup>Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.<sup>13</sup>For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that,<sup>15</sup>if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.<sup>16</sup>Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
The Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, following teachers whose consciences are seared and who forbid marriage and certain foods. Paul answers with creation: everything God made is good and to be received with thanks, made holy by God’s word and prayer.

Then he turns to Timothy. Refuse silly myths and train yourself for godliness, which, unlike bodily training, pays out in this life and the next. Do not let anyone despise your youth; be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Give yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching. Let your progress be seen. Watch your life and your doctrine closely, for in this way God will save you and your hearers.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit has warned that in the last times some will desert the faith, drawn by deceiving spirits and teaching that comes from demons, spread by hypocrites whose consciences have been burned numb. These teachers forbid marriage and ban certain foods, though God made food to be eaten gratefully by believers who know the truth. Paul insists that everything God created is good and nothing should be refused if it is received with thanks, because God’s word and prayer make it holy.
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The Ephesian error was ascetic — impressive for what it gave up — and Paul answers it not by negotiating but with Genesis 1: everything God made is good, created to be received with thanksgiving (vv.3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Seared consciences are made one over-ruling at a time, through ordinary men saying what they know to be untrue (v.2).

Now: Grace at the table sanctifies a common meal (v.5): neither refuse the gift nor grab it, but take it and say thank you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 4 moves from the truth the church upholds (3:15–16) to the lies that attack it, and then to the kind of minister Timothy must be. Chapter 3 ended with a hymn to Christ: manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, taken up in glory. Chapter 4 opens with the opposite sound, the voice of spirits that deceive. First, the danger (vv. 1–5): the Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, led by demonic teaching passed on by hypocritical liars. These teachers forbade marriage and demanded abstinence from certain foods. Paul answers that everything God created is good and is to be received with thanksgiving, because it is made holy by God’s word and prayer. Second, Timothy’s own life and ministry (vv. 6–16): he is to teach these things, nourishing himself on sound doctrine and rejecting silly myths. He must train himself for godliness, which is worth far more than physical exercise because it has promise for this life and the next. The Christian labours because his hope is in the living God, the Saviour of all people, especially of believers. Timothy must not let anyone despise his youth but must be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. He must devote himself to reading Scripture publicly, exhorting and teaching, and not neglect the gift given at his ordination. He must give himself wholly to these things, watch both his life and his doctrine closely, and persevere, for in so doing he will save both himself and his hearers. The chapter that begins with demons ends with a young man reading the Bible aloud to a congregation, and that is the whole strategy of God against the lie.

The setting. The false teaching had an ascetic strand: it treated the material world, marriage and certain foods as spiritually dangerous. This may have mixed Jewish food laws with early Greek ideas that matter is inferior to spirit, ideas that later grew into Gnosticism. The teachers may also have believed that the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), so that believers should already live like angels, who do not marry (Luke 20:35–36).

Now the Spirit expressly says. The word is rhētōs: in so many words, explicitly, in plain terms. Paul is not inferring this from general principles or reading the mood of the times. He is reporting something the Holy Spirit has stated, through Jesus himself (Matthew 24:10–12; Mark 13:22), through Paul’s own earlier warnings (Acts 20:29–30; 2 Thessalonians 2:3), and through the prophets of the early church. And the tense is present: the Spirit says. The warning was not spoken once and filed. It still stands, and it still speaks to every congregation that reads it. There is comfort hidden in that. The church has never been taken by surprise by apostasy. Its Lord saw it coming, named it, and told his people in advance, which means that when it happens it is not evidence that he has lost control but evidence that he spoke the truth.

That in later times. The phrase (hysterois kairois, subsequent seasons) does not mean some distant final period at the edge of history. The New Testament treats the whole stretch between Christ’s first and second comings as the last days (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18). The later times began when Christ came, and Paul plainly treats what follows as a description of Ephesus in his own day. The prophecy was being fulfilled in the room where the letter was read, and it has been fulfilled in some room in every generation since.

Some will depart from the faith.
