What a person does with unstructured freedom is one of the more revealing facts about him, and it is worth asking of every retirement, every empty evening, every free Saturday.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should only help widows who pray constantly. It describes the character of a genuine widow who is to be enrolled for regular church support. Nor does “dead while she lives” mean a final verdict; she may still repent.

I am widowed and lonely. How can I set my hope on God when it hurts this much? Grief is not a lack of faith. The widow in this verse is not someone who has stopped feeling her loss; she is someone who has taken her loss to God, again and again, night and day. Setting your hope on him does not mean pretending; it means telling him the truth and asking him for help, as the psalmists do. Begin there, even with a few words. Let the church carry you: accept the meals, the visits, the invitations, even when it is hard. And know that your prayers matter. A widow who prays is not on the edge of the church’s life but at the centre of it.

In a sentence. The widow who is really in need, left on her own, has put her hope in God and keeps on praying and asking him for help night and day. But the widow who lives for pleasure is dead while still alive.

On a Tuesday. If you have time on your hands, retired, widowed, between jobs, ask what you are spending it on. Pick one person or one need to pray for daily this week, by name. And if you know a widow in your church, ask her what you can pray for, and then ask her to pray for you. She may be the most powerful intercessor you know.

For worship. If you are alone, set your hope on God, as she did. Your prayers are a real ministry to his church. He is the God who is near to the brokenhearted, the husband of the widow and the father of the fatherless. He has never once turned away a woman who came to him in the night. Anna waited and prayed for decades in the temple courts, and one day an old man took a baby in his arms, and she saw the redemption of Jerusalem with her own eyes. The God who answered her answers still. And the Son who rose from the dead is the living Hope for every widow, because he has promised that death will not have the last word over the husband she lost in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. Verse 7 is the hinge. Two things follow from it. First, these are commands (parangellō), not suggestions: Timothy is to issue them with the authority already established (1:3; 4:11). Second, the purpose is that they may be without reproach (anepilēmptos, giving no grounds for accusation), and the word is the one used of overseers in 3:2. The same standard applied to leaders is here applied to widows and to families caring for their own: no one should be able to accuse them, whether of neglect or of self-indulgence. Paul is not merely arranging finances; he is protecting the reputation of Christian households in a watching city.

But if anyone does not provide for his relatives. Then verse 8, one of the fiercest sentences Paul ever wrote. “Provide for” (pronoeō) means think ahead for, plan for, take care of. It is not crisis rescue but forethought. “Relatives” (idiōn) are his own people, the extended family.

And especially for members of his household. “Household” (oikeiōn) means the immediate family, those in his home. The closer the relationship, the greater the duty.

He has denied the faith. Read both halves slowly. To fail here is not a lapse in a secondary duty. “Denied” (arneomai) means disowned, renounced, the same verb used of Peter in the courtyard (Mark 14:68). It is a denial not in words but in deeds. Refusing to care for one’s family contradicts the Christian faith, which teaches love and honouring parents. Practice can deny what the lips confess (Titus 1:16). A man may recite the creed accurately and, by leaving his mother destitute, have denied every word of it.

And is worse than an unbeliever. That is the sharper edge. Pagans looked after their own; family obligation was a recognised virtue across the ancient world, no gospel required. So a Christian who neglects his relatives has not merely fallen below a Christian standard. He has fallen below the ordinary decency of people with no faith at all, and brings shame on the name of Christ. It is also worth saying plainly what this does to a common assumption. Spirituality here is not measured by devotion, insight or ministry activity. It is measured by whether the people related to you have what they need.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a person who is unable to provide, through illness, poverty or circumstance, has denied the faith. The point is unwillingness, a refusal to take responsibility. Nor does it mean only men provide; verse 16 applies the same duty to believing women. The verse deserves to be felt before it is applied, and applied without cruelty. It does not settle every hard case; some families are estranged for grave reasons, some relatives cannot be helped by any amount of money, and some carers are already at the end of their strength. Paul is not writing about those situations. He is writing about people who could and do not, and who have arranged their religion so as not to notice.

Does this apply to a husband who will not work or support his family? Yes, directly. A man who is able to work and support his wife and children and refuses, or who spends on himself what his family needs, is the person this verse describes. Scripture expects able-bodied people to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). A wife and children left in want by such a man are not obliged to pretend all is well, and the church should not pretend either: the elders should lovingly confront him and, if he persists, treat it as a matter of discipline, while making sure his family is cared for. Financial neglect can also be part of a pattern of control or abuse; where it is, the church must protect the vulnerable, not the abuser.

How do I balance providing for my family with giving to the church and the poor? Begin with the order Paul gives: your own household is your first earthly responsibility, and neglecting it is not generosity but disobedience. But provision is not the same as luxury, and the Bible also commands generous giving to God’s work and to the poor (2 Corinthians 9:6–8; Galatians 6:10). Most of us have more room for both than we think, once wants are separated from needs. Plan ahead, as the word provide implies: budget, save for your family’s future, and give first rather than from what is left. Then trust the God who feeds the sparrows to keep his promises to those who honour him.

In a sentence. Give these instructions too, so that no one can accuse them. Anyone who fails to look after his own relatives, especially his immediate family, has denied the faith by his actions and is worse than an unbeliever.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone in your family who needs your care that you have been avoiding? Take one practical step toward them this week. Look ahead as well as around: is there an ageing parent whose needs you have not planned for, a sibling who is quietly struggling, a will you have not written? Provision is forethought. Do one piece of it today.

For worship. The faith that can be denied by neglect is the faith of a God who never neglects. He provided for Adam before Adam knew he needed anything; he fed Israel with bread from heaven for forty years; he clothes the lilies and numbers the hairs on our heads. He thought ahead for us before the foundation of the world, and in the fullness of time he sent his Son. Our heavenly Father knows what we need before we ask him. He is the true Provider, and every Christian household that cares for its own is a small picture of his faithful, forethinking love.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.

Let a widow be enrolled. Now the criteria for the official list. “Enrolled” (katalegō) means put on a list, registered, an actual roll of names receiving regular support. There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in return devoted themselves to prayer and service (v. 5), perhaps caring for orphans, visiting the sick, and ministering to women. It was something like an order of widows, which is attested in the early church.

If she is not less than sixty years of age. Sixty was considered the beginning of old age. A practical threshold: past the age of likely remarriage, and past the age of earning a living. Paul is not being arbitrary; he is drawing the line where genuine long-term dependence begins. It also meant she would probably not want to leave the role to remarry (vv. 11–12).

Having been the wife of one husband. Literally a one-man woman (henos andros gynē), the mirror of the phrase used of overseers in 3:2, and best read the same way: faithful in her marriage. It is not a rule against having remarried after widowhood, since Paul tells younger widows to marry in verse 14, and he would hardly command something that disqualifies them later.

And having a reputation for good works. “Reputation” (martyroumenē) means being testified to, well attested: a track record of faithful service, known to all. Then the reputation is spelled out, and it is a list of unglamorous things.

If she has brought up children, has shown hospitality. “Brought up children” (eteknotrophēsen) is the ordinary work of years, her own children or perhaps orphans she took in. “Shown hospitality” (exenodochēsen) is welcoming strangers, opening her house, as the overseer must (3:2).

Has washed the feet of the saints. The lowest job in the household, given to the least slave, and the one Jesus did in the upper room (John 13:5, 14; Luke 7:44). It stands for all kinds of humble service, and it is the mark of a woman who has followed her Lord to the basin and the towel.

Has cared for the afflicted. “Cared for” (epērkesen) means helped, relieved; “the afflicted” (thlibomenois) are those under pressure, in distress: perhaps the sick, the poor, the persecuted. And it says something about a woman now dependent herself. Before she needed help she gave it, which is precisely why the church now owes her.

And has devoted herself to every good work. “Devoted herself” (epēkolouthēsen) means followed after, pursued diligently. The list is summarised in that phrase, and the whole shape of it should be weighed. Not one item is public, spectacular or recorded anywhere. Raising children, feeding guests, washing feet, sitting with the sick: these are the credentials Paul asks the church to verify. A woman is put on the roll because of a lifetime of things nobody wrote down.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should refuse all help to widows under sixty or without this record. Paul is describing the criteria for the enrolled list with its lifelong commitment, not for emergency help. Any person in genuine need may receive help (Galatians 6:10).

Should churches keep a list of widows today? Churches today rarely keep a formal roll, and nothing here requires one. Much of what the list did is now partly met by pensions and state provision. But the principle remains: real need, met first by family and then by the church, with care to support those who are genuinely alone, and wisdom to make support a blessing rather than a trap. Many churches meet this through deacons, who know the widows and the needy by name and make sure no one is overlooked (Acts 6:1–6). And the honour remains: older women who have given a lifetime of quiet service should be valued, visited and drawn on for their wisdom and prayer, not left at the edge.

In a sentence. A widow may be put on the list only if she is at least sixty years old, was faithful to her husband, and is well known for good deeds: bringing up children, welcoming strangers, washing the feet of God’s people, helping those in trouble, and giving herself to every kind of good work.

On a Tuesday. What will your reputation be in thirty years? Begin now to build a record of humble, faithful service. Not the kind that gets a mention in the notices, but the kind this list describes: a meal taken round, a guest welcomed, a sick friend sat with, a child patiently raised. Do one of them this week, and tell no one.

For worship. Heaven’s list of honour is not the world’s. God does not record the speeches and the titles; he records the cup of cold water, the washed feet, the guest made welcome. Nothing done for his people is forgotten by him (Hebrews 6:10). And the One who first knelt with the basin was the Lord of glory, who knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, took a towel. He made humble service the badge of greatness, and on the last day the King will say to women whose names were never written anywhere but in his book: you did it to me.
verseByVerse.note: There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in turn served it.

verseByVerse.quote: But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.

But refuse to enroll younger widows. These three verses are the difficult ones. “Refuse” (paraiteomai) means decline, reject, the same verb used of the silly myths in 4:7. Not because younger widows are less worthy, but for their own good.

For when their passions draw them away from Christ. The verb (katastrēniasōsin) pictures an animal pulling against its rein: to grow restive against, to feel impulses that pull away. Natural desire for marriage and companionship is not wrong (v. 14), but here it pulls them away from a commitment they had made to Christ.

They desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. That sounds at first like a condemnation of remarriage, until verse 14, where Paul tells these same younger widows to marry. So he plainly is not against it. Something else is going on, and the phrase “former faith” (tēn prōtēn pistin, their first pledge) is the clue. Most likely, enrolled widows made a pledge to devote themselves to Christ and the church’s service for the rest of their lives, without remarrying. A young woman who makes that commitment and later finds she cannot keep it has broken a promise, and the problem is the broken pledge, not the marriage. Breaking it would bring condemnation (judgement, censure) because it broke a vow made to God (Numbers 30:2; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). Possibly too they might marry unbelievers (1 Corinthians 7:39). Paul wants to avoid putting young women in a position where they would be tempted to break a vow. Which makes this a piece of pastoral realism rather than severity. His judgement is that a woman in her twenties should not be asked to bind herself for life, because many will not manage it and the failure will damage them. The kindest policy is not to let them make the vow.

Besides that, they learn to be idlers. Then verse 13 names the second danger, and it is entirely practical. “Idlers” (argai) are the inactive, the unoccupied. Note they learn: this is not a character flaw these women arrive with. It is something the arrangement teaches them. Put a young woman on a stipend with no dependants, no work and no structure, and she will fill the days somehow; with their needs met by the church and no household of their own to run, idleness was a real danger.

Going about from house to house. The houses of a congregation are open to her, and the traffic in other people’s business begins: visiting homes, perhaps under the guise of ministry, but actually spreading gossip. The false teachers also worked through house visits (2 Timothy 3:6).

And not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not. “Gossips” (phlyaroi) are babblers, speakers of nonsense. “Busybodies” (periergoi) are meddlers, busy with other people’s affairs, the same root as 2 Thessalonians 3:11, where Paul saw the same thing among idle men at Thessalonica: not busy, but busybodies. Saying what they should not may mean spreading the false teaching, or revealing private matters learned in visiting homes. The diagnosis generalises, because it is not about women and not about widows. Idleness is never neutral. Remove a person’s proper work and the energy does not evaporate; it goes into other people’s affairs. Paul’s remedy in the next verse is correspondingly practical: give them something real to do.

What it does not mean. It does not mean younger widows are worse people or that all of them would behave this way. Paul is giving practical wisdom based on observed patterns. Nor does “condemnation” mean eternal damnation or loss of salvation; it is the censure due to a broken vow.

How do I know if I am gossiping? Ask three questions before you speak about someone who is not present. Is it true, and do I actually know it, or am I passing on what I heard? Is it mine to tell, or was it shared in confidence, or is it simply none of my business? And would I say it the same way if the person were standing here? Gossip often wears the clothes of concern: let me tell you so you can pray. If you genuinely need help with a situation, go to someone who can help, such as an elder, not to someone who will merely enjoy knowing. And when someone brings gossip to you, you can kindly stop it: ask whether they have spoken to the person directly.

Does this teach that Christians should not make lifelong vows? No. Marriage is a lifelong vow, and so is the covenant made in church membership. What Paul warns against is binding people, especially the young, to vows they are unlikely to keep and that Scripture does not require, such as lifelong celibacy. He is wary of the very thing the false teachers promoted in 4:3. Vows to God are serious and must be kept (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5), which is exactly why they should not be made lightly. Jesus warns against rash oaths (Matthew 5:33–37). Make the promises God asks of you, keep them by his grace, and do not add others that he has not asked for.

In a sentence. Do not put younger widows on the list, because when natural desires pull them away from the commitment they made to Christ, they want to marry and so bring judgement on themselves for breaking their first pledge. Besides, they get into the habit of idleness, going round from house to house; and not only idle, but chatterers and meddlers, saying things they should not.

On a Tuesday. Watch your conversations this week: are you speaking what builds up, or what you should not? Notice especially what you say about people after they have left the room, and when you are bored. If you have unstructured time, give it somewhere good to go before it finds somewhere bad: a person to serve, a skill to learn, a task to finish.

For worship. The Lord who knows our frame does not lay on us burdens too heavy to bear. He is the wise Shepherd who will not let his young sheep run into a fold where they will be hurt, and the faithful God who keeps every vow he has ever made. He swore by himself to Abraham, and he has never once broken his word. And the tongue that so easily wounds can be made new: the Spirit who came as tongues of fire gives words that heal. Christ never spoke a word he should not; even his silence before his accusers was perfect. His mouth was full of grace, and he will one day make ours the same.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.

So I would have younger widows marry. “I would have” (boulomai) means I want, I direct, the same word as 2:8. Paul does not merely permit remarriage; he prefers it. Marriage is good (4:3), and Paul counsels it for younger widows. Set that against chapter 4, where the false teachers were forbidding marriage. Paul’s answer to a genuine pastoral risk is not more restriction but ordinary life: a husband, children, a household to run. He is sending these women into the very things the ascetics despised, and calling it the safer road. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is entirely lawful (Romans 7:2–3; 1 Corinthians 7:39), provided it is only in the Lord.

Bear children, manage their households. “Manage their households” (oikodespotein) is a strong word: to rule the house, to be mistress of the home. The wife has real authority and responsibility in running the home (Proverbs 31:10–31). Busy with a meaningful calling, they would not fall into idleness.

And give the adversary no occasion for slander. The “adversary” (antikeimenos, opponent) is either a human enemy of the church who would seize on scandal, or Satan himself. “Occasion” (aphormē) is a military word: a base of operations, an opening. The church is being watched, and its arrangements can hand ammunition to people looking for it. That concern has appeared repeatedly: the overseer well thought of by outsiders (3:7), conduct that does not disgrace the name. Christians’ behaviour should give critics no legitimate ammunition (Titus 2:5, 8). Paul takes seriously what a congregation looks like from the street.

For some have already strayed after Satan. This is not hypothetical. It had happened. “Strayed” (ektrepō) means turned aside, gone off the road, as in 1:6. Some younger widows had already fallen into sin, perhaps immorality, perhaps following the false teachers. Following false teaching is following Satan (4:1). Whatever the arrangement had been doing to young widows in Ephesus, it had already cost some of them.

If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Then verse 16, which closes the argument. The “believing woman” (pistē) is addressed directly: the duty of verse 8 is not the men’s alone. Perhaps a well-off woman who has widows in her extended family, or in her household. “Care for” (eparkeitō, relieve, assist) is the same word as verse 10, where the widow cared for the afflicted. What she once did, others now do for her.

Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows. “Burdened” (bareō) means weighed down. The principle is stated as plainly as it can be. Every family that supports its own frees the church’s limited resources for the women who have nobody. This is not meanness; it is the arithmetic of love. A congregation that carries people whose families could carry them will run out before it reaches the destitute, and the destitute are the ones the whole chapter exists to protect.

What it does not mean. It does not command every younger widow to remarry; it is Paul’s counsel in general, and singleness remains honourable (1 Corinthians 7:8, 40). Nor does it limit women to the home; it describes a good and worthy calling, not the only one.

How does this apply today? The church still has a duty to care for members in real need who have no family to help, and families may not pass their own duty to the church or the state (v. 8). Churches today may not keep a formal roll of widows, but the principle remains: real need, met first by family and then by the church.

Is it disloyal to my late husband or wife to remarry? No. Marriage is for this life; death ends the bond (Romans 7:2), and Jesus taught that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30). Paul here actively encourages remarriage for younger widows, and it was God who said it is not good for the man to be alone. Love for a spouse who has died is not betrayed by a new marriage; many find that a good first marriage prepared them to love again. Take time, grieve honestly, seek counsel, and marry only in the Lord. And be patient with children or friends who find it hard; their grief may move at a different pace.

In a sentence. So my counsel is that younger widows marry, have children and run their homes, giving our opponents no foothold for slander; for some have already turned aside to follow Satan. If any believing woman has widows in her family, she should help them, so that the church is not weighed down and can help the widows who have no one else.

On a Tuesday. Is there a widow in your extended family or church you could help this week, with a meal, a visit, or a practical task? Ask her what would actually help: a lift to the shops, help with paperwork, a gutter cleared, an evening of company. And ask yourself whether the way your household lives gives the watching street any reason to speak badly of Christ, or any reason to wonder at him.

For worship. God is the great Householder who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6). He gives husbands to widows and children to the barren, homes to the homeless and a family to the friendless. He does not despise ordinary life; he fills it with his presence, so that a kitchen and a nursery can be as holy as a temple. And over every widow stands the Bridegroom whose own Bride the church will never be widowed, because he died and rose, and lives for ever, and is coming back for her.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elders who lead well deserve double honour, especially those who labour at preaching and teaching, for Scripture says a working ox is not to be muzzled and the worker deserves his wages. An accusation against an elder must be backed by two or three witnesses; those who persist in sin are to be rebuked publicly, as a warning to others. Timothy must apply these instructions without prejudice or favouritism, and must not be hasty in laying hands on anyone or share in others’ sins. Paul adds a personal word: he should drink a little wine for his frequent stomach trouble. Some people’s sins and good deeds are obvious; others come to light later, but none remain hidden.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gospel Quoted as Scripture

Verse 18 introduces both Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying of Jesus recorded at Luke 10:7 with ‘the Scripture says’ — among the earliest signs that the written words of Jesus were already counted as Scripture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Elders are hard to accuse (v.19) and hard to hide behind (v.20); a church needs both verses.

Now: Verse 23 shows Paul correcting a good man's over-scrupulous mistake, and verse 25 promises that unrecorded goodness cannot stay hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,” and, “The laborer deserves his wages.”

Let the elders who rule well. “Elders” (presbyteroi) hold the same office as the overseers of 3:1–7. “Rule” (proistēmi) means lead, direct, care for: the word used of managing a household (3:4), and so a word with a father’s care in it rather than a manager’s distance. “Well” (kalōs) means excellently. Not all elders lead equally well; those who do deserve recognition.

Be considered worthy of double honor. “Honor” (timē) is the same word as in verse 3, where it plainly included money, and the two Scripture quotations Paul immediately produces are both about paying workers, which settles it. This is about the church’s obligation to support its elders financially. “Double” (diplēs) probably means ample, generous honour rather than literally twice a figure, or perhaps honour in two forms: respect and remuneration. The point is that the support should be ample and not grudging. Elders who give themselves to the work should be supported by the church.

Especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. The word for labour is kopiaō: work to exhaustion, the word for a man at the end of a long day. Paul chose it for preaching (logos, the word) and teaching (didaskalia) deliberately. Whatever else pulpit work looks like from a pew, it is not restful. All elders must be able to teach (3:2), but the especially implies that some devote themselves particularly to the ministry of the word, and these particularly deserve support, since their work takes their whole time and strength.

For the Scripture says. Paul gives two quotations under the single heading Scripture, and it is worth noticing that before we see why.

You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain. The first is from the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4). Oxen walked over the harvested grain on the threshing floor to separate it from the husk, and the law said they must be free to eat as they worked. Paul reads the law’s kindness to animals as establishing a principle about people, as he does at length in 1 Corinthians 9:9–11: if God cares that an ox is fed from its labour, how much more those who labour in the gospel.

And, The laborer deserves his wages. The second is not from the Old Testament at all. These are the words of Jesus as recorded in Luke 10:7 (compare Matthew 10:10). Weigh what Paul has just done. He introduced both quotations with the Scripture says, and the second is from a Gospel. Remarkably, Paul places a saying of Jesus, apparently from Luke’s written Gospel, alongside Deuteronomy, both called Scripture. This is one of the earliest indications anywhere that the words of Jesus, in written form, were already being regarded as Scripture alongside the Old Testament, within Paul’s own lifetime, and stated without argument, as something his readers would accept. Peter does something similar with Paul’s letters (2 Peter 3:16). Within the apostolic generation, the words of Jesus and the apostolic writings were already recognised as Scripture, equal in authority to the Old Testament. The New Testament’s own writers were already treating each other this way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should be in it for money (3:3; 6:5). Nor does it mean every elder must be paid; some, like Paul at times, may choose to support themselves. And it does not create two separate offices: teaching elders and ruling elders are both elders, with different emphases in their labour.

Where does the idea of teaching and ruling elders come from? From the especially of this verse, which implies that some elders laboured in preaching and teaching and some did not, or not to the same degree. Presbyterian churches speak of teaching elders (ministers) and ruling elders; many Baptist and independent churches speak simply of elders, some of whom are set apart and paid to preach. Both read this verse honestly, and both agree on the essentials: there is one office of elder, all must be able to teach, and some give themselves especially to the ministry of the word and should be supported to do it. Faithful churches differ on the details of government, and this text does not settle them all.

How much should a church pay its pastor? Scripture gives no figure, but it gives a spirit: double honour, ample and not grudging. A good test is whether the pastor can live without distraction at a level comparable to the people he serves, provide for his family (5:8), offer hospitality (3:2) and buy books, without either luxury or anxiety. A church that keeps its minister poor to keep him humble has misread this verse, and so has a minister who demands more than his people can bear. Many churches set the salary in relation to the average income of the congregation. And remember that honour includes more than money: respect, prayer, encouragement and a willingness to be taught.

In a sentence. Elders who lead well should be thought worthy of generous honour and support, especially those whose hard work is preaching and teaching. For Scripture says, “Do not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker has earned his pay.”

On a Tuesday. Does your church support its ministers generously? Thank your pastor this week, and give faithfully so that those who labour in the word are cared for. Write him a note naming one specific way God has used his preaching in your life. Most pastors hear criticism every week and specific thanks rarely, and a single sentence can carry a tired man for a month.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest cares even for the ox on the threshing floor. Not one sparrow falls without the Father, and no labourer in his field goes unpaid in the end. And the Word that tells us to honour those who preach is a Word that comes to us whole: the Law of Moses and the sayings of Jesus, bound together by the one Spirit into one Scripture, so that the voice from Sinai and the voice from the hills of Galilee are the voice of the same God. The Chief Shepherd himself laboured to exhaustion for his sheep, and sat weary by a well at midday, and he will give his faithful under-shepherds the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.note: The two sayings come from Deuteronomy and from Jesus’ words as recorded in Luke — a sign that the Gospels were already being received as Scripture.

parallels.desc: You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.

Do not admit a charge against an elder. “Admit” (paradechomai) means receive, accept, entertain; “charge” (katēgoria) is an accusation. Elders are especially vulnerable to accusations, from disgruntled members, false teachers, or simple misunderstanding. A man in public office is a target. Accusations cost the accuser nothing and can end a ministry before anything is established. Timothy must not take every complaint seriously, and is not to open proceedings at all on the word of one person.

Except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. The rule comes straight from the law, the standard for any legal charge in Israel (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15), applied by Jesus to church discipline (Matthew 18:16) and by Paul himself (2 Corinthians 13:1). So the protection is real and it is deliberate. It protects leaders from malicious or careless accusations and ensures justice. That is not indifference to wrongdoing; it is the ordinary requirement of justice, and a church that ignores it will destroy good men on rumour.

As for those who persist in sin. But the protection is not a shield, and verse 20 is the other half. Note the participle (tous hamartanontas, present tense): those who keep on sinning, continuing, going on with it after being dealt with. Most likely these are elders who, after the charge is established, continue in their sin without repentance. It could also refer more generally to any church member, but the context suggests elders. This is not a first response.

Rebuke them in the presence of all. “Rebuke” (elenchō) means expose, convict, reprove. In the presence of all means publicly, before the church, or possibly before the other elders. Leaders sin publicly in the sense that their sin affects the whole church; the correction must be equally public. That is the exact reverse of how churches usually handle it. The instinct is to protect the institution: settle it quietly, move the man on, tell nobody. Paul’s instruction is that an elder who persists in sin is rebuked in front of everyone, precisely because his position was public.

So that the rest may stand in fear. “The rest” may be other elders or the whole church. “Fear” (phobos) is a healthy fear of sinning, a sobering reminder that leaders are accountable (James 3:1). Hold the two verses together and you have a workable and demanding standard. Hard to accuse, and hard to hide behind. A church that keeps only verse 19 becomes a place where leaders are untouchable; one that keeps only verse 20 becomes a place where any grievance can ruin a man. Both, or neither works.

What it does not mean. It does not mean elders are above correction; the opposite. Nor does it mean that a victim’s report of abuse should be dismissed for lack of witnesses; corroborating evidence, patterns of behaviour and the testimony of multiple victims can serve as witnesses, and civil authorities must be involved in criminal matters (Romans 13:1–4). The principle is careful justice, protecting both the accused and the vulnerable.

I have been harmed by a church leader and there were no other witnesses. Will I be believed? You should be heard, carefully and seriously, and this verse must never be used to silence you. The two or three witnesses rule concerns what is needed to establish a charge, not whether a report may be made or investigated. Abuse usually happens in private, and Scripture’s own standard allows for evidence beyond eyewitnesses: patterns of behaviour, other people who come forward, messages, records. If the matter involves a crime, report it to the police; the church must not handle criminal abuse internally, and should help you do so. Speak to another elder or a trusted leader outside the situation. God is the defender of the oppressed, and a church that protects an abuser to protect its reputation has abandoned this very passage.

What should I do if I hear an accusation against my pastor? Do not repeat it. If someone brings it to you, ask whether they have spoken to the person directly or to the other elders, and encourage them to do so, or to go to the authorities if it is criminal. If you yourself have a concern, take it to the elders, not to the congregation or social media. Then pray, and wait for a fair process. Being slow to believe an accusation is not the same as refusing to believe it; it means letting the truth be established before you act on it, as you would want done for yourself.

In a sentence. Do not accept an accusation against an elder unless it is backed up by two or three witnesses. Those who keep on sinning must be rebuked publicly, so that the others will be afraid to sin.

On a Tuesday. Be slow to believe or spread an accusation against a leader. And pray that your church’s leaders would be accountable and above reproach. Pray by name this week for each of your elders: for their purity, their marriages, their humility, and for the courage to deal with sin in their own number when it appears.

For worship. God is perfectly just. He never condemns the innocent and never clears the guilty, and his courtroom has no favourites and no cover-ups. He hears the cry of the wronged when no human witness stood with them, and he protects the falsely accused when every voice is against them. And at the centre of history stands a trial where this rule was broken: the Son of God was condemned on the word of false witnesses who could not agree (Mark 14:56). The one true Elder who never sinned was publicly shamed for the sins of others, so that sinners who come to him may stand before God without fear.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.

In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels. This is the most solemn sentence in the letter, and the solemnity is the point. It is an oath-like formula (2 Timothy 4:1). Paul swears Timothy in, as a witness is sworn before testifying, and he names three parties watching: God, Christ Jesus, and the elect angels. The angels are the surprising item. “Elect angels” (eklektōn angelōn, chosen angels) are the angels who did not fall with Satan, kept by God’s choice (contrast 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). Paul mentions them elsewhere as observers of church life (1 Corinthians 4:9; 11:10; Ephesians 3:10), Peter says they long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12), and they will accompany Christ at the judgement (Matthew 25:31; Luke 9:26). The picture is of a courtroom with an unseen gallery: what Timothy does about a difficult elder is done in front of a congregation that includes more than he can see. Timothy carries out discipline before the court of heaven.

I charge you to keep these rules. “Charge” (diamartyromai) means solemnly testify, adjure, warn earnestly. “These rules” are the instructions about elders and discipline (vv. 17–20), perhaps the whole chapter. Why such weight for what is, after all, church administration? Because of what Paul is guarding against, and he names it twice.

Without prejudging. “Prejudging” (prokrima) is literally pre-judgement: prejudice, having decided in advance. Do not decide a case before hearing the evidence.

Doing nothing from partiality. “Partiality” (prosklisis) is literally leaning toward, inclination, favouritism: not leaning one way. Do not favour friends, the wealthy, the influential, or those you like. God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11; James 2:1–9; Deuteronomy 1:17). Both failures are the same failure from opposite sides, and both are the natural human response. Timothy will like some of these elders and find others difficult. He will have friends, and men who have opposed him. When a charge comes in, he will know before he hears it which way he wants it to go, and that is exactly what Paul puts him under oath about. This is one of the hardest things asked of anyone in leadership, and it is why the oath is here. Rules for discipline are easy to write and easy to keep when the accused is a stranger. The test is the case where you already know whose side you are on, and Paul’s answer is not a better procedure but a reminder of who is watching.

What it does not mean. It does not mean angels judge us. They witness; God judges. Nor does the election of angels mean they are redeemed as humans are; Christ did not take on angelic nature or die for angels (Hebrews 2:16). God simply chose and kept them.

What does it mean that angels are elect? It means God chose and kept some angels so that they did not fall when Satan and others rebelled. Their standing, like ours, rests on God’s sovereign choice, not on their own strength. That is a quiet confirmation of the doctrine of election: even in heaven, those who stand, stand by grace. But there is a difference. The elect angels never fell and so needed no Saviour; elect sinners fell and were redeemed by Christ, who became man, not angel, to save us. That is why the angels look on with wonder at the church (Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12). They have seen God’s power and holiness from the beginning; in us they see his mercy.

How do I avoid partiality when someone I love is involved? Admit the bias first; you cannot correct what you will not name. Then put distance between your feelings and the decision: hear both sides fully before you form a view, ask what you would conclude if the names were reversed, and involve others who do not share your attachment. In church matters, a leader with a close relationship to someone involved should often step back from the decision altogether. And remember, as Paul tells Timothy, who is watching. Fairness is not coldness; it is loving everyone involved, including the person who is not your friend, enough to give them the same justice.

In a sentence. Before God, before Christ Jesus and before the chosen angels I solemnly order you to follow these instructions without deciding in advance, and to do nothing out of favouritism.

On a Tuesday. Notice today where you have already decided before you have heard: about a colleague, a family member, someone in church you find difficult. Go and hear the other side. And in the small judgements of the day, the email you answer, the child whose account you believe, act as one who knows the gallery is full.

For worship. Remember that heaven watches your conduct. Let that make you fair, honest and impartial in every judgement you make. And let it lift your eyes. We live and serve before the living God, before the risen Christ Jesus who will judge the living and the dead, and before ten thousand times ten thousand holy angels who never tire of praising him. They watch the little church in Ephesus, and the little church you belong to, because there the manifold wisdom of God is on display. The God who chose angels to stand and sinners to be saved shows no partiality: rich and poor, Jew and Greek, come to him by the same blood, and are welcomed by the same grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.

Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands. “Hasty” (tacheōs) means quickly, too soon. The laying on of hands is, in context, ordination: the public act by which the church sets a man apart, as the elders did over Timothy himself (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). Some have thought it refers to restoring repentant sinners, but the context of elders (vv. 17–21) favours ordination. Paul’s instruction is about speed. Do not do it quickly. This picks up 3:6, where a recent convert must not be made an overseer lest he be puffed up and fall, and 3:10, where deacons must first be tested. Take time to observe a man’s life before appointing him. Ephesus needed leaders; the church was under pressure and its existing teachers were part of the problem. The temptation to fill posts fast would have been considerable, and Paul says no. Rushing to fill a vacancy with an untested man invites disaster, as Ephesus had learned.

Nor take part in the sins of others. Then the reason, and it is startling. “Take part” (koinōneō) means share, participate in, be a partner. Paul is saying that a man who ordains hastily shares in what the ordained man subsequently does. Not that he commits the sin, but that he is implicated in it, because he put him there. Endorsing someone makes you a partner in their conduct (2 John 11). That is a heavy doctrine of responsibility and it deserves to land. Whoever recommends, appoints or installs is not a neutral party who can later say he could not have known. Paul’s assumption is that with proper testing (3:10) he could often have known, and that haste is itself the fault.

Keep yourself pure. “Pure” (hagnos) means clean, chaste, free from moral defilement: free from complicity in others’ sins, and personally holy. It follows naturally rather than changing the subject. A man who appoints carelessly does not stay clean; the compromises attach to him. The purity in view is the same thing Paul told him to model in 4:12, and here it is defended by an administrative discipline, which is a useful reminder that a great deal of personal holiness is protected or lost in decisions that look purely procedural.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a church that ordained a man who later fell is guilty of his sin, if it acted with care. The point is not to act carelessly. Nor does it mean we may never be associated with sinners; Jesus ate with them (Luke 15:1–2).

How long should a church take before appointing someone? Scripture sets no fixed period, but it sets a principle: long enough for the man’s character to be genuinely known (3:2–7, 10). That usually means years of observed faithfulness, not months of enthusiasm. A gifted speaker can impress quickly; the qualities Paul lists, self-control, a well-ordered home, a good reputation with outsiders, gentleness, can only be seen over time. Talk to his wife, his colleagues, those he has served under. Watch how he handles disappointment and correction. The greater the responsibility, the longer the testing. And the same applies, in proportion, to youth leaders, small group leaders and anyone entrusted with the vulnerable.

In a sentence. Don’t rush to lay hands on anyone to appoint him, and don’t make yourself a partner in other people’s sins; keep yourself clean.

On a Tuesday. Before you recommend or endorse someone for a position, take time to know them well. Your endorsement is a responsibility. The same goes for the references you write, the friend you vouch for, the people you put forward at work. And ask where your own purity is being quietly lost in decisions that seem merely practical: the corner you let someone else cut, the thing you signed off without reading.

For worship. The Lord Jesus never laid hands on anyone in haste. He spent the whole night in prayer before he chose the twelve (Luke 6:12–13), and he knew from the beginning who would betray him. He knows every heart; nothing is hidden from him. And this is our comfort: the Head of the church is never deceived. Men may be hasty, but he is not, and he keeps his church even through our mistakes. The One who calls is holy, and he makes his servants pure, washing them in his own blood and clothing them in his own righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.

No longer drink only water. It is one of the strangest verses in the New Testament: a piece of medical advice dropped into a passage about elders and discipline, and it is a small window into a friendship. “Drink only water” (hydropotei) means be a water-drinker. Timothy apparently abstained from wine entirely. Why? Almost certainly on principle, perhaps to distance himself from drunkenness, or to avoid any suspicion, or in reaction to the false teachers, or as an act of devotion. Paul has just told him to keep himself pure (v. 22), and this letter’s opponents were ascetics who forbade marriage and food (4:3). A conscientious young minister in that environment, wanting to be above reproach and not a drunkard like the men excluded in 3:3, might well have gone teetotal to be safe, and made himself ill doing it. Paul adds that purity does not require asceticism.

But use a little wine for the sake of your stomach. “A little” (oligō) means moderation, not excess. In the ancient world, water was often contaminated, and wine was used medicinally (Luke 10:34). Wine mixed with water could help prevent illness and settle the stomach. Paul’s correction is gentle and entirely practical. Not your theology of wine is mistaken, but: take a little, for your stomach. And note the restraint on both sides: a little, and for your stomach. This is not a licence any more than it is a prohibition.

And your frequent ailments. “Frequent ailments” (pyknas astheneias) are recurring weaknesses, illnesses. Timothy was often sick; this was not a single episode. Paul, who had performed miraculous healings (Acts 19:11–12), does not simply heal him here, but recommends practical medicine. Even in the apostolic era, healing gifts were not used at will, and God’s people used ordinary means (2 Timothy 4:20; Philippians 2:25–27).

A window into a friendship. The verse also says something about the man who wrote it. Paul has been dictating solemn instructions about elders, witnesses and the elect angels, and in the middle of it he remembers that his friend is unwell and stops to say so. It is the same apostle who asked for his cloak and his parchments (2 Timothy 4:13). Great theology and ordinary care for a person’s body sit in the same paragraph without embarrassment. And there is a lesson for the scrupulous. Timothy’s mistake was a good man’s mistake: trying to be blameless and overshooting into something that damaged him. Paul does not praise the rigour. He tells him to stop.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must drink wine, or that those who abstain are wrong; abstinence for good reasons is a matter of freedom (Romans 14:21). Nor does it license drunkenness, which Scripture condemns (Ephesians 5:18). It means using medicine is not a lack of faith, and that ascetic rules are not the path to holiness.

Why did Paul not simply heal Timothy? Even the apostle who had done extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12) did not heal at will, and here he prescribes a remedy for his closest friend. He left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God does not always heal miraculously, illness is not always a sign of sin or weak faith, and using medicine is no lack of trust. The miracles of the apostles were signs confirming the message in the founding era (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Today we pray for the sick, and God often answers, sometimes beyond what doctors expect (James 5:14–15); but we also take the medicine, and both are ways of looking to him.

I am often unwell, like Timothy. Does it mean God is displeased with me, or that I am less useful? No. Timothy was one of the most trusted men in the apostolic church, and he was frequently ill. Paul himself served with a thorn in the flesh that God would not remove, because his power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Illness can limit what you do, and that is a real grief, but it does not lower your standing before God or your worth to his church. Use the means: rest, see the doctor, take what helps. Bring the weakness to God honestly. And serve in the ways your strength allows; prayer offered from a sickbed is not second-class ministry.

In a sentence. Stop drinking only water and take a little wine to help your stomach and your frequent illnesses.

On a Tuesday. Take care of your body. Using medicine and seeking help when you are sick is wise stewardship, not weak faith. If you have been putting off a doctor’s appointment out of a sense that it is unspiritual to worry about yourself, make it. And if you have taken on a rule for yourself that is quietly harming you, ask a wise friend whether it is godliness or scrupulosity.

For worship. The God of all glory cares about a young man’s stomach. The Spirit who inspired the doctrine of the Trinity and the mystery of godliness also inspired a sentence about indigestion, so that we would never imagine our bodies are beneath his notice. Jesus touched lepers, took a fevered woman by the hand, and wept at a friend’s tomb. He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, and one day he will raise these weak and ailing bodies in power, with no more frequent ailments, no more pain, and no more death.

verseByVerse.quote: The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.

The sins of some people are conspicuous. These verses return to the subject of choosing elders (v. 22), and they are the realistic postscript to it. “Conspicuous” (prodēlos) means openly evident, obvious beforehand. Some people’s sins are obvious; they disqualify themselves at once, and no examination is needed.

Going before them to judgment. The image is of sins walking ahead like heralds, reaching the court before the accused does, announcing their guilt before they arrive. Everyone already knows. In the church’s evaluation, and ultimately at God’s judgement, these sins are already known.

But the sins of others appear later. “Appear later” (epakolouthousin) means follow after. Other people’s sins follow along behind and catch up eventually: hidden at first, they come to light only over time, sometimes long afterwards. This is why Timothy must not be hasty (v. 22): time reveals character. And this is honest in a way church manuals usually are not. Paul has just laid down a careful procedure, test them first (3:10), do not be hasty (v. 22), require witnesses (v. 19), and now he admits the procedure will not catch everything. Some appointments will go wrong despite proper care. He does not pretend otherwise, and he does not respond by tightening the rules further. What he offers instead is the assurance underneath the whole thing: nothing stays hidden. Sins that do not appear now will appear later, if not in this life then at the judgement. That is why haste is unnecessary as well as unwise: a man who waits is not risking that the truth will never come out.

So also good works are conspicuous. Then verse 25 turns it round, and this is the kinder half. The same law runs in the other direction. Some goodness is visible and gets its recognition.

And even those that are not cannot remain hidden. Much goodness does not get noticed, and Paul says it cannot stay hidden either. Good works done quietly will eventually come to light. Timothy should not overlook a modest, faithful man because his virtues are not on display; patient observation will reveal them. And at the last day God will reveal everything (1 Corinthians 4:5; Matthew 6:4). Think back to the widow of verse 10 with her lifetime of unrecorded work: children raised, guests fed, feet washed, sick people sat with. Nobody wrote any of it down. It is not lost. Hold that, if your faithfulness has gone unnoticed, and if you have watched someone else get the credit. Both columns are being kept, and both will be read out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should judge harshly or suspiciously. It means patient, careful observation before appointing leaders. Nor does it mean good works save; they show the reality of faith (James 2:18).

If all my sins will come to light, should I be afraid of the judgement? Not if you are in Christ. For the believer, the sins that will be exposed have already been judged, at the cross, and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). The light of that day will show what grace forgave, not a debt still owing. That is why the best thing to do with hidden sin is to bring it into the light now: confess it to God, and where it is wise and fitting, to a trusted believer (James 5:16; 1 John 1:7–9). Hidden sin festers; confessed sin is cleansed. What should alarm us is not the light but the hope that we can keep anything from it.

In a sentence. Some people’s sins are plain to see and go ahead of them to judgement; others’ sins only come to light afterwards. In the same way, some good deeds are obvious, and those that are not cannot stay hidden forever.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you are hoping will never come out? Bring it to God today, and if it involves someone you have wronged, begin to put it right. And do one good thing this week that no one will ever know about unless God tells them: an anonymous gift, a prayer for an enemy, a job done well that nobody will check.

For worship. God sees what is hidden, both sin and good. Confess hidden sins today, and do hidden good works without seeking credit; your Father who sees in secret will reward you. Nothing escapes his eye, and nothing is lost in his memory. He knows the sins we hide and has covered them with the blood of his Son; he knows the kindnesses we forgot and has written every one of them down. On the last day the Lord will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness, and then each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5). The Judge of all the earth will do right, and for those in Christ his judgement will be the unveiling of grace.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers,<sup>2</sup>older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.<sup>3</sup>Honor widows who are truly widows.<sup>4</sup>But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.<sup>5</sup>She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day,<sup>6</sup>but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.<sup>7</sup>Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach.<sup>8</sup>But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.<sup>9</sup>Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband,<sup>10</sup>and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.<sup>11</sup>But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry<sup>12</sup>and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith.<sup>13</sup>Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.<sup>14</sup>So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander.<sup>15</sup>For some have already strayed after Satan.<sup>16</sup>If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.<sup>17</sup>Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.<sup>18</sup>For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."<sup>19</sup>Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>20</sup>As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.<sup>21</sup>In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.<sup>22</sup>Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.<sup>23</sup>No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.<sup>24</sup>The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later.<sup>25</sup>So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.

6.title: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain
6.overview:
The last chapter ties the letter together. Slaves are to honour their masters, so that God’s name is not slandered. Then the root of the false teaching is exposed: these men thought godliness was a way to make money. Paul answers that “godliness with contentment is great gain”, since we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

Timothy, the man of God, must flee all this and pursue righteousness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness, fighting the good fight until Christ appears, the King of kings who dwells in unapproachable light. The rich are not told to give everything away, but to hope in God, who gives richly for enjoyment, and to be rich in good works. Finally: guard the deposit, and grace be with you all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christian slaves should treat their masters with full respect, so that God’s name and the teaching are not brought into disrepute. Those whose masters are believers should not take liberties because they are brothers, but serve them all the better, since those who benefit are fellow believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Paul Does and Does Not Say

Paul gives slaves a reason for their conduct that has nothing to do with their masters' rights — the honour of God's name (v.1) — and sets it beside his condemnation of slave-trading (1:10) and his plea for Onesimus (Philem 16): a principle planted inside the institution that would in time dissolve it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Equality in Christ, Paul says, should make a slave serve a believing master better, not worse (v.2).

Now: The strategy took far too long, and Christians defended slavery with verses like this while ignoring 1:10 — yet abolition came largely from people arguing from this book.

verseByVerse.quote: Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 6 brings the letter to a close by returning to its two great concerns: the false teachers and the kind of man Timothy must be. It begins with a word to Christian slaves (vv. 1–2): they are to honour their masters, so that God’s name is not slandered, and not take advantage of believing masters. Then Paul exposes the false teachers once more (vv. 3–5): proud, ignorant, addicted to controversy, and treating godliness as a way to make money. This leads to a great passage on wealth and contentment (vv. 6–10): godliness with contentment is great gain; we came with nothing and will leave with nothing; the desire to be rich is a trap, and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Then the charge to Timothy (vv. 11–16): as a man of God, he must flee these things and pursue righteousness, fight the good fight of faith, and keep the commandment until Christ appears, which God will bring about at the right time; and Paul breaks into a doxology to the blessed and only Sovereign, who dwells in unapproachable light. A word to the rich follows (vv. 17–19): they must not be proud or trust in riches, but in God, and be rich in good works and generous, storing up treasure for the age to come. The letter ends with a final appeal (vv. 20–21): guard the deposit, avoid what is falsely called knowledge, and grace be with you all. Notice the shape: at the very centre of a chapter about slaves, money and quarrels, the letter rises into one of the highest descriptions of God in the Bible. Paul cannot talk about wealth for long without being carried up to the only One who is truly rich.

The setting. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world; perhaps a third of the population of a city like Ephesus were slaves. Slavery in Rome was not based on race, and many slaves were educated, skilled, could own property, and could hope for freedom. But they were legally the property of their masters, and could be cruelly treated. The church contained both slaves and masters, as brothers in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16). Some Christian slaves may have thought that their new equality in Christ freed them from duty to their masters, perhaps encouraged by the false teachers. These two verses need honest handling, because the New Testament’s treatment of slavery is one of the things people most often hold against it. Slaves were in the congregations, some of them, as verse 2 shows, owned by fellow Christians, and a movement calling for immediate abolition would have been crushed as sedition within a year, with its members killed and the gospel extinguished with them.

Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants. “Under a yoke” (hypo zygon): the yoke was a picture of servitude and burden (Leviticus 26:13), and God himself is the one who broke the bars of Israel’s yoke and made them walk upright. “Bondservants” (douloi) are slaves. Paul does not pretend the condition is light; he names it a yoke. He acknowledges the burden of their condition.

Regard their own masters as worthy of all honor. “Masters” (despotai) are owners, lords; our word despot comes from it. “All honor” (pasēs timēs) is full respect. Slaves are to give their masters respect, even unbelieving masters.

So that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Here is the reason, and it changes everything. “Reviled” (blasphēmeō) means slandered, blasphemed. If Christian slaves were rebellious or lazy, outsiders would say that Christianity destroys social order. The gospel’s reputation was at stake (Titus 2:9–10). But notice what Paul does not say. The slave is not told to obey because his owner deserves it or because the arrangement is just. He is given a reason for his conduct that has nothing to do with his master’s rights. He is told that he is a witness: that the reputation of God is, astonishingly, in the hands of a slave. The man with the least standing in Ephesus is entrusted with the honour of the highest name in the universe.

Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers. Verse 2 addresses a real problem that had evidently arisen. “Disrespectful” (kataphroneō) means despise, look down on. Some had reasoned, quite understandably, that equality in Christ meant the old arrangement no longer bound them: he is my brother, so I need not work hard for him. Paul’s answer is not to deny the equality. He affirms it in the same breath, calling the master a brother, believing and beloved. Spiritual equality does not cancel earthly responsibilities.

Rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved. “Serve all the better” (mallon douleuetōsan) means serve them even more; “benefit” (antilambanomai) means take part in, receive. Their brotherhood is a reason to serve better, not worse: they are serving those whom God loves. And there is a quiet revolution in the word beloved. The slave is told to see his owner as one whom God loves; the owner, reading the same letter aloud in the same room, is being told that his slave is his brother.

Where Christians differ: does the New Testament approve of slavery? Critics have accused the Bible of endorsing slavery, and slaveholders once used such texts to defend it. Verdict: The New Testament regulates an institution it did not create and could not abolish by decree, while planting the principles that would undermine it. It condemns slave-trading (1:10), tells slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), commands masters to treat slaves justly and remember that they too have a Master (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1), and declares slave and free one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by Scripture’s own law (Exodus 21:16). Christians who fought for abolition, like William Wilberforce, did so from these principles. That is the strategy: not a revolt that would have been drowned in blood, but a principle planted inside the institution that would eventually dissolve it. It took far too long, and Christians defended slavery for centuries by quoting verses like this one while ignoring 1:10 and Philemon. That is a grief and a shame to the church. But when abolition finally came, it came largely from people arguing from this book.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slavery is good or God’s design. It does not mean Christians should tolerate injustice. It means believers in every station of life are to live so as to adorn the gospel. The principle applies to employees today: work diligently and respectfully, especially for Christian employers.

Does this mean I must put up with an abusive boss? No. An employee today is not a slave: you are free to leave, to complain through proper channels, and to seek justice, and you should when you are mistreated (1 Corinthians 7:21 shows Paul valued freedom where it was available). What carries over is the attitude: honest work, respect for those in authority, no sulking, cutting corners or badmouthing behind their backs, so that your conduct commends Christ. But respect is not complicity. You must never do what is sinful because you are told to (Acts 5:29), and harassment, abuse or illegal practice should be reported, not endured in silence. Working well and standing up for what is right are both ways of keeping God’s name from being reviled.

What about slavery and trafficking today? Christians must oppose it with all their strength. Modern slavery, forced labour, debt bondage and sex trafficking are exactly the kidnapping that God’s law punished with death (Exodus 21:16) and the slave-trading that Paul condemns in this very letter (1:10). Nothing in these verses gives them any cover. In practice that means praying, supporting organisations that rescue and restore victims, asking where the goods you buy come from, and refusing to look away when something seems wrong in your community. The gospel that made Onesimus a beloved brother still sets captives free.

In a sentence. All who live under the yoke of slavery should count their masters as deserving full respect, so that God’s name and our teaching are not slandered. Those whose masters are believers must not look down on them because they are brothers; they should serve them even better, because those who benefit from their work are fellow believers whom God loves.

On a Tuesday. Work today as if Christ were your employer. Your diligence and respect can make the gospel attractive. Notice the moment you are tempted to do less because no one will check, or because your manager is a Christian and will understand. Do the job well, speak well of the people above you, and let your work be the sermon your colleagues actually hear.

For worship. The Lord of glory took the form of a doulos. He who owned the universe was sold for the price of a slave, thirty pieces of silver, and he washed feet, and he served all the better those who did not deserve it. He is the Master in heaven who shows no partiality, before whom slave and free, employer and employee, stand on the same ground. And he is the Redeemer, the One who buys slaves to set them free. In his house there are no slaves, only sons and daughters, and the slave who reveres his name in a Roman kitchen will sit at the marriage supper of the Lamb beside kings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul describes anyone who departs from the healthy teaching of the Lord Jesus as swollen with pride and lacking understanding, with a sick appetite for disputes and arguments about words that breed envy, quarrels, slander and suspicion. Such people treat religion as a route to profit. But real profit is godliness joined to contentment, since we arrived in the world with nothing and will leave with nothing; with food and clothing we should be satisfied. The desire to get rich is a trap that leads to foolish and harmful cravings and finally to ruin. Love of money lies at the root of every kind of evil, and some, chasing it, have strayed from the faith and wounded themselves with many sorrows.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Root Beneath the Quarrels

Beneath the Ephesian error was a business — ‘godliness is a means of gain’ (v.5) — and its fruit was relational damage rather than doctrinal error (v.4). The love of money, a root of all kinds of evils (v.10), enables every sin rather than having one of its own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul grants the false teachers their word ‘gain’ and attaches it to contentment (v.6).

Now: Verse 9 warns those who desire to be rich — a condition available at every income.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.

If anyone teaches a different doctrine. Paul returns to the false teachers one last time, and now he traces their error to its root, which turns out not to be intellectual at all. “Teaches a different doctrine” (heterodidaskalei) is the same word as 1:3, forming a bracket around the letter.

And does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Agree with” (proserchomai) means come to, adhere to, attach oneself to. “Sound” (hygiainousi) is the medical word again: healthy, wholesome. “The words of our Lord Jesus Christ” are either the teachings of Jesus himself, or the apostolic gospel about him, which carries his authority.
