True doctrine is healthy; it produces spiritual health.

And the teaching that accords with godliness. Note the test: teaching is measured by whether it accords with godliness, by what kind of life it produces. That has been the letter’s yardstick since 1:5. True doctrine leads to a godly life. False doctrine does not.

He is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. “Puffed up” (typhoō) is the inflation word again (3:6): swollen with air, or blinded by smoke, conceited. “Understands nothing” (mēden epistamenos) means knows nothing. And the pairing is deliberate and devastating: maximum self-regard, zero comprehension. The two go together more often than not. For all their claims to knowledge (v. 20), they understand nothing of real importance.

He has an unhealthy craving for controversy. The Greek is a striking reversal. “Unhealthy craving” (nosōn) is literally being sick, diseased, the opposite of the sound teaching just named. Paul’s picture is of a man with an appetite that is itself a sickness: he does not merely tolerate argument, he needs it. Take away the controversy and he would not know what to do with himself. “Controversy” (zētēseis) means speculative questions, disputes, as in 1:4.

And for quarrels about words. “Quarrels about words” (logomachias) are word-battles, fighting over terms: arguments about technicalities and hair-splitting, not substance (2 Timothy 2:14).

Which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction. Look at what it produces. Five words, and not one is a doctrinal error. They are all relational damage. “Envy” (phthonos) is jealousy. “Dissension” (eris) is strife, rivalry. “Slander” (blasphēmiai) is abusive speech. “Evil suspicions” (hyponoiai ponērai) are malicious suspicions, assuming the worst. “Constant friction” (diaparatribai) is mutual irritation, people rubbing against each other until the skin is raw. You can know a teaching by its fruit (Matthew 7:16–20). Paul judges the teaching by its wreckage: a congregation where people suspect each other and cannot stop arguing has a teaching problem, whatever is on its statement of faith.

Among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth. “Depraved” (diephtharmenōn) means thoroughly corrupted, rotted. “Deprived” (apestermenōn) means robbed, stripped. They once had access to the truth, but have been robbed of it, or have turned from it.

Imagining that godliness is a means of gain. Then the root, and it is the last word of the paragraph. “Means of gain” (porismos) is a source of profit, a money-making scheme. There it is. Beneath the genealogies and the quarrels about words was a business. These men had discovered that religion pays: that a reputation for spiritual insight brings money, standing and a following. They charged for their teaching, flattered the wealthy, and built a following for profit (Titus 1:11; 2 Peter 2:3). This remains the most reliable question to ask about a teacher whose doctrine seems off. Not only is this true, but what does he get out of it? Paul puts the financial motive at the bottom of the whole Ephesian trouble, and the next verses are about money because of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all disagreements in the church are sinful or that theological precision does not matter. Paul himself defends doctrine carefully. The problem is a sick craving for controversy, especially over trivia, and an approach that produces division rather than godliness.

How can I tell the difference between defending the truth and loving controversy? Look at three things. The subject: is it something Scripture treats as central, such as the person of Christ, the gospel, the authority of the Bible, or is it a speculation Scripture does not settle? The manner: are you gentle, patient and willing to listen, or do you enjoy winning and look for the next fight (2 Timothy 2:24–25)? And the fruit: does the conversation leave people closer to Christ and to each other, or does it leave envy, suspicion and friction? A healthy defender of the faith would rather not argue, and does so for the sake of others. A lover of controversy argues for the pleasure of it, and would be lost without an opponent.

How do I recognise a teacher who is using religion for gain? Watch the money and the message together. Be wary when giving is tied to promised returns, when a teacher’s lifestyle is lavish and unaccountable, when pressure is applied to give more, or when the message flatters the wealthy and fits suspiciously well with what the teacher needs. Ask whether there is real accountability: elders, published finances, a church that can correct him. Gain need not be money; it can be fame, a platform or power over people. A faithful teacher can be paid (5:17–18), but he is not driven by it, and his teaching makes you want Christ, not him.

In a sentence. If anyone teaches something different and does not hold to the healthy words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that leads to godliness, he is swollen with pride and understands nothing. He is sick with a craving for disputes and fights about words, which breed jealousy, conflict, abuse, malicious suspicion and endless friction among people whose minds are corrupt and who have been robbed of the truth, people who think that godliness is a way to make money.

On a Tuesday. Before you enter a theological argument, ask: is this about something that matters, and will my manner produce godliness or friction? Look back over your last few online comments or church conversations and ask which of the five words they produced. And examine your own motives in serving: what do you get out of it, and would you still do it if you got nothing?

For worship. The words of our Lord Jesus Christ are healthy words, and he is the Great Physician whose teaching heals. He never once argued for the pleasure of winning, though he silenced every opponent; he never used his ministry for gain, though he was Lord of all; he had nowhere to lay his head. His words produce not envy but love, not suspicion but trust, not friction but peace. Never man spoke like this man. And his truth does not puff up; it bows the proud and lifts the humble, and it will be standing when every quarrel about words has fallen silent.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.

But godliness with contentment is great gain. Paul takes their phrase and turns it inside out. They imagined godliness was a means of financial gain; Paul says godliness is great gain, but only when combined with contentment. The word they wanted is granted, there is real profit here, but it is attached to something they had no interest in. “Contentment” (autarkeia) is the Stoic word, the one Paul used at Philippians 4:11 and filled with different content. For the Stoic it meant self-sufficiency, independence from circumstances through inner strength, needing nothing outside yourself. For Paul it means having enough because of who supplies you: sufficiency in Christ, being satisfied with what God provides (Philippians 4:11–13; 2 Corinthians 9:8). The greatest wealth is to be godly and content.

For we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. Then two arguments, and the first is unanswerable. Job said it (Job 1:21), and so did the Preacher (Ecclesiastes 5:15; compare Psalm 49:17). It is not a religious claim at all; it is an observation anybody can verify, and it has never once been disproved. We arrive naked and leave naked. The force of it is in the bracketing. Whatever a person accumulates is held for the middle stretch only. Nothing crosses either boundary. Possessions are temporary, on loan; they do not last beyond death. And most of us, if pressed, know this perfectly well and live as though an exception might be made. Why stake your life on what you cannot keep?

But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content. Then the second argument. Two items. Not comfort, not security, not a modest sufficiency by local standards: food and covering. The word (skepasmata, coverings) can include shelter, so perhaps three. The basic necessities. When we have these, we have enough to be content. Jesus taught the same: do not be anxious about food and clothing, for your Father knows you need them (Matthew 6:25–33). That is a genuinely uncomfortable verse and should not be softened into a general commendation of simplicity. Paul has set the bar at survival. He is not saying it is wrong to have more; he will tell the rich in verse 17 that God gives us everything to enjoy, which rules out asceticism. He is saying that everything above food and clothing is surplus, and that a Christian should know it is surplus.

The real test. Which is the actual test, and it is not about income. Anyone can name a figure at which they would be content; the honest question is whether contentment arrived when the last increase did. If it did not, it will not arrive with the next one either.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must be poor, or that owning more than the bare minimum is sinful. Paul addresses the rich in verses 17–19 without telling them to give everything away. Nor does contentment mean passivity; we may work to improve our situation (1 Corinthians 7:21). It means our hearts are at rest in God whatever our circumstances.

How do I actually learn contentment? Paul says he learned it (Philippians 4:11–12); it is not a temperament but a trained habit of the heart, and its secret is Christ, through whom he could do all things. Practise gratitude daily, naming specific gifts, because thanksgiving and discontent cannot live long in the same heart. Notice what feeds your wanting, the adverts, the scrolling, the comparisons with friends, and starve it. Give generously, because giving loosens the grip of things. Remember the bracket: you will leave with nothing. And above all, feed on what does satisfy: the God who has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you, which is the very reason Hebrews gives for being content (Hebrews 13:5).

Is it wrong to want a better job, a pay rise or a nicer home? Not necessarily. Wanting to provide better for your family, to use your gifts more fully, or to have room for hospitality can be good desires. Paul assumes people may improve their situation. The question is what the wanting is doing to you. Ask: am I anxious, envious or restless about it? Would I be at peace with God if it never came? Am I prepared to sacrifice integrity, family or church to get it? If you can want it with open hands, pray for it and work for it. If it has become the thing you cannot be happy without, it has become an idol, and contentment means laying it down.

In a sentence. Godliness really does bring great profit, when it comes with contentment. We brought nothing into the world and we can carry nothing out of it; so if we have food and clothes, we will be satisfied with that.

On a Tuesday. List five things you have today that you need. Thank God for each. Then ask him to free your heart from wanting more. Name the one thing you most often think, if only I had that. Bring it to God by name, and thank him instead for one thing you already have that you once longed for.

For worship. The Son of God came into the world with nothing: born in borrowed space, laid in a feeding trough, wrapped in cloths. He left it with nothing: stripped of his clothing, while soldiers gambled for it, buried in a borrowed tomb. And in between he was perfectly content, because his food was to do the will of the One who sent him. He became poor so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). In him we have more than food and clothing: we have the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, and an inheritance that will never perish. Godliness with contentment is great gain, because the godly have God.

parallels.desc: Naked I came from my mother's womb

verseByVerse.quote: But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.

But those who desire to be rich. Note the object of the warning. Not the rich: Paul will address them separately in verse 17, and does not tell them to divest. “Desire” (boulomenoi) means want, resolve, set their will on: those determined to become rich, whose goal in life is wealth. The danger is in the desiring, which is a condition available at every income.

Fall into temptation, into a snare. The verbs describe a descent. “Fall” (empiptō) is to fall into, as into a pit. They fall into temptation (peirasmos) and a snare (pagis), the bird-trap word from 3:7, something that closes on you before you have seen it. The pursuit of wealth exposes people to endless temptations: dishonesty, neglect of family, idolatry, oppression.

Into many senseless and harmful desires. Then many desires (epithymias, cravings, lusts), senseless (anoētous, foolish, unreasonable) and harmful (blaberas, injurious, damaging), which arrive in company, because wanting one thing teaches you to want others. Greed breeds other cravings, and none of them satisfy.

That plunge people into ruin and destruction. And finally these plunge people (bythizō), a verb used of a ship going down, dragged under, sinking to the bottom. “Ruin” (olethros) and “destruction” (apōleia, perdition, eternal loss) together describe total, final ruin, in this life and the next (Matthew 16:26; Luke 12:20–21). The rich fool built bigger barns and was told, this night your soul is required of you.

For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. Then the famous line, and it is famously misquoted. Three corrections in one sentence. It is not money but the love of it (philargyria, love of silver, avarice); money is a tool and Paul is about to tell wealthy Christians what to do with theirs. It is not the root but a root (rhiza, with no definite article in Greek); Paul is not claiming every sin traces here, and pride and lust do fine without it. And it produces all kinds of evils (pantōn tōn kakōn) rather than every single evil; the point is the variety. There is almost no wickedness that money-love cannot eventually produce: theft, murder, adultery, war, lies, broken families. That is why it is so dangerous: it does not have a characteristic sin, it enables every sin. And at bottom it is idolatry (Colossians 3:5; Matthew 6:24). You cannot serve God and money.

It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith. “Craving” (oregomenoi) is reaching out for, stretching toward. “Wandered away” (apeplanēthēsan) means been led astray. Wandered, not renounced. Nobody sets out to leave Christ for money. The word suggests drifting off the path while looking at something else, which is exactly how it happens. The love of money has led some to abandon the faith, perhaps including the false teachers: like Judas, who sold his Master for silver (Matthew 26:14–16), and Demas, who loved this present world (2 Timothy 4:10).

And pierced themselves with many pangs. The verb (peripeirō) is violent: run through, impaled, as on a spit. And the reflexive is the sting. Nobody did this to them. “Pangs” (odynais) are pains, griefs, sorrows: anxiety, guilt, broken relationships, emptiness, regret. The griefs money-love produces are self-inflicted, and they come to the person who got what he wanted.

Where Christians differ: does God promise wealth to the faithful? The prosperity gospel teaches that God wants every believer to be rich, and that faith, giving or positive confession will produce wealth. Verdict: This passage directly refutes it. Paul warns that the desire to be rich is a trap that leads to destruction. Jesus warned against storing up treasure on earth (Matthew 6:19–21) and said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23–25). God promises to provide what we need (Philippians 4:19), not wealth. Teachers who promise wealth are precisely those who think godliness is a means of gain (v. 5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean money itself is evil, or that wanting to provide for one’s family is wrong (5:8). Nor does “wandered from the faith” mean true believers can be lost; those who abandon the faith reveal that their faith was not genuine (1 John 2:19).

How do I know if I love money? Love shows itself in what you think about, what you fear losing, and what you will sacrifice for. Ask: Do I think about money more than about God? Am I anxious when it is short, proud when it is plentiful? Do I resent giving, or give only what I will not miss? Would I bend the truth, cut a corner or neglect my family to get more? Do I envy those who have more? Does the prospect of losing it terrify me more than the prospect of losing fellowship with Christ? Nobody answers all of these well. The cure is not guilt but a better love: look at Christ, who though he was rich became poor for you, and give something away today as an act of worship.

Is it wrong to save, invest or have a pension? No. Scripture commends the ant that stores up in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the wise who plan ahead (Proverbs 21:20), and providing for your family includes thinking about the future (5:8). Saving becomes sin when it is driven by fear rather than faith, when it becomes the place your security truly rests, or when it crowds out generosity. The rich fool’s problem was not that he had barns but that he built bigger ones for himself alone and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21). Save wisely, give generously, and hold it all loosely, remembering whose it is.

In a sentence. But people who are set on getting rich fall into temptation and into a trap, and into many foolish and destructive cravings that drag them down to ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root from which every kind of evil grows. Some people, reaching for it, have strayed from the faith and stabbed themselves through with many sorrows.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: how much of my time, thought and energy goes into getting more money? Is it drawing me away from Christ? Look at your bank statement as a spiritual document: it shows what you love. Then make one concrete change this month: a regular gift you will feel, a purchase you decline, a conversation with your spouse about what is enough.

For worship. Judas sold the Son of God for thirty pieces of silver, and the Son of God let himself be sold, so that sinners pierced with self-inflicted griefs could be healed by his wounds. He was pierced for our transgressions, the wounds we deserved and the wounds we gave ourselves. Money promised Judas everything and left him with a field of blood; Christ, who had no silver, gives the pearl of great price to all who come to him with empty hands. He is the treasure hidden in the field. Those who find him go and sell all they have, and count it joy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In contrast, Timothy, God’s man, must run from all this and chase after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance and gentleness. He must fight hard in the contest of faith and seize the eternal life to which he was called when he confessed his faith publicly. Paul solemnly charges him, before God who gives life and before Christ, who testified before Pilate, to keep this command spotless until Christ appears. God will bring that about at the right time: the blessed and only ruler, King over all kings and Lord over all lords, the only one who is immortal, living in light no one can approach, whom no one has ever seen, to whom be honour and power for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
Titles Thrown at Idols

‘Only Sovereign’, ‘King of kings and Lord of lords’, ‘who alone has immortality’ (vv.15–16) are aimed at Artemis and the emperor; and the God who dwells in unapproachable light is reached only through the one mediator (2:5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy confessed Christ among friends; Jesus confessed before Pilate, who could kill him (vv.12–13).

Now: Flee and pursue (v.11): some temptations must simply be run from, and a man who only avoids will eventually be caught.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.

But as for you, O man of God. The contrast is emphatic (sy de, but you). Against the men who imagine godliness is gain, against those who desire to be rich, stands one person, addressed directly. And the title is striking, and not a general compliment. “Man of God” (anthrōpe theou) is the Old Testament’s standing description of the prophets and leaders: Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6), Elijah (1 Kings 17:18) and Elisha (2 Kings 4:9), men who stood for God against a drifting people. It marks a person who belongs to God, represents him and speaks for him. Paul lays that mantle on a young minister in Ephesus who has been having a difficult time of it, and in 2 Timothy 3:17 he extends it to every believer equipped by Scripture.

Flee these things. Then two verbs, and the Christian life is in both. “Flee” (pheugō) means run away from, escape, and it is present tense: keep fleeing. “These things” are the love of money, pride, controversy and greed (vv. 3–10). It is the word used of Joseph leaving his garment in her hand rather than staying to argue with Potiphar’s wife (Genesis 39:12). Some temptations are not to be engaged, reasoned with or managed. Distance is the only reliable tactic, and a man who stays to test his own strength has already decided how it ends (1 Corinthians 6:18; 10:14; 2 Timothy 2:22).

Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. “Pursue” (diōkō) is the word used of hunting and of persecution: chase it down, run after it. And the pairing matters. Fleeing alone leaves a vacuum, and a man who is only avoiding things will eventually be caught by one of them. You have to be running toward something. Christian life is not only negative; flee one thing and chase another. Six virtues, and they fall into three pairs. Righteousness (dikaiosynē, upright conduct) and godliness (eusebeia, devotion to God): right living toward people and toward God. Faith (pistis, trust, faithfulness) and love (agapē): the inner life of a believer, the two that have run through this letter since 1:5. Then steadfastness and gentleness, which is the interesting pair: hypomonē, the staying power that does not buckle under weight, and praupathia, a rare word meaning meekness, mildness of temper. Those last two together are the answer to what this chapter has described. A man dealing with quarrelsome teachers and constant friction needs to be immovable and unaggravated at the same time: to face opposition with endurance and without harshness, to hold the ground without becoming like the people pushing him. That is a hard combination, and it is exactly the one Paul asks for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we pursue these to earn God’s favour. We pursue them because we already have it. Nor does the title “man of God” make Timothy a special class of Christian; every believer belongs to God.

What does fleeing look like in practice? It means arranging your life so that the temptation has less access to you. For money: unsubscribe from the shopping emails, stop browsing what you cannot afford, avoid the friendships built around getting and spending. For sexual sin: filters and accountability, no being alone where you know you are weak, leaving the room or switching off at once. For controversy: closing the thread, not reading the comments. Fleeing is not cowardice; it is wisdom about your own weakness. And it is always paired with pursuing: put something good in the space you have cleared, or the old thing will come back with friends (Matthew 12:43–45).

In a sentence. But you, man of God, run from all this, and chase after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness.

On a Tuesday. Name one thing you need to flee and one virtue you need to chase this week. Do both on purpose. Be specific: not greed in general but the app you open when bored; not love in general but the colleague you have been avoiding. Then plan the escape and the pursuit as concretely as you would plan a journey.

For worship. Christ is the true Man of God. He fled nothing out of fear, yet he never once lingered with temptation: in the wilderness he answered the devil with the word and sent him away. He pursued righteousness and fulfilled it; his godliness was perfect devotion to the Father; his faith held in Gethsemane; his love went to the end; his steadfastness endured the cross, despising the shame; and his gentleness was such that he would not break a bruised reed. He is meek and lowly in heart, and he gives rest to all who come. All six virtues we are told to chase are the features of his face, and the Spirit is making us like him.
verseByVerse.note: “Man of God” is an Old Testament title for prophets such as Moses, Samuel and Elijah.

verseByVerse.quote: Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.

Fight the good fight of the faith. The verb (agōnizou) comes from the arena: contend, compete, struggle, strain. It is the root of our word agonise, and it is present tense: keep fighting. Paul has used the military and athletic images throughout (1:18; 4:7–8), and the image here may be athletic, a race or wrestling match, as much as military. “Good fight” (kalon agōna) is the noble contest. Note the definite article: the good fight of the faith. Not any struggle a Christian happens to be in, and not merely a private battle with a besetting sin. Paul means the one contest that matters, waged over the faith itself, the deposit he will name in verse 20: a contest for the faith, the body of truth, and in faith, trusting God. Paul uses the same words of his own life at its end: I have fought the good fight (2 Timothy 4:7).

Take hold of the eternal life. The verb (epilabou) means to seize, grasp, lay hold of, and it is aorist: grab hold decisively. That sounds odd applied to eternal life, which Timothy already has as a gift (John 5:24). But this is Paul’s regular pattern: what God gives, you are then told to lay hold of; work out your salvation because God works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). The possession is secure and the grip is still commanded. Eternal life must be grasped, lived in, and pressed toward as the prize at the end of the race (Philippians 3:12–14).

To which you were called. “Called” (eklēthēs) is God’s effectual call, which brought Timothy to faith (Romans 8:30; 2 Timothy 1:9). The call is God’s act; our grasping is the response his grace enables. Timothy did not wander into eternal life; he was summoned into it by the voice that raises the dead.

And about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses. Then the memory Paul reaches for. “Confession” (homologia) is a public declaration, an acknowledgement. The good confession was probably made at Timothy’s baptism, when he publicly confessed Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9–10), or perhaps at his ordination: a public occasion where he said in front of people what he believed. “Many witnesses” are the congregation who heard it. He must live up to what he declared before them. Paul does this repeatedly in these letters. When a man is flagging, he sends him back to what was said over him and by him at the beginning (1:18; 4:14). That is a practical kindness. Feelings about ministry come and go; the fact that you stood up in front of witnesses and confessed Christ does not, and on the days when nothing else is steady it is a fixed point you can put your weight on. And the phrase is about to be used of someone else. In the very next verse Christ himself makes the good confession before Pilate, which tells Timothy what company he is in, and what such confessions can cost.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eternal life is earned by fighting. It was given when he was called. Fighting and grasping are the way the called live. Nor does the confession at baptism mean that baptism saves; it is the public sign of faith.

What is the fight, for an ordinary Christian? It is the daily contest to keep believing and living the gospel against everything that pulls the other way. Inwardly, it is the fight against unbelief, doubt and the sins that would choke faith. Outwardly, it is holding to the truth when the world, or even a church, drifts from it, and speaking of Christ when it costs you. Its weapons are those God supplies: the Word, prayer, the fellowship of the church, the Lord’s Supper (Ephesians 6:10–18). It is not fought by aggression toward people; Paul has just told Timothy to pursue gentleness. And it is a good fight: one that ends in victory, because the Captain has already won it.

Why does it matter that I made a public confession? Because faith in Christ is not meant to be private. Jesus said that whoever confesses him before men, he will confess before his Father (Matthew 10:32). For a believer, baptism is the appointed place for that first public confession, made before witnesses who can later remind you of it and hold you to it. If you are a believer and have never been baptised, this verse is an invitation: speak to your pastor. If you have been, look back on it when faith feels weak. You did not imagine it. You stood before God and his people and said Jesus is Lord, and the God who called you then has not changed his mind.

In a sentence. Strive hard in the noble contest of the faith. Lay hold of the eternal life God called you into, the life you publicly confessed before many witnesses.

On a Tuesday. Where is the fight for you this week: a doubt you have been nursing, a sin you have stopped resisting, a conversation where you will need courage to own Christ? Name it, and take up the Word and prayer against it. And tell one person this week, plainly, that you belong to Jesus.

For worship. Remember your own confession of faith, at your baptism or conversion. Thank God for calling you, and renew your commitment to him today. The call came from him before the confession came from you. He spoke your name before you spoke his. And the fight we are given is good because the Captain of our salvation has already fought the decisive battle and won it, disarming the rulers and authorities and triumphing over them in the cross. We do not fight for victory; we fight from it. The eternal life we are told to grasp is held already in the hand of Christ, and no one will snatch us out of it.
verseByVerse.note: The “good confession” was probably made at Timothy’s baptism or ordination.

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,

I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things. The second solemn oath of the letter (compare 5:21), and both witnesses are chosen for the occasion. “Charge” (parangellō, command) is the keyword of the letter (1:3, 5, 18). “Gives life” (zōogoneō) means preserves alive, gives life to. God is the giver and sustainer of all life, which is precisely what a man needs to remember if the charge might cost him his own. The God who gives life to all things is the God who will raise Timothy if he dies for his faith.

And of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession. Jesus himself made the good confession: before Pilate, he declared that he was a king, whose kingdom is not of this world, and that he came to bear witness to the truth (John 18:33–37; Mark 15:2). He did so knowing it would cost him his life. Timothy’s confession (v. 12) follows the pattern of his Lord’s. That reference to Pilate is doing careful work. Timothy made his good confession before many witnesses, in a room full of friends. Jesus made his before a magistrate who could kill him, and did. Paul sets the two side by side without comment. Confession before a supportive congregation is real; confession before a hostile authority is the same act with the price attached, and Timothy is being told which one he is signed up to.

Suffered under Pontius Pilate. It is also worth noticing that Paul anchors this in a datable event. Pontius Pilate is a name from provincial administration, recoverable from Roman records and an inscription found at Caesarea. The mention of Pilate anchors the gospel in real history, as the later creeds would do with the words suffered under Pontius Pilate. The faith Timothy is charged to keep is not a philosophy but something that happened at a particular hour in front of a particular official.

To keep the commandment. “Keep” (tērēsai) means guard, preserve, obey. “The commandment” (tēn entolēn) is probably the whole charge Timothy received, the gospel and its demands, all that Paul has entrusted to him (1:18; 6:20), which he will call the deposit in verse 20.

Unstained and free from reproach. Two adjectives describe how it is to be kept. “Unstained” (aspilos) means spotless, without blemish. “Free from reproach” (anepilēmptos) means irreproachable, as of elders (3:2). These may describe the commandment (keep it pure, uncorrupted) or Timothy (keep it so that you are spotless), and in practice both are true, because a man’s life can put a mark on the message he carries.

Until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Appearing” (epiphaneia) means manifestation, glorious appearance: a word used in the Greek world for the appearance of a god or the arrival of an emperor. The Pastoral Letters often use it for Christ’s return (2 Timothy 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13). And the timescale is the whole of it: not until the trouble in Ephesus resolves, or until Paul arrives, but until Christ appears. The assignment has one end date, and it is not in Timothy’s diary. Timothy must keep faith until then, whether that comes in his lifetime or after.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul expected Christ to return before Timothy died; he says God will bring it about “at the proper time” (v. 15). It means the return is the horizon of faithful ministry.

What will Christ’s appearing be like? Public, visible and glorious. Scripture describes one return of Christ at the end of the age, not a secret coming: he will come on the clouds with power and great glory, every eye will see him, the dead will be raised, and he will judge the living and the dead and make all things new (Matthew 24:30; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7). It will be terror to those who rejected him and unspeakable joy to those who love his appearing (2 Timothy 4:8). We do not know the day, and we are not told to calculate it. We are told what Timothy was told: keep faith until then, and live so that you would be glad to be found doing what you are doing.

What if I am afraid to confess Christ before people who could harm me? Look at the One who went first. Christ did not ask Timothy to do anything he had not already done, before a far more dangerous judge. Fear is not itself sin; it is the soil in which courage grows. Pray for boldness, as the apostles did (Acts 4:29). Remember that the Spirit gives words in the hour of need (Matthew 10:19–20). Use wisdom: you are not commanded to court danger needlessly. And if you have failed, as Peter did in the courtyard, remember that the risen Lord restored him and later gave him courage to die for him (John 21:15–19). The God who gives life to all things holds yours.

In a sentence. In the sight of God, who gives life to everything, and of Christ Jesus, who bore witness to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, I order you to keep this commission spotless and above reproach until our Lord Jesus Christ appears,

On a Tuesday. Think of the place where it is hardest for you to own Christ: the office, the family dinner, the group chat. Ask God this morning for one opportunity there, and take it. And live today as if the appearing could be tonight, not in fear, but so that nothing you are doing would need to be hidden from him.

For worship. Thank Christ who confessed the truth before Pilate at the cost of his life. Ask for courage to confess him before whoever you face this week. He stood bound before the governor of Judea, the true King before a borrowed throne, and told the truth knowing it meant the cross. He did not deny us when we would have denied him. He witnessed the good confession, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and on the third day rose again. And the God who gives life to all things has given him the name above every name, and one day he will appear, and every knee will bow.

verseByVerse.quote: which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.

Which he will display at the proper time. The mention of Christ’s appearing sets Paul off, and the letter breaks into its second doxology (compare 1:17). It reads like something already sung. “Display” (deixei) means show, bring about, reveal. “At the proper time” (kairois idiois) means in his own seasons, as in 2:6. God the Father will bring about Christ’s appearing at the moment he has appointed (Acts 1:7; Mark 13:32). Not before, not after. Nobody hurries it and nobody delays it.

He who is the blessed and only Sovereign. Then the titles, and every one of them is a stone thrown at an idol. “Blessed” (makarios) is the word from 1:11: perfectly and self-sufficiently happy. God is not a lonely or needy being who made us to fill an emptiness; he is supremely happy in himself, Father, Son and Spirit, and he creates out of fullness. “Only Sovereign” (monos dynastēs) means the only ruler, the only potentate, and the only is pointed, in a city with a temple to Artemis and a cult of the emperor. All earthly rulers, including the emperor who claimed divine titles, are under him.

The King of kings and Lord of lords. Literally King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule. This was imperial vocabulary. Eastern monarchs used the formula, and it attached to the man in Rome. Paul takes the highest title available in the political world and says it belongs to someone else. It is a title of the supreme God (Deuteronomy 10:17; Psalm 136:2–3), and in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16 it is given to Christ, the Lamb who conquers. Timothy is to keep his charge until that King appears.

Who alone has immortality. “Immortality” (athanasia) is deathlessness. Not merely that God happens to live forever, but that deathlessness belongs to him by nature and necessarily, and to nobody else in that way. God alone has life in himself (John 5:26). All other beings, including angels and human souls, continue because he sustains them; he continues because of what he is. Believers will receive immortality as his gift at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53–54). The false teachers were peddling secret knowledge about intermediary beings, and Paul says there is one immortal.

Who dwells in unapproachable light. “Unapproachable” (aprositon) means inaccessible. God’s holiness and glory are like blinding light that no creature can approach on its own (Exodus 33:20; Psalm 104:2; Isaiah 6:1–5). And the paradox is deliberate. Light is what makes seeing possible, and here it is what prevents it: not darkness keeping God hidden but excess of brightness. Moses was told no one may see God’s face and live. The obstacle is not that there is too little to see.

Whom no one has ever seen or can see. God in his essence is invisible (1:17; John 1:18). We see him only as he reveals himself, supremely in Christ: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9), the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). In glory, believers will see him in Christ (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4). And that is where the doxology lands in a letter about false teachers claiming special access. Nobody has seen him, nobody can, and no technique will get you nearer. Which makes the line Paul has already written the more astonishing: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (2:5). The unapproachable light came out to meet us.

To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen. “Dominion” (kratos) is might, power, rule. The proper response to such a God is worship, and Paul does not argue for it; he simply gives it. Theology that does not end in doxology has not yet understood its subject.

What it does not mean. “Who alone has immortality” does not mean human souls cease to exist at death. Humans have an immortality given by God; God alone has it by nature. Scripture teaches a conscious intermediate state and the eternal existence of all people (Luke 16:22–26; Matthew 25:46). Nor does “no one can see” contradict the promise that the pure in heart will see God; we will see him as he reveals himself in the glorified Christ.

If God dwells in unapproachable light, how can I pray to him? Through Christ. On your own you could not approach this God for a moment; Isaiah, seeing only the edge of his glory, cried that he was undone. But the One who dwells in that light sent his Son into our darkness, and through his blood we have confidence to enter the holy places by the new and living way he opened (Hebrews 10:19–22). So you come not in your own name but in his, and you are welcomed as a child. Hold both truths together when you pray: the awe of verse 16, which keeps prayer reverent, and the access of the gospel, which makes it bold (Hebrews 4:16).

Why does Paul break into praise in the middle of instructions? Because for Paul doctrine and worship are one thing. He cannot mention Christ’s appearing without being carried up to the God who will bring it about. It is a lesson in how to read the Bible and how to live: every truth about God is meant to end in adoration. If your study of Scripture never moves you to praise, slow down and ask what the passage shows you of God. And it is a comfort in hard places: Timothy, facing false teachers and difficult elders, is reminded that the One he serves is the only Sovereign, and that every throne in Ephesus is beneath his.

In a sentence. an appearing that God will bring about at the time he has chosen, God the blessed and only ruler, King over all kings and Lord over all lords, the only one who is deathless by nature, who lives in light no one can approach, whom no one has ever seen or is able to see. To him belong honour and power for ever. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Take these two verses into your prayers this week and pray them back to God phrase by phrase: blessed, only Sovereign, King of kings, alone immortal, dwelling in light. When the news makes some earthly ruler seem all-powerful, say this doxology aloud. And when you are anxious about the future, remember who sets the proper time.

For worship. Spend a few minutes in silence before this God: blessed, sovereign, immortal, dwelling in light. Then thank him that in Christ you may approach him. He needs nothing, and gives everything. Emperors rise and are forgotten; he reigns. Every king who ever lived is dust; he alone has immortality. Seraphim cover their faces before him; yet this God took flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. The light no one can approach came near, so that one day we, who could not look on him and live, will see his face and live for ever. To him be honour and eternal dominion. Amen.

parallels.desc: man shall not see me and live

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives instructions for wealthy believers: they must not be arrogant or rely on riches, which are uncertain, but rely on God, who generously gives us all we need to enjoy. They should be rich in doing good, generous and willing to share, so laying up treasure that will last and grasping the life that is real life. Finally Paul urges Timothy to protect what God has entrusted to him, steering clear of irreverent chatter and the contradictions of so-called knowledge, which has led some away from the faith. He ends with grace for them all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guard the Deposit

The paratheke of verse 20 is property left for safekeeping, to be returned exactly as received — not developed or made more interesting — against ‘what is falsely called knowledge’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul does not tell the rich to divest but to hope in God, who gives everything to enjoy (v.17), and to get rich in good works (v.18).

Now: The closing grace is plural (v.21): after pages addressed to Timothy, Paul turns to the whole room.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.

As for the rich in this present age. Now Paul turns to the rich in the congregation, and it matters enormously what he does not say. He does not tell them to divest, and he does not treat wealth as a sin requiring repentance. He gives them instructions for handling it. These are those who are already wealthy, as distinct from those who desire to be (v. 9). “In this present age”: their riches belong to this passing world only. There were wealthy believers in Ephesus, a prosperous commercial city.

Charge them not to be haughty. Two dangers first. “Haughty” (hypsēlophronein) means high-minded, arrogant, thinking oneself superior, and it is the natural drift of money: it quietly persuades a person that he is a different sort of human from the people who do not have it, and that he does not need God (Deuteronomy 8:11–17).

Nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches. “Set their hopes” (ēlpikenai) means fix their hope. And the phrase is exact: not on uncertain riches but on the uncertainty of them (adēlotēti, unreliability). Wealth’s defining property, for the purposes of hope, is that it might not be there. Riches can sprout wings and fly away overnight (Proverbs 23:5; Luke 12:16–21). They are a foolish foundation for hope.

But on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. Stop on that, because it is one of the most generous sentences in the New Testament, and it comes from the man who has just said food and clothing are enough. “Richly” (plousiōs) is a play on the word rich: the truly rich one is God, who gives abundantly. And the purpose named is enjoyment (eis apolausin): not merely use, not bare sufficiency. God is not stingy; he gives good things for our pleasure. This is the final answer to the ascetics of chapter 4 who forbade marriage and food. The God who gives us things means us to be glad of them. Wealth is not evil; it is a gift to be enjoyed with thanks (4:4), not trusted.

They are to do good, to be rich in good works. Then four things for the rich to do, and they build. “Do good” (agathoergein) is the general instruction. “Be rich in good works”: and there is the deliberate wordplay. They are rich in one currency, and Paul tells them to get rich in another. Real wealth is measured in good deeds, not in money.

To be generous and ready to share. “Generous” (eumetadotous) means ready to give, liberal, open-handed. And “ready to share” (koinōnikous) is a further step, from the fellowship word: not merely willing when asked, but holding what they have as common property with people who need it.

Thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future. “Storing up treasure” (apothēsaurizontas) means laying up in store; “foundation” (themelion) is the base a building stands on. The image is Christ’s own: treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy (Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 12:33; 16:9). And it turns the whole thing round. Giving money away is here described as an investment, the only one whose returns are guaranteed.

So that they may take hold of that which is truly life. “Truly life” (tēs ontōs zōēs) is life that is really life; some later manuscripts read eternal life. It is the same verb as verse 12, and the same implication. What the rich are currently holding is not, in Paul’s estimate, quite life. Life measured by possessions is not real life (Luke 12:15). There is a realer thing available, the life of God, now and forever, and the way to lay hold of it is to let go of the other.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the rich earn salvation by giving. Generosity is the fruit of faith, and the treasure laid up is God’s gracious reward. Nor does it command the rich to give away everything; Paul does not condemn wealth but its misuse.

Does generosity earn heaven? No. Good works are the fruit of saving faith (Ephesians 2:8–10), and the reward is God’s grace. Paul is telling the rich to use their wealth for others because they have something better to hope in. He sets no fixed amount; the measure is a generous heart and a ready hand (v. 18).

Am I rich? Most readers of this probably are, by any global or historical measure. If you have regular meals, a home, clothes beyond what you need and some money left at the end of the month, you are among the rich in this present age, even if you feel stretched compared with those around you. That feeling is itself one of the dangers: we measure ourselves against people who have more, and so never notice we are the ones Paul is addressing. Read verses 17–19 as written to you. Not to make you guilty, but to free you: from pride, from false security, and into the joy of using what God has given for others.

How much should I give? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage, but it gives a direction and a spirit. Give regularly and in proportion to what God has given you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the church that feeds you (5:17–18; Galatians 6:6), and to the poor, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point and then grow beyond it; for some on very low incomes, faithful giving will be smaller. The test of verse 18 is not the amount but readiness: a hand that opens quickly, and a heart that enjoys it.

In a sentence. Tell those who are wealthy in this present world not to be proud and not to rest their hope on riches, which are so uncertain, but on God, who gives us everything in abundance for our enjoyment. Tell them to do good, to be wealthy in good deeds, to give freely and share willingly, so laying up for themselves a solid foundation for the age to come, and so taking hold of the life that is truly life.

On a Tuesday. If you are rich by world standards (and most readers of this are), give something generously this week, and enjoy what God has given you with thanks. Do both on purpose: give a gift you will notice, to someone or something that needs it, and then sit down to a good meal and thank God for it without guilt. Generosity and enjoyment are not rivals; they are both ways of saying that God is the Giver.

For worship. The truly rich One is God, and he is not a miser. He richly provides us with everything to enjoy: sunlight and bread, music and friendship, the laughter of children and the taste of fruit. And his greatest gift was not a thing at all. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He shared everything; he held nothing back, not even his own Son. Every generous Christian is a small reflection of that open hand, and every gift given in his name is treasure laid up with him, in the city whose foundations he himself has laid.

verseByVerse.quote: O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called “knowledge,”

O Timothy. The letter’s last direct address, and the vocative gives it the sound of a hand on the shoulder. It is a personal, emotional appeal, as Paul closes.

Guard the deposit entrusted to you. “Guard” (phylaxon) means keep safe, protect, like a sentry. The word for deposit is parathēkē, a technical term from banking and law: property placed with someone for safekeeping. In a world without secure storage you left valuables with a trustworthy man, and the obligation on him was absolute: not to invest it, improve it or use it, but to return exactly what he received. That is Paul’s picture of the gospel and of Timothy’s job. The deposit is the gospel, the apostolic truth (2 Timothy 1:12–14). It was entrusted to Paul (1:11) and now to Timothy, and it is not his. Timothy is not its owner but its guardian. His task is not to develop it or make it more interesting. He must not add to it, subtract from it, or let it be stolen or corrupted. He must hand it on intact (2 Timothy 2:2).

Avoid the irreverent babble. “Avoid” (ektrepomenos) means turn away from. “Irreverent” (bebēlous) is godless, profane, as in 4:7. “Babble” (kenophōnias) is empty sounds, empty chatter. The false teaching was all noise and no substance.

And contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge. “Contradictions” (antitheseis) are opposing arguments, counter-claims; our word antitheses. “Falsely called” (pseudōnymou) means falsely named. And “knowledge” is gnōsis, the very word that would name the great heresy of the next century, Gnosticism, with its promise of secret understanding available only to the spiritual elite. Whether or not developed Gnosticism existed yet, the instinct plainly did, and Paul names it: falsely called. It advertises knowledge and does not have any. Against this, the Christian gospel is public, open to all, and centred on the historical Christ.

The whole letter in one verse. Set the two halves together and you have the whole letter in one verse. On one side a deposit: fixed, received, handed on, not yours to alter. On the other an endless production of new material that sounds impressive and is empty noise. Every generation faces the same choice, and the second is always the more exciting of the two. And note what guarding requires. Not aggression: Paul has ruled out the quarrelsome man (3:3) and the craving for controversy (6:4). A guard does not chase; he stays where he was posted, and the thing he was given is still there in the morning.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid learning or scholarship. True knowledge of God is commanded (2 Peter 3:18). The problem is false claims to secret or superior knowledge that contradict the gospel.

I am not a pastor. How do I guard the deposit? Every believer has been entrusted with the gospel, and you guard it first by knowing it: read the Bible whole, learn a sound confession or catechism, and be able to say clearly what the gospel is. Guard it in your home by teaching it to your children. Guard it in your church by supporting faithful preaching, asking questions when something sounds wrong, and being slow to embrace new ideas that cannot be found in Scripture. Guard it in your own life by holding to it when it is unfashionable. And pass it on: tell someone else. The deposit is guarded best not by being buried but by being faithfully handed to the next person (2 Timothy 2:2).

Are there modern forms of falsely called knowledge? Yes. Any teaching that claims a secret key to the Bible, a hidden message only insiders can see, or a spiritual experience that lifts some believers above ordinary Christians follows this pattern. So does the claim that the church misunderstood Jesus until some recent discovery or theory, or the idea that real spirituality lies in techniques beyond the Word, prayer and sacraments. Scripture is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17); it is not a code for an elite but light for all God’s people. When a teaching makes you feel you must get past the plain meaning of the Bible to find the real truth, turn away.

In a sentence. Timothy, guard what has been placed in your care. Turn away from godless, empty talk and from the counter-claims of what is wrongly called knowledge,

On a Tuesday. Could you explain the gospel clearly to a friend in two minutes? Try it this week, aloud, even if only to yourself, and then to someone else. And notice the voices you are listening to: books, podcasts, videos. Are they helping you guard the deposit, or offering you something more exciting than it?

For worship. Thank God that his truth is not hidden for an elite, but openly revealed in Christ and in Scripture for all who believe. He did not give his gospel to the clever and the initiated; he hid these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children, for such was his gracious will. And the deposit is safe, not finally because Timothy guarded it, but because God does. Paul knew whom he had believed, and was convinced that he is able to guard what has been entrusted until that day (2 Timothy 1:12). The gospel has passed through twenty centuries of hands, many of them weak, and it reaches us whole, because the Lord of the gospel keeps his Word.
verseByVerse.note: “Knowledge” may point to early forms of the teaching later called Gnosticism.

verseByVerse.quote: for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.

For by professing it some have swerved from the faith. The letter ends where it began. “Swerved” (ēstochēsan) is the archer’s word, missing the mark, the same word as 1:6, where certain persons had swerved and wandered into vain discussion. Here the same verb closes the argument. Paul has come full circle, and the shape is deliberate: this is what the whole letter has been about. Note the mechanism once more: by professing it (epangellomenoi, claiming, promising, making a show of). Not by studying it or being tempted by it, but by claiming it. The moment a man announced he had this knowledge, he was committed to a position, and the faith had to be adjusted around it. Public claims have a way of taking their maker where he did not intend to go. The warning is sober: it can happen.

Grace be with you. Then the last words, which no letter of Paul’s is without. And the you is plural (meth’ hymōn). Much of the letter has addressed Timothy personally, O Timothy, guard the deposit, and at the very end Paul turns to the room. This letter was always going to be read aloud to the congregation, and he knows it. The elders being assessed, the widows on the roll, the rich being charged, the slaves with believing masters, and the men who wanted to be teachers: grace to all of them. All of them needed grace. After all the warnings, the last word is grace: God’s undeserved favour, which alone keeps us in the faith. It is the same last word as every letter he wrote, and it is the right one here. This has been a demanding letter: qualifications, disciplines, warnings, a list of the lawless, two men handed over to Satan. It closes with the only thing that was ever going to make any of it possible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean those who are truly in Christ can finally fall away. Those who swerve from the faith show that they did not truly belong (1 John 2:19). But we must take the warning seriously, for it is one of the means by which God keeps his own.

Someone I love has swerved from the faith. Is there hope? Yes, while they live there is hope. Some who wander are true believers in a season of backsliding, and the Shepherd goes after his lost sheep (Luke 15:4–7); Peter denied Christ and was restored. Others were never truly converted, and the God who raises the dead can still call them. You cannot tell from outside which it is, and you do not need to. Keep praying for them by name, without giving up. Keep loving them and keep the door open, without pretending all is well. Speak of Christ when there is an opening, gently. And entrust them to the God who is mighty to save. Grace is the last word of this letter, and it is not too late for grace.

In a sentence. for some, by laying claim to it, have missed the mark of the faith. Grace be with you all.

On a Tuesday. Read the whole of 1 Timothy again this week in one sitting, as the church at Ephesus would have heard it. Then pray for your church as Paul did: for its leaders, its widows, its rich and its poor, its teachers and its young. And end the day as the letter ends, by asking grace for the people you have found hardest to love.

For worship. End by praying for grace to keep you, your church, and those you love in the true faith until Christ appears. Grace, to a difficult church, from an apostle on the road, about a deposit that had to be carried one more generation. It was. And it has been carried every generation since, not because the carriers were strong, but because the grace was. The God of all grace called us, keeps us, and will bring us home. The first word of the gospel is grace, and so is the last. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.note: “You” here is plural: the letter was meant for the whole church to hear.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled.<sup>2</sup>Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.<sup>3</sup>If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness,<sup>4</sup>he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions,<sup>5</sup>and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.<sup>6</sup>But godliness with contentment is great gain,<sup>7</sup>for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world.<sup>8</sup>But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.<sup>9</sup>But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.<sup>10</sup>For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.<sup>11</sup>But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.<sup>12</sup>Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.<sup>13</sup>I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession,<sup>14</sup>to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>15</sup>which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords,<sup>16</sup>who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.<sup>17</sup>As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.<sup>18</sup>They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,<sup>19</sup>thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.<sup>20</sup>O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"<sup>21</sup>for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
